News.title: BBC visits hospital in Kathmandu as families wait for news
News.content:
A deadly flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border has killed at least 150 people, with hundreds still missing.

The missing include more than 100 from India, 54 from the US, and 33 from the UK, as well as more than 100 from Nepal itself, according to Nepal's tourist board.

The BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is in a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopter for treatment.

News.title: Woman who died in fire with niece, 7, was 'beautiful soul', mother tells BBC
News.content:
A woman killed in a house fire has been described by her mother as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".

Natalie McDonald, 34, died along with her seven-year-old niece, Valentina Foster, in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of Wednesday.

Cleveland Police said the fire had also left a 48-year-old woman in a critical condition in hospital alongside another three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and were in police custody, the force said.

Lisa Kirton, Natalie's mother, told the BBC her daughter was "lovely, bright and bubbly" and "everybody loved her".

She said Valentina, also known as Tina, had been spending the summer holidays with the family.

"She was a cute little kid," Kirton said. "I can't believe it, seven years old - it's just a disgrace."

She also said Natalie's 15-year-old daughter and a friend had managed to escape through an upstairs window.

The friend, she said, had "kicked out a window" and "had saved their lives".

News.title: New thunderstorm warnings for parts of UK as rain set to continue
News.content:
Met Office yellow warnings for thunderstorms will remain in force for most of Thursday as downpours and thunderstorms move northwards across the UK.

Southern England was first to see the rain overnight, with a yellow warning continuing until 08:00 BST in the south-east.

A wider warning area covers all of Wales and large swathes of England and lasts until 22:00, with downpours bringing the risk of localised flash flooding and travel disruption.

The wettest areas could potentially see 75mm (3in) of rain, accompanied by large hail, lightning and gusty winds.

It will also feel rather humid for many.

Spells of rain are set to continue over the weekend - a bank holiday for England, Wales and Northern Ireland - accompanied by windy conditions in the south.

News.title: World's first patient to undergo live AI-assisted brain surgery has tumour removed
News.content:
The world's first patient to have brain surgery with live artificial intelligence assistance has successfully had his tumour removed.

Rhys Hibbert, a father-of-two from Bedfordshire, could have lost his sight without the operation, said surgeons at University College London Hospital.

The AI tool analysed a video feed of the operation as it happened and advised surgeons on how to avoid crucial but hidden vessels and nerves in the brain. It allowed them to safely remove as much of the tumour as possible.

"From a patient safety perspective, I can see absolutely the benefit. There are no road signs inside our head," said Hibbert.

Until 18 months ago, 48-year-old Hibbert, a customer services manager, was fit and healthy, going on a two-mile walk every lunchtime.

It was on one of these walks that he fell unconscious and started fitting in the road.

A brain scan revealed he had an 11mm (0.433in) non-cancerous tumour growing on the pituitary gland - a marble-sized organ at the base of the skull.

The gland secretes vital hormones that help with processes like growth, metabolism and regulating blood pressure and temperature.

Crucially it sits very close to the carotid arteries which are vital vessels that supply blood to the brain, and the optic nerves that control vision.

As Hibbert's tumour began to press on his optic nerves, it narrowed his peripheral vision.

News.title: Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama dies aged 97
News.content:
Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama, who became famous later in life for her work in sculptures and installations, has died aged 97, her company has confirmed.

The statement announced, "with profound sorrow... the passing of Yayoi Kusama at a hospital in Tokyo on August 14, 2026, at the age of 97".

"Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry," it said.

Kusama, who had voluntarily lived in a pyschiatric hospital for decades, was known for her bright-red wig and quirky polka-dot ensembles.

"She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.

"We will carry forward Kusama's wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world."

Kusama became one of the world's most recognisable artists and a global cultural icon in her 80s and 90s, after having been mostly overlooked for decades.

Poorly received by a masculine-dominated art scene of New York in the 1960s, Kusama caused a stir with her exhibitions of phallic sculptures, including a fabric couch, and frequent displays of nudity.

In 1965, her work "Infinity Mirror Rooms", in which mirrors and lights create seemingly endless spaces, attracted millions of visitors. Later, her polka-dot and pumpkin works became highly sought-after.

However, she became distressed when her ideas were copied or "inspired" by her male contemporaries â including Andy Warhol, Claes Oldenburg and Lucas Samaras â whose works would be displayed at more prestigious galleries.

News.title: Meta's $18bn settlement may hasten reckoning for social media on child safety
News.content:
As part of the settlement, the social media giant has agreed to make a number of changes to the way Instagram and Facebook operate for its youngest users.

Some experts say it is long overdue.

The new safety barriers include a two-hour time limit across both platforms, which will be a default setting for known teen users. But direct messaging on the platforms will not count towards the daily use limit.

Notifications will be muted between midnight and 06:00 and on school days between 08:00 and 15:00.

Likes on posts and content will also be entirely hidden on the platforms for teens.

Most of these new features will be made either default or an option for teens within six months.

However, new efforts by Meta to better identify which users on its platforms are children will take up to a year to be rolled out.

I would be surprised if these measures remain within the confines of the US for very long, as other countries will almost certainly be keen to adopt them too.

Meta also says the new features will only truly help children if all of its rivals adopt them as well.

It's a highly competitive industry, but given the global backlash against social media and its impact on children, perhaps others like TikTok and Snapchat may have to follow suit.

The question then is whether children will still bother with them, once they are deliberately toned down into a much blander offering.

And perhaps that would bring the social media era to a natural end, as existing adults gradually aged out of it.

Arturo Bejar, the ex-Instagram engineer turned whistleblower, says the proof of the pudding will be in whether the new teen safety features are effective.

"At the end of the day, Meta needs to be held accountable for results, not efforts," he told me.

Additional reporting from Kali Hays

News.title: Burnham calls summit of Welsh, Scottish and Northern Irish first ministers
News.content:
Burnham said: "I am in South Wales today because the answers to the UK's challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places that know their own strengths, and from a government willing to listen and then act.

"Good jobs in every community, in every part of the UK. That is what I want every leader in this country signed up to."

He will meet the Welsh government's deputy first minister Sioned Williams at the visit.

Williams said the visit was "a positive example of governments working together to improve people's lives".

She will call for a "fair share of the UK government's steel fund", an "energy social tariff to support those facing fuel poverty and struggling with high energy bills", and high standing charges in Wales to be addressed.

She added: "Wales is an energy-rich nation. People should see that reflected in good jobs, stronger communities and lower bills."

The National Economic Council was created by the Gordon Brown administration in 2008, and has been revived by Burnham.

A previous meeting brought together government ministers and English local authority mayors.

Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to discuss "how we will drive good growth in every postcode across the UK" with the first ministers.

The Welsh government said: "We look forward to discussing shared challenges, including ensuring growth and investment in all the countries represented, and support for families facing the continuing cost-of-living crisis.

"This is alongside further discussions with the UK government to progress broader priorities in Wales, including fair funding and extending devolution."

Plaid Cymru has pressed the UK government for discussions over more powers and funding for the Senedd - Wales's parliament - and the Welsh government in Cardiff.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth had his first meeting with the new prime minister on the sidelines of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in July.

At the time, ap Iorwerth said it was "too early" to know whether the new Labour prime minister would agree to his calls.

Downing Street said then that the prime minister wanted an "open and ongoing dialogue" with the first minister.

News.title: Susan Sarandon leads tributes to Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Tim Curry
News.content:
But he was perhaps best known for his zany role as the cross-dressing Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.

He first played the part on stage before the movie adaptation that propelled him to cult stardom.

Sarandon, who played the heroine Janet Weiss in movie, praised Curry as "a funny, sexy, original".

"Thank you Tim for meaning so much to so many people."

Curry's longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz confirmed he "passed away peacefully at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles on August 25".

Australian actress Nell Campbell, who starred alongside Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, told the BBC: "I feel like the head of our family has just died because he was the head of the Rocky Horror family."

Welsh actor Luke Evans, who played Frank-N-Furter in a Broadway revival, called Curry "a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm".

In a letter he recently wrote to Curry, Evans thanked him for his fearlessness and for "creating something so enduring, and for inspiring generations of actors to be a little braver than they thought they could be".

The official Rocky Horror Picture Show on Broadway account similarly thanked the late actor for "giving the world a little more freedom, a little more fearlessness, and through the tears in our eyes, the courage to BE IT" - a nod to Curry's delivery of the famous line from the musical: "Don't dream it, be it."

In a statement to Entertainment Weekly, writer and composer Richard O'Brien, who co-wrote the musical and film, remembered the actor as "a wonderful man by nature who was also a wonderful performer".

"He never sought attention and never put himself before the roles that he played," O'Brien said. "He was, in short, a good egg and class act."

News.title: Nepalese authorities say 33 UK nationals missing after flash floods
News.content:
According to the company's travel logs, shared with the Press Association, the age of the missing British citizens ranges from 13 to 65.

Alpine Eco Trek said the youngest member of the group is believed to be a 13-year-old girl, according to PA.

It also reported four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing.

The company's manager Kumar Adhikari said he was in contact with the guides until 08:40 when they were expected to be at Tibet's immigration office, but their phones were disconnected.

"We were hoping that inside it was safe," he told PA, "but later the video came from China's government which [showed] even Tibet's side was hit by the flood."

Adhikari said he was "slowly responding to" the families of the Britons but has been unable to give them any updates, adding he has been in contact with the British consulate and forwarded them copies of the clients' passports.

"I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next...We are in pain at the moment, deep pain."

Another tour company impacted by the flash floods, Himalayan Glacier US, told the BBC they have lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff who where making a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which included two British citizens.

Kailash Journeys also reported a group of 27 guests and staff missing, with a spokesperson saying they were last in contact with them early Wednesday morning local time.

A list of names provided to the BBC included two men who are British citizens.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he is "deeply concerned" by news of the flash flooding, and wrote on social media: "All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home".

In a joint statement with Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland, the UK embassy in Nepal urged British nationals in Nepal to "exercise caution in affected areas".

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.

Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believed to have flown into the country privately from California, and landed in Birmingham shortly before midday.

A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said "this is not something we would comment on".

There did not appear to be a police presence as Harry and his family left the airport, a source told the BBC.

Last week, it was reported that the couple would be relocating to the UK in August. They will not return to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.

It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in school and the new term is due to start next week.

Though not confirming the family's arrival in the UK, a spokesman for the Sussexes did say their chickens were staying in California, but they were bringing their dogs Mia and Pula with them.

The chickens, which the couple rescued, have regularly featured on Meghan's Instagram account and also appeared in her Netflix programme.

News.title: Stourbridge fires that razed 19 homes accidental
News.content:
Two fires that destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge were started accidentally in fields where farming machinery was in use, according to West Midlands Fire Service.

Investigators established agricultural equipment was being used in the vicinity of fields immediately before the fires were first reported. The service would not confirm the type of machinery.

The first fire started in a field near Racecourse Lane at about 13:27 BST on 13 August, while a second began shortly afterwards in a field near Quarry Park Road.

The day after the fires the government sent out an emergency alert to millions of people across England and Wales, warning them against "any activity that could start a fire".

News.title: King and Queen to visit the Caribbean in autumn tour
News.content:
King Charles III and Queen Camilla will travel to the Caribbean later this year, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The royal pair will travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, with the King also visiting the Bahamas and Guyana as part of the eight-day trip.

The tour - planned for 27 October to 4 November - will "celebrate the communities, cultures and nature within the Commonwealth family," the palace said on Wednesday.

It marks the first time the King has visited the Caribbean since 2021, when he travelled to Barbados to see the country officially removed Queen Elizabeth II as its head of state and become the world's newest republic.

The monarch, who was the Prince of Wales at the time, acknowledged the "appalling atrocity of slavery" the Caribbean island suffered during a speech he made.

He also visited Antigua and Barbuda in 2017 following the widespread devastation caused by Hurricanes Irma and Maria, and made official visits to Guyana in 2000 and the Bahamas in 1973.

He travelled across the Atlantic Ocean earlier this year when he visited Bermuda in May, where he is also head of state.

The trip marked his first royal visit as monarch to a British overseas territory and came after a state visit to the US.

News.title: US designates Palestine Action a terrorist group
News.content:
The US has imposed sanctions on Palestine Action, designating it as a terrorist group.

The US Department of the Treasury said it had "taken action" against the UK-based group, which it accused of supporting "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020".

Supporting Palestine Action became illegal in the UK in 2025 after the government banned it under anti-terror legislation.

The group's co-founder Huda Ammori responded in a social media post, saying: "As a Palestinian and Iraqi, the fact the country which destroyed both my homelands is calling me a terrorist, is beyond hypocritical."

In a statement to the BBC, Ammori said the group's actions had "always been about saving lives", adding the ban should be a "wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and democracy".

Announcing the move in a statement on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear.

"Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated."

The sanctions imposed include freezing any assets belonging to the group that are either based in the US or in the control of US citizens.

The US ban on the group is part of a wave of sanctions announced by the Trump administration against what it says are far-left terror organisations around the world.

The Department of Treasury accused Palestine Action of having supported "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government".

Palestine Action, which used so-called direct action tactics against Israeli-linked arms companies in the UK, has been facing an ongoing legal battle to get its UK ban overturned.

In June, Court of Appeal judges ruled the UK government made a "justified and proportionate" interference on freedom of expression rights.

But Palestine Action has since been given permission to challenge the decision at the Supreme Court.

More than 2,000 people are facing potential trial after being arrested for protesting against the ban by allegedly declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group during mass demonstrations.

Separately, four of its members were jailed in June for a break-in at a defence firm that caused more than Â£1m worth of damage, with one person sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

News.title: Boy, 15, arrested over stabbing at Brent Council HQ
News.content:
On Wednesday, one man who works in the area told BBC London the stabbing "felt normal".

"These things happen every single day here, in London and in the area. It's not a big surprise," he said.

"You see things like this happen all the time. You read the news and every single day there's something going on. If it's in Harrow, or Wembley, or Neasden, or Willesden or wherever, it doesn't come as a surprise."

However, one woman who lives in the area said the stabbing "came as a shock".

"I've never felt unsafe around here and it's a bit concerning," she said.

Student Demi said he felt "uneasy" after the stabbing.

"It's not really an unsafe area," he said. "It's a bit out of the ordinary.

"These things happen, unfortunately, but it's a bit strange to have it happen here."

Kate, another local resident, said: "Usually we feel very safe. We're fortunate living in this area because there are lots of security patrols and there are always people around.

"Stabbings are terrible tragedies, but it could happen anywhere, and I know there are areas of London that have to deal with that every day.

"I still feel safe. We're fortunate to live here with so much security; I wish that everyone lived in such an area."

News.title: Call with couple in Iran prison 'enormous relief'
News.content:
The family of an East Sussex couple detained in Iran say they have spoken to them for the first time in three months.

Lindsay and Craig Foreman were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges, which they both deny, and are being held in Evin prison.

Lindsay's son, Joe Bennett, said hearing his mum's voice was "an enormous relief" and encouraged the government to visit the couple as the UK embassy in Iran reopened last week after closing due to ongoing security concerns in the region.

A Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) spokesperson confirmed staff had returned to the embassy and said the pair's health and welfare was a "top priority".

Bennett, who lives in Folkestone, said the 12-minute phone call was their first official conversation since the couple ended their hunger strikes.

He said his mother told him she and her husband were "slowly rebuilding their strength" after losing a substantial amount of weight.

"Just hearing mum's voice properly again was an enormous relief," he added.

"We only had 12 minutes, but after everything that has happened, those 12 minutes meant a great deal."

Bennett said his mother and her partner had remained "mentally resilient" and "determined to return home".

Bennett claimed the conversation was "monitored" and conducted with an interpreter present, limiting what could be discussed.

He is now calling for the UK Government to take "swift action" to arrange an urgent consular visit and ensure the couple receive appropriate medical care.

He also hopes to meet with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and for the government to use all available diplomatic and legal channels to secure their release.

He said the family was particularly concerned the couple did not receive a full medical assessment following their hunger strikes.

News.title: Inquest begins into death of Jason Arday
News.content:
An inquest has begun into the death of Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row.

He was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, days after resigning from his post.

His appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment.

Senior coroner Dr Julian Morris said on Wednesday: "The various reports have given me reason to suspect that Professor Arday died an unnatural death 12 days ago."

He told London Inner South Coroner's Court: "It therefore follows that I must open an investigation."

The Metropolitan Police said at the time that Arday's death was being treated as unexpected and was "not believed to be suspicious".

Arday was found "unresponsive" by family members at his home in Battersea, the inquest heard on Wednesday. Despite resuscitation efforts he was pronounced dead, the inquest was told.

The 41-year-old had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

He said controversy about his work had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The claims emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Such scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

After his death, his family issued a statement saying they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage surrounding the former Cambridge professor before his death.

Arday's memoir is due to be published in the UK on Thursday. The publisher, Simon & Schuster, announced on Monday that the book will be released as planned, with his family saying: "It is only right that we honour his wishes."

Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, who was known for her signature polka dots, has died. She was 97.

An announcement made on her official website by her company on Thursday said ​that she died on 14 August. It did ​not give a cause of death.

Kusama was one of Japan’s most respected contemporary artists. She was widely exhibited around the world, including at the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York.

Repetitive motifs were her trademark, sometimes resembling netting, swirls or worms – but most often dots. They danced proudly on her canvases or appeared as sparkling balls or dots of light in her installations.

Frustrated with ⁠the confining nature of Japanese society, Kusama ​left for New York at 27, where she ​quickly made a name for herself with her paintings, inspired by hallucinations of flashing lights, dots and flowers she ​had seen since childhood.

She also wrote, took ​part in anti-war activities during the 1960s, and reportedly influenced ‌artists ⁠such as Andy Warhol.

open image in gallery People look at Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama's sculpture 'Pumpkin' in Kensington Palace Gardens in London in 2024 ( Reuters )

Kusama, who was candid about her mental health struggles, said that New York gave her neuroses.

Around 1977, a few years after ​returning to ​Japan, she ⁠voluntarily entered a mental hospital and lived there for decades, being driven ​to her nearby studio each morning.

"I ​still ⁠see hallucinations even now," Kusama said in 2017.

"Dots come flying everywhere – on my dress, the floor, ⁠things ​I'm carrying, throughout the house, ​the ceiling. And I paint them."

Kusama described polka dots as “fabulous” in a 2012 interview with the Associated Pres.

open image in gallery Artist Yayoi Kusama with her artwork ‘Love arrives at the Earth Carrying with it a Tale of the Cosmos’ at the Tate Modern gallery in 2012 ( Reuters )

“I want to create 1,000 paintings, maybe 2,000 paintings, as many as I can draw,” she said.

“I will keep painting until I die.”

In her later years, Kusama enjoyed fame. She signed on with fashion brands like Louis Vuitton as well as other licensed products like teacups, T-shirts and key chains with her illustrations, including replicas of her likeness that were used in show windows and other marketing.

In 2008, Christie’s auctioned her work for $5.8 million, and in 2016, she won the most prestigious award Japan gives its artists, the Order of Culture.

“She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul,” the studio's statement said.

“We will carry forward Kusama’s wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world.”

Nearly 1,500 people are missing across Nepal and Tibet, authorities said on Thursday, as rescuers used helicopters to search a Himalayan valley devastated by flash floods a day earlier.

Police in Nepal said they expect the death toll, already above 160, to rise further as search teams reach areas cut off since Wednesday.

Almost 600 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism officials said, with travellers from more than two dozen countries unaccounted for.

open image in gallery The red dotted line shows the route of the flooding along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers ( The Independent )

The largest group, 177 people, were from India, followed by 63 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.

In Tibet's Gyirong county, the missing tally stood at 558, including 260 foreign nationals, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.

The disaster began when a landslide of ice and rock struck the Lhende river, a tributary that meets the Bhotekoshi roughly 20km northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing with Tibet, according to an initial analysis of satellite imagery cited by Nepal's disaster management authorities.

The collapse sent a debris-laden surge down the Lhende into the Bhotekoshi, then into the Trishuli river, carrying mud, rock and water through the border town of Gyirong on the Tibetan side before crossing into Nepal's Rasuwa district.

Chinese authorities have since warned of a further risk from a separate, still-dammed lake upstream of the border crossing in Gyirong county, which they said could complicate rescue efforts.

open image in gallery An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal's Nuwakot district on 27 August 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Villages including Manakamana and Khadga Bhanjyang, both in the flood's direct path, were largely destroyed.

Downstream, the surge passed through Nuwakot and Dhading districts, where families gathered near an army training centre being used as a base for helicopter rescue operations.

Survivors described the water arriving without warning.

Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old being treated in hospital, told Reuters he tried to pull his wife to safety as mud engulfed their home. "As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher," he said.

"I tried to grab my wife's hand and take her to the terrace, but she was swept away by the mud." He was airlifted to safety four hours later.

Another survivor said he saved himself by clinging to a mango tree as he watched the house where he had been working disappear.

open image in gallery A muddy area viewed from a helicopter, in the aftermath of flash floods, in Rasuwa district, Nepal 26 August 2026 in this still image obtained from social media video ( Reuters )

More than 5,000 army and police personnel have been mobilised to search for survivors and recover bodies, Raja Ram Basnet, a spokesperson for Nepal's army, told Reuters.

Helicopters have been dropping tents, food and other emergency supplies provided by India to communities cut off by the disaster.

The flood's reach has extended well beyond Nepal's own river system. India's National Disaster Response Force said a sudden rise in the Trishuli River was detected at Furke Khola, around 160km from the Indian border, and warned the flood wave was expected to continue downstream into the Gandak river.

open image in gallery An aerial view shows a collapsed bridge along with houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal's Nuwakot district on 27 August 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Response teams have been deployed to vulnerable districts in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh as a precaution.

Early reports had suggested a separate earthquake triggered the glacial collapse, but the US Geological Survey has since clarified that the magnitude-4.4 reading it initially logged was in fact the seismic signature of the glacial rock-and-ice collapse itself, rather than a distinct tremor that caused it.

"This is a very unique disaster, in terms of intensity and speed, which had a distinct blueprint of impact on communities, and activities around immediate response and recovery," Nader Naderpajouh, who leads the Organising Risk and Resilience research lab and is Head of the School of Project Management at the University of Sydney, said.

open image in gallery Members of a rescue team stand amid mud and debris following devastating floods, in Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, 27 August 2026 ( Reuters )

"The reports suggest the flood and landslide were caused by a buildup of water in the glacier, which was triggered by seismic activity.

"With global warming, there is an expectation that similar patterns of disasters will recur. We can benefit from the implementation of a warning system, similar to those triggered for tsunami warnings after 2004's tsunami."

The disaster has drawn pledges of support from several governments. The US said it was sending a disaster response adviser and $500,000 in assistance, while Canada, Australia and the United Nations have also offered help.

Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, spoke to his Nepali counterpart, Balendra Shah, to convey condolences and pledge "all possible humanitarian assistance."

Blind Date will be returning to our screens with a brand new host, more than 20 years after ITV’s Cilla Black-fronted programme went off air.

The dating show, which has been revived a handful of times over the years, is moving to a streaming service for the first time, with Disney+ producing and airing the episodes.

Fresh from her stint on The Traitors US, Maura Higgins will be on hosting duties when the new series arrives next year.

While Disney+ has promised that Blind Date will be “reimagined for contemporary audiences – bigger, better, and bolder than ever”, it will be sticking to the original format, which saw contestants choose between three potential dates hidden by a wall.

“Fans can expect a host of innovative format twists and a spicy dose of drama,” Disney+ said in a press release.

open image in gallery Higgins has been building her profile in the US in recent months ( AFP/Getty )

Higgins made her small screen debut with an (iconic) stint on the 2019 series of Love Island, reaching the final alongside Curtis Pritchard.

The 35-year-old went on to host Love Island USA: Aftersun before appearing on the Stateside version of Celebrity Traitors earlier this year, where she yet again delivered a golden reality television moment. Later this year, Higgins will appear in another US version of a British favourite – Dancing with the Stars.

Angela Jain, Head of Content, Disney+ EMEA, has said the Irish star is “the perfect match for our version of Blind Date”.

“Her distinctive straight-talking humour, coupled with her experience as a reality dating show contestant, means we know she has the gravitas plus the wit to bring Blind Date to new audiences,” she continued.

With Cilla Black on hosting duties, Blind Date first aired on ITV in 1985. At its peak, the Saturday night programme pulled in a whopping 18.2 million viewers per episode. The programme brought its presenter, who was already a chart-topping singer, to an even wider audience and turned many of her frequently used lines into popular catchphrases.

open image in gallery ‘Blind Date’ brought Cilla to an even wider audience ( PA )

Black hosted the show until it was taken off air by ITV in 2003. The broadcaster eventually settled on Take Me Out as a replacement in the primetime Saturday night slot, with Paddy McGuinness fronting 11 series between 2010 and 2019.

Meanwhile, ITV aired two one-off Blind Date specials in 2006 and 2013, before Channel 5 tried to revive the show in 2017, almost two years after Black’s death at the age of 72. That version was presented by Black’s longtime pal and fellow Liverpudlian Paul O’Grady – but it was sadly axed after four series due to struggling ratings.

A small plane carrying four people crashed into shallow waters next to a remote coastal town in Alaska on Wednesday, killing everyone on board, according to officials.

The Piper PA-24 was heading for the airport in the small town of Seldovia after taking off from Anchorage, according to a statement from the Alaska Department of Public Safety. Seldovia's airport is about 136 miles (219 kilometers) southwest of Anchorage.

After it crashed, it was submerged in about 15 feet (4.6 meters) of water in the Seldovia Slough near the shore, said Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief. Troopers had to wait until the tide went out in order to reach it.

Troopers were able to get the bodies of the four adults out of the plane. They're being sent to the medical examiner’s office and their names will not be released until next of kin are notified, according to the Department of Public Safety.

It was not immediately clear what may have caused the crash.

The NTSB is investigating.

U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, of Alaska, said he'll be getting a briefing from the NTSB and Federal Aviation Administration as they work to figure out what went wrong.

"These tragedies are heartbreaking and unacceptable, which is why aviation safety and infrastructure in Alaska continue to be a top focus of mine," he said in a post on Facebook.

Less than a week earlier, another plane crashed at a remote military site in western Alaska, killing all eight people on board. The aircraft had been making its second runway approach in heavy fog and its pilots could not see the gravel airstrip, authorities said.

Former Loose Women presenter Carol McGiffin has said that the long-running ITV show should be axed as it “seems to be in its final throes”.

The broadcaster, 66, served as an anchor and panellist on the mid-morning chat show regularly from 2000 until 2013, before returning for a five-year stint in 2018.

Three years on from her exit, McGiffin has spoken out about the future of Loose Women and declared that it’s time for ITV to wrap it up.

“There’s nothing worse than having to watch someone you love die a slow, painful death but it’s also painful to watch when something you loved dies a slow death,” she wrote in her latest Best magazine column.

open image in gallery Carol McGiffin on ‘Loose Women’ ( ITV )

“And so it is, in my opinion, with Loose Women. It’s been happening for a while but now it seems to be in its final throes.”

She went on to say that the show used to be “full of humour, with strong sassy women, innuendo and risqué topics” and was a “joy to do and an even bigger joy to watch”.

“Watching now it’s a sad shadow of its former self, boring, strained, unfriendly and with too many rich, whinging women going on about the menopause or their terrible lives,” she continued, adding: “Time to let it go.”

The Independent has contacted ITV for comment.

McGiffin left Loose Women in 2023, revealing at the time that she was left “upset” after she was “forced” into the decision due to an unsatisfactory contract.

“The problem was, ITV were insisting, for the first time since I went back in 2018, that if I wanted to carry on doing the show, I would have to sign a contract that was totally unjust and unworkable for me, so I had to say ‘no thanks,’” she said. “I feel quite upset about it, if I’m honest, because although it is my decision, I felt it was one I was being forced to make.”

open image in gallery Nadia Sawalha recently claimed that she had been ‘bullied’ off the show ( ITV )

In the years since, Loose Women has faced major cuts and controversies. Last year, ITV announced its plans to overhaul its daytime output, slashing the budgets for shows including Good Morning Britain (GMB), Lorraine, This Morning, and Loose Women.

The changes resulted in hundreds of job losses across daytime, with Loose Women also forced to lose its live studio audience after moving to a smaller studio in Covent Garden. In January, it was reported that there had been “some meltdowns” over the reduced dressing room space.

Meanwhile, earlier this month, former panellist Nadia Sawalha claimed that she had been “bullied off” the series due to her vocal support for Palestine.

She claimed the channel’s decision arose from “escalating campaign of smears, complaints, hostile media coverage and targeted calls to have me removed” from the series, and threatened legal action against ITV. The broadcaster did not respond to requests for comment at the time.

Rupert Grint is set to reprise his role as Ron Weasley, 15 years after we last saw him alongside Daniel Radcliffe and Emma Watson in the final Harry Potter film.

The actor, who is now 38, will join the cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on Broadway in February 2027.

The two-part play – penned by Adolescence screenwriter Jack Thorne, from an original story developed with JK Rowling – focuses on the next generation of Hogwarts students and will see Grint play an older version of the loveable but occasionally hapless Ron.

Grunt said in a statement: “Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can’t wait to meet him again in this stage of life.

“There is something so full-circle and so special about stepping back into Ron’s shoes now when we are both fathers; it is somehow both very familiar and completely new. And the joy of being back on Broadway, this time in a role that defined so much of my life is truly exciting.”

open image in gallery The original Harry Potter trio landed their roles in 2000 ( Getty )

Producers Sonia Friedman and Colin Callender said: “Rupert is not simply revisiting a role from his past. He is continuing a journey he began as a child and carrying it forward with all the life and experience he has gained since filming concluded, including a career that has taken him from film to television to acclaimed stage work on both Broadway and the West End.

“His return creates a powerful bridge between the story audiences first fell in love with and the story of family, legacy and the passage of time that Harry Potter and the Cursed Child carries forward.”

Grunt’s stint in Cursed Child will begin on 2 February 2027 – just a few weeks after Tom Felton’s run as Draco Malfoy comes to an end.

The Slytherin star returned to his role in November last year, but with ticket sales booming, his stint was recently extended until January 2027.

Grint is currently scheduled to appear in The Cursed Child until 30 May 2027. The ticket presale will begin on Tuesday 1 September.

open image in gallery Grint will make his debut in the play next May ( AFP/Getty )

The announcement comes after the the latest casting news for HBO’s Harry Potter TV series, which will debut on Christmas Day. It was announced that Kit Harington will play Gilderoy Lockhart, replacing Nicholas Hoult after the Nosferatu actor dropped out due to “scheduling issues”.

Warwick Davis is the only star from the films confirmed to reprise their role in the series. He will return as Professor Filius Flitwick, joining the likes of John Lithgow, Katherine Parkinson and Paapa Essiedu.

News.title: Savio scores on debut as Spurs cruise past Charlton in Carabao Cup
News.content:
It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest big-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his new club.

Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.

But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.

“A perfect day for him,” said De Zerbi. “His biggest improvement is to increase the number of goals. He is one of the best wingers, but the best wingers score many goals and I spoke with him two days ago, and we put the goal at 10-12 goals.

“We need 10-12 goals from the wingers. Last season, we suffered too much because the number of goals were not enough.”

News.title: German airport worker dies of malaria after mosquito imported on plane
News.content:
Five airport workers in Frankfurt have been infected with malaria and one has died after being bitten by a stowaway mosquito, health officials have said.

The employees are thought to have been infected in early July, but their diagnosis was delayed due to a lack of travel history to malaria-endemic regions, according to the Robert Koch Institute, Germany’s federal agency responsible for disease control.

It is believed that they were bitten by mosquitoes which arrived at the airport on a plane, most likely from Africa, where 95 per cent of global malaria cases are found.

The five surviving airport workers – who are all male and are said to work in different parts of the facility and in different jobs – are undergoing medical care.

Traps have now been installed across the airport in an attempt to catch any remaining mosquitoes and analyse their origin, according to an airport spokesperson.

It is not the first time that Frankfurt Airport, Germany’s busiest travel hub, has recorded a case of malaria, according to the Robert Koch Institute, which added that there was another incidence in 2023.

More than 610,000 people die of malaria every year, the overwhelming majority children under five in Africa who are unable to quickly access treatment.

The disease, which is caused by a parasite carried by infected mosquitoes, is largely curable if treated early with antimalarials.

In Britain and Europe, there are thousands of imported cases of malaria every year reported in returning travellers from Africa and Asia – but local transmission is exceedingly rare.

Of the 5,000 or so cases recorded in Europe every year, typically just five are caught locally – either from an airport or from a non-infected European mosquito picking up the disease from a sickened person and spreading it to others.

Early symptoms include fever, headaches, and chills, which can quickly develop into multi-organ failure.

Vaccines were made available for the first time in 2024 and are licenced for use in young children in Africa, although they are thought to be only between 30 and 50 per cent effective at preventing the disease.

News.title: Livestock bacterial disease spreading among humans in Europe
News.content:
In Barcelona, researchers found further evidence that the bacterium was spreading between people.

Nine cases identified between December 2025 and March 2026 were caused by strains that differed by just zero to four genetic mutations, suggesting the infections were part of a recent transmission chain rather than separate cases acquired from animals.

The bacterium can survive in crusted areas on the skin for up to 42 months, according to Dr McHale, raising questions about the role of contaminated surfaces, equipment and shared spaces.

People should not be alarmed by the infection, which is treatable with a course of antibiotics, he added.

This could make hygiene particularly important in places such as saunas, where people may have prolonged skin contact with others and with shared surfaces.

Saunas have historically been a destination for gay and bisexual men seeking social and sexual contact.

Dating apps such as Grindr have since made casual encounters in these environments far easier to arrange, experts say.

“What we’re seeing is the kind of in-person venues like saunas being combined with apps,” said Rusi Jaspal, a Professor of Psychology at the University of Brighton and expert on wellbeing among gay men.

“Someone might, for example, be in a sauna but also have their app on, and that might be a way of getting people to come to the sauna. So they’re not only attracting people who are already in the sauna, but who might be outside of that environment and coming in.”

Progress and complacency

Professor Jaspal believes the success of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), which protects against HIV, has also played a role.

“I think that is a really big contributor,” he said. “On the one hand, obviously it’s fantastic that PrEP is there. It prevents HIV; it’s extremely effective against HIV. But it’s not effective against other infections.”

He argued that because PrEP has removed the fear of HIV that shaped gay men’s sexual behaviour for decades, some men are now having condomless sex with more partners, in the belief that other infections are treatable in a way HIV once was not.

“Because they think, well, everything else is treatable – gonorrhoea, syphilis, it’s all treatable – they’re going to just not use condoms,” he said. “That is not only creating more of a risk of infection, but I think people are having more partners as well.”

Sexual contact is not the only route by which the bacterium appears to be spreading.

In Norway, ten cases have been linked to martial arts, with some infections occurring during training in Norway and others during trips to Thailand.

One case report described a 34-year-old Muay Thai fighter who developed recurrent pustular lesions after returning from a training trip, later confirmed as D. congolensis through whole-genome sequencing.

Dr McHale said the bacterium tends to take hold where the skin has already been compromised in some way.

“Predisposing factors for infection include cutaneous microtrauma, for example, from ultraviolet radiation, tick exposure and insect bites, and maceration of the skin,” he said.

Dermatophilus congolensis is notoriously difficult to grow in culture, meaning infections can easily go undiagnosed or be mistaken for more common skin conditions.

Researchers in Barcelona have warned that cases could be going unrecognised because sexual health clinics do not routinely test for the bacterium.

But Professor Jaspal believes the legacy of the HIV/Aids epidemic explains why this cluster was identified so quickly.

He said the crisis of the 1980s, when confusion and stigma allowed the virus to spread largely undetected, forced public health bodies to build far stronger surveillance and communication systems for outbreaks among gay and bisexual men.

That same infrastructure, he argued, has since been used to manage subsequent threats such as mpox – and now this obscure bacterium – far more effectively.

“I think we are quite rightly identifying cases early on, so that we can then communicate that risk to people and encourage precautions to protect themselves,” Professor Jaspal said. “That is really, really important.”

News.title: The five best coastal places to retire in the UK
News.content:
How equity release can help you purchase a seaside property

UK homeowners aged 55 or over may be able to use equity release in two main ways: either to help fund the purchase of a second home, or to buy a new home and release equity from that property as part of the same legal transaction. Seeking professional advice is key to understanding which option may be right for you.



The most popular equity release product is a lifetime mortgage. A lifetime mortgage is a loan secured against your home. It will reduce the value of your estate and could affect your entitlement to means-tested benefits. There is no obligation to make monthly repayments with a lifetime mortgage, although you can choose to make some if you wish. Instead, the full amount plus interest is only repaid when the last homeowner dies or enters permanent long-term care, and this is usually done with the sale of the home.



You must always seek professional help when considering equity release. Make sure your adviser is looking at products from lenders that are members of the Equity Release Council. The Equity Release Council, the industry trade body, requires its members to offer plans that comply with its product standards.

News.title: Households warned of ‘worse to come’ as energy bills rise
News.content:
Households have been warned there is “worse to come” on energy bills after Ofgem raised its price cap to a three-year high.

On Wednesday, the regulator announced typical annual household gas and electricity prices will rise by £60 from October.

The 4pc rise follows a 13pc jump in July as the Iran war pushed up global oil and gas prices.

Analysts at Cornwall Insight, the energy consultancy, said there was no relief in sight for households in January if the conflict in the Middle East continues.

It said a further 9pc rise should be expected in the new year, putting an average January bill up to £1,872 a year, £149 higher than the prices coming into effect from October.

The forecast underlines the challenges faced by Andy Burnham as he stakes his reputation on lowering the cost of living.

Mr Burnham on Wednesday said he recognised rising energy bills were “difficult” for people, adding the government had decided to remove VAT from electricity bills to “give people that little bit of help”.

Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the Prime Minister said: “We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.

“We’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”

However, the latest increase to the price cap effectively wipes out the £45 reduction from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, hinted on Wednesday there could be more action from ministers “to protect families from unaffordable bills”, with the Budget due to be held on October 28.

Commenting on the price cap, Craig Lowrey, of Cornwall Insight, said there was a risk of “more hardship” by January.

“Where January bills land will depend on whether the situation in the Middle East calms down in the next couple of months.”

He added that low European gas stocks heading into the winter meant bills were unlikely to fall.

Elsewhere Ms Fahnbulleh appeared to suggest that investment in net zero projects was contributing to higher household bills.

Asked on LBC if the rise in bills could not solely be blamed on the Middle East conflict, but also on political choices to pay for renewable subsidies, she replied: “Well, no, so it is both.”

However, she later insisted it was “simply not true” that net zero was adding to bills, when questioned by Sky News.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

Sports.title: Liverpool close in on £115million Bradley Barcola transfer with Premier League clubs to spend £1BILLION before deadline
Sports.content:
LIVERPOOL are closing in on an agreement for Paris Saint-Germain star Bradley Barcola.

The Reds are in the hunt for a new star on the wing following the departure of Mohamed Salah at the end of last season.



The French champions originally quoted suitors for the 23-year-old with a price tag of £145million.

But the Times claim that a deal could now be struck for something in the region of £115m.



That fee would provisionally make him the club’s second most expensive signing ever, just less than the £125million paid for Alexander Isak last summer.

The monster sum could be part of a late Premier League transfer rush reaching sums of over £1 BILLION.

Several deals have neared or broken the £100m mark so far this summer, including Elliot Anderson‘s move to Manchester City and Morgan Rogers‘ switch to Chelsea.

While other deals in that region are still under negotiation, with Enzo Fernandez linked to a City move, while Arsenal battle for Julian Alvarez‘s signature.

Nicolas Jackson‘s £65million agreement to move to Aston Villa looks like a reasonable fee in comparison, but still constitutes a record for the side.

Sports.title: Tottenham 5 Charlton 1: £85million Savio shines on debut as Spurs get over woeful Brentford loss in style
Sports.content:
SAVIO sparkled on his debut as he scored and assisted from the bench as Tottenham thrashed Charlton.

The Brazilian, who arrived from Manchester City for £85million this week, showed off his dancing feet as he masterminded two goals in quick succession.



Manager Roberto De Zerbi has splashed over £320m on new signings this summer already, with Omar Marmoush expected to walk through the door from City in the coming days too.

But who can blame the Italian when his big-money arrivals are having this kind of impact.



Tottenham are on the back of two dismal domestic campaigns and something has had to change in North London.

Turns out breaking the bank to bring in a host of new star players could be the answer.



New £85m midfielder Mateus Fernandes also made his full debut, while there wasn’t even space in the matchday squad for £100m man Sandro Tonali and fellow new arrival Marcos Senesi.

But it was Savio, who failed to impress often at City, was the star of the show following his 70th-minute introduction.

His contribution helped Spurs win just their second domestic game at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in over EIGHT MONTHS.

Nathan Jones’ visiting Charlton side paled in comparison, not least because the Addicks boss had made ten changes to his side that beat West Ham at the weekend.

Jones has 19-year-old striker Micah Mbick leading the line, while his goalkeeper, Tiernan Brooks, has never played a game in England’s top four leagues and joined from National League Gateshead in the summer.

Former Southampton chief Jones was hoping to rest most of his stars for their Championship clash with Preston this weekend, but was forced to introduce Danny McNamara and skipper Lloyd Jones after just 15 minutes.

Centre-back partnership Collins Sichenje and Billy Koumetio were both forced off with injuries.

Koumetio hobbled off holding his hamstring after treatment from a Charlton physio, while Sichenje was seemingly inconsolable as he was taken off on a stretcher following an innocuous knock in the box.

Despite Tottenham’s squad being laden with newly-acquired firepower, it was academy ace Mikey Moore that got things kicking.



The wideman, who spent last season on loan with Rangers, cut in from the right flank and unleashed a venomous strike that left Brooks helpless.

Moore is expected to join German side Cologne before the window closes next week, especially following the signings of Savio and Marmoush.

Any hope of a dramatic comeback was killed by substitute Kevin Danso, who rose up to nod home a floated free-kick with his first touch of the game.



Even with three goals flying in, perhaps the loudest cheer of the night came when Savio was introduced for a 20-minute debut cameo.

Sports.title: When is the Champions League 2026/27 draw? Start time, FREE stream and pots as Arsenal and Man Utd learn fate
Sports.content:
EUROPE’S footballing elite will attempt to dethrone back-to-back supremos PSG as the Champions League gears up for its next electrifying instalment.

Last season’s final saw the Parisian powerhouse sneak past Arsenal after an agonising penalty shoot-out in Budapest crushed the Gunners’ bid to bag North London’s first Champions League crown.



Luis Enrique and his glittering array of attacking talent are strongly tipped to extend their continental dominance and secure a three-peat, having also thumped Inter Milan 5-0 in the 2024/25 curtain-closer.

Hot on their heels will be vengeful Premier League champions Arsenal, alongside German giants Bayern Munich and a Barcelona side bursting with eight top talents from Spain’s World Cup-winning squad.



Five Premier League sides will do battle with Europe’s big boys, with Manchester City, Manchester United, Aston Villa and Liverpool all in the draw for the league phase along with Mikel Arteta‘s runners-up.

A staggering six English clubs reached the last 16 in a record-breaking 2025/26 competition, but the initial euphoria quickly fell flat after four failed to progress further and Liverpool were outclassed by PSG in the quarter-finals.

The fight for the most coveted prize in European club football will kick off with a league phase once more, and SunSport has all the crucial details for the draw.

When is the Champions League draw?

The draw for the league phase of the 2026/27 Champions League will take place on Thursday, August 27.

Proceedings are scheduled to begin at 5pm BST.

Uefa’s headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland, will host the event.

How to watch the Champions League draw FREE

The Champions League draw will be broadcast live and will be available to watch FREE on Uefa.com, Uefa.tv and the Uefa app.

TNT Sports 1 will also air the draw on regular TV, and subscribers will be able to stream it via HBO Max.

Alternatively, you can follow all the ties as they get confirmed on the night through SunSport’s live blog of the draw.

How does the Champions League league phase draw work?

Europe’s premier club competition will once again follow a Swiss System, commencing with a 36-team league phase in which each side plays eight times, evenly split between matches at home and on the road.

The continent’s top 36 teams are seeded into four pots containing nine similarly-matched teams, as determined by their five-year Uefa club coefficient.



Beginning with the top pot, a ball will be physically drawn before the automated software randomly draws two opponents from each pot, in an attempt to ensure every club faces an equally balanced set of rivals.

As stipulated by Uefa’s country protection rule, sides in the same league cannot play each other, and clubs cannot play more than two opponents from any one country.

The top eight teams in the final league standings automatically qualify for the last 16, while those who finish ninth to 24th are whittled down by two-legged play-off ties.

Savio grabbed a goal and assist on a dream debut as Tottenham thrashed Charlton to progress into the third round of the Carabao Cup.

The Brazilian, signed from Man City for £85m on Tuesday, was introduced as a second-half substitute and took just 11 minutes to open his account, adding to the hype surrounding his arrival in north London.

Roberto De Zerbi named a strong side to face the Championship opposition, with many senior names included in the starting XI after Spurs' dreadfully disappointing defeat to Brentford in their Premier League opener.

It was youngster Mikey Moore who finally broke down a stubborn Charlton defence though, smashing the ball through the hands of Tiernan Brooks to score his first Tottenham goal. That lead was quickly doubled just five minutes later, with Dominic Solanke smartly finishing after the visitors failed to clear their lines.

Several other high profile names were introduced after an hour, including Kevin Danso who headed home from a Mateus Fernandes free-kick with his first touch. However, Spurs fans will only thinking about the magic of Savio after he came on in the 71st minute.

The forward cut inside from the right and fired smartly into the bottom corner to add Spurs' fourth, before his scrappy effort deflected off veteran Ben Davies for a fifth just three minutes later.

There was still time for Charlton to find a consolation courtesy of the head of Lloyd Jones, but it meant little as Spurs cruised into third round, where they will meet Liverpool at Anfield.

'He lit the place up' - All the reaction from Savio's electric Spurs start

Sky Sports' Jermaine Beckford:

"A lot can happen in just one minute of football. Even more can happen in 20. As we have just seen, that's enough time to make yourself a cult hero.
