His remarks come as weatherman warned of increased rainfall in the coming months, with Nairobi among the urban areas requiring heightened preparedness because of its exposure to flooding and the impact of heavy rainfall on roads, settlements and other critical infrastructure.

Sakaja said the county has so far brought together the disaster management teams, Kenya Red Cross, Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA) and Kenya National Highways Authority (KeNHA) under a coordinated programme worth Sh2.4 billion to strengthen Nairobi’s flood resilience.

Of the amount, Sh2 billion has been set aside for drainage and flood-mitigation works targeting 19 roads in flood-prone areas.

The projects are at an advanced stage, with tenders awarded and contractors expected to commence implementation after completion of the necessary processes.

Sakaja reiterated that the programme will complement ongoing county interventions under the Nairobi Regeneration Programme, which includes the rehabilitation and upgrading of critical infrastructure across the city.

“The Sh2 billion will support a comprehensive drainage overhaul that complements the ongoing Nairobi Regeneration Programme. Our goal is to permanently address the flooding challenges that have affected the city for many years,” Sakaja said.

He said the focus is not only on responding to floods after they occur, but on addressing the infrastructure weaknesses that have historically made Nairobi vulnerable to flooding.

To strengthen preparedness, the county has established five specialised sub-committees under the multi-agency framework.

The committees include Infrastructure and Drainage; Emergency Response and Evacuation; Shelter and Relief; Security and Traffic and Communication.

While the Infrastructure and Drainage committee will coordinate the clearing and improvement of drainage systems, rivers and other critical infrastructure, the Emergency Response and Evacuation committee will oversee rapid response, rescue and evacuation operations whenever emergencies occur.

The Shelter and Relief committee will prepare safe shelters and coordinate the provision of food, water, medical assistance and other essential support to affected residents.

The Security and Traffic committee will coordinate security, traffic management and emergency access, while the Communication committee will strengthen early-warning systems, public alerts and timely dissemination of information.

Sakaja said the county is also mobilising personnel, equipment and other resources to clear blocked drains, remove silt and waste and strengthen emergency response systems in areas identified as vulnerable.

He urged residents and their associations, businesses and other stakeholders to play an active role in flood preparedness by keeping drainage areas clear and paying attention to official warnings.

The county chief said residents in high-risk areas will be provided with timely information on emerging weather conditions and the actions they should take when heavy rains occur.

“We don’t want people to panic. We want people to be proactive, to listen to information and to work with us. The multi-agency team is in place, and we are preparing before the rains intensify,” Sakaja said.

According to him, the multi-agency approach will also help eliminate jurisdictional gaps by bringing together national and county agencies to operate as one coordinated team.

He said the combination of drainage upgrades, emergency preparedness, early-warning systems and coordinated response would strengthen Nairobi’s resilience and reduce disruption caused by heavy rains.

The multi-agency team is expected to meet next week to review progress, coordinate ongoing works and further push the city’s El Niño preparedness agenda.

World.title: Public officers eyeing elective posts to resign by February 10 - IEBC
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon addressing the press at a past press conference. [File, Standard]

Public officers seeking to contest elective positions in the 2027 General Election have until February 10, 2027, to resign from office, the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has announced.

IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon said the deadline falls exactly six months before the August 10, 2027, General Election, which the Commission has confirmed will be held on a Tuesday.

“Any public officer who intends to contest in this election must resign from public office by Wednesday, 10th February 2027, which is exactly six months before the election,” Ethekon said.

The IEBC said adherence to the timelines will be non-negotiable, noting that they are legally binding and essential to ensuring an orderly electoral process.

Under the timetable, political parties must submit their membership lists and details of candidates participating in party primaries by March 16, 2027.

Party primaries and any related disputes must be concluded by May 8, while independent candidates are also required to meet their legal obligations by the same date.

Presidential aspirants will have until May 24 to submit lists of supporting voters drawn from a majority of Kenya’s counties.

Candidate registration will begin on May 29, with specific deadlines applying to the various elective positions.

The official campaign period will commence after candidates are registered, but not earlier than May 29, 2027.

Ethekon warned political parties, candidates and their supporters against breaching the prescribed campaign period, saying any electioneering outside the legal window will be unlawful.

The restrictions cover campaign posters, billboards, political caravans and other forms of campaigning.

Campaigning will close on August 7, 2027, 48 hours before Kenyans head to the polls.

“The law prescribes when election campaigns may commence,” Ethekon said, urging political parties, candidates and their supporters to strictly comply with electoral laws and regulations.

The deadline is among key milestones unveiled by the electoral commission as political parties, aspirants and other stakeholders begin preparations for the next General Election.

World.title: Schools will open on August 24 as scheduled, Ogamba says
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Students heading home during recent demonstrations. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

The Ministry of Education said the official academic calendar remains unchanged.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, August 19, Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba insists that learners will return to school on Monday, August 24, 2026.

The CS has dismissed reports circulating on social media claiming that the reopening of schools for the third term has been postponed, warning parents, teachers, learners and education stakeholders against relying on unauthorised online notices.

“We wish to clarify that the academic calendar for Basic Education institutions and Teacher Training Colleges remains unchanged,” the CS said.

The clarification comes two days before the scheduled reopening of schools, amid reports circulating on social media platforms suggesting that the government had pushed back the start of Term III.

"Our attention has been drawn to misleading information circulating on various social media platforms, purporting that the academic calendar for basic education institutions and Teachers Training Colleges has been changed," he stated.

The Ministry termed the reports “FALSE” and urged members of the public to completely disregard them.

Ogamba said the Ministry had directed Regional Directors of Education, County Directors of Education and Sub-County Directors of Education to ensure strict compliance with the approved academic calendar contained in a circular dated October 9, 2025.

According to the Ministry, pre-primary, primary, junior, senior and secondary schools will begin Term III on Monday, August 24. The term will run for nine weeks and end on October 23, 2026.

The reopening marks the final academic term of the school year, with schools expected to implement the approved programmes as they prepare learners for the end-of-year national assessments and examinations.

Diploma Teachers Training Colleges will also resume academic operations on August 24, with their third term scheduled to conclude on November 6, 2026.

The Ministry further confirmed that the national assessment and examination calendar has not been altered for KPSEA, KILEA, KJSEA, KPLEA and KCSE are scheduled to begin from October 26, 2026, as earlier announced.

The Ministry also reminded schools that extracurricular activities and visits to secondary schools will remain banned during Term III.

The latest clarification is part of efforts by the government to prevent confusion among parents, learners and teachers as schools prepare to reopen.

Ogamba urged education stakeholders to obtain information through official Ministry communication channels, rather than social media posts whose authenticity cannot be established.

“Parents, teachers and learners and members of the public are advised to strictly rely on the Ministry's official communication channels and field officers for accurate information," he said.

World.title: Ring hopes new encryption tech will ease surveillance fears around its home security cameras
World.content:
New York — Many Americans feel growing unease about the proliferation of cameras — in people’s hands, on homes and businesses, in public spaces for police use — that seem to be capturing our every move, sparking Many Americans feel growing unease about the proliferation of cameras — in people’s hands, on homes and businesses, in public spaces for police use — that seem to be capturing our every move, sparking backlash protests and users ditching or destroying devices

Now Ring, one of the largest home security camera providers in the United States, is rolling out a new encryption technology that it hopes will give customers more confidence about the privacy of their cameras and footage.

It is the latest move by a security camera company to address consumers’ privacy and surveillance fears. Earlier this month, law enforcement technology firm Flock introduced new police auditing and accountability controls.

Ring’s update effectively means customers don’t have to worry about any third parties, including law enforcement and Amazon itself, viewing their home security footage without their consent, according to the Amazon-owned company. That was already Ring’s policy, but the new form of encryption reinforces that on a technical level.

The technology is called TAKE — an acronym for “throw away the key.” When stored in the cloud, a user’s videos will be kept in what Ring says is effectively a secure digital vault to which only the user has the key. The company says it will only get the virtual key to run features like video search for a limited time with a customer’s approval and then will “throw away the key,” so Ring doesn’t have ongoing access to the videos.

Ring will roll out the new encryption as the default security setting on all of its cameras starting in September.

“People are always going to have questions about, like, how do you store it? How do you protect it?” Ring founder Jamie Siminoff told CNN. “As a company we’ve done, I believe, a really good job with that, but this is the physical way of now giving them confidence … this is the show, not just tell.”

Ring has long faced criticism over its relationship with law enforcement.

The company faced intense scrutiny earlier this year after a Super Bowl ad about a lost dog feature prompted surveillance fears. Weeks later, Ring canceled a controversial partnership with Flock.

Ring says TAKE provides a similar level of protection as end-to-end encryption, where sensitive data is effectively scrambled when traveling between one trusted endpoint (like a camera) and another (like a customer’s phone) and no outsider can access it. But the company says the new technology is more effective for the multi-device, multi-user configurations used by many Ring customers.

Ring users can still voluntarily share footage with law enforcement if police request it through the company’s Neighbors app.

Ring began offering end-to-end encryption in 2021, following calls from privacy advocates, but it restricted how people could use their devices. The company says it will retain end-to-end encryption as an option starting in September.

The new technology may address some users’ fears about who can access Ring camera footage. But even non-Ring users have raised concerns about privacy violations when they walk by a neighbor’s home or walk up to a friend’s front door.

Siminoff said he hopes that Ring’s new encryption will help ease those fears, too — at least to some extent.

“I think there is an anxiety of, like, I just don’t know what’s happening with this (footage),” Siminoff said. “I think people will hear about this and then feel more comfortable when they see a Ring camera, knowing that there’s a default encryption on it, that it’s locked to the specific person.”

World.title: Iranians split over proposed law to criminalize contact with foreign media
World.content:
Iranian politicians are divided over a move by the country’s parliament to approve a bill that would criminalize communications with media outlets deemed hostile to the Islamic Republic.

The bill is yet to become law, with some Iranian members of parliament raising concerns that the wording is too broad and could affect essential activities. Moein Khazaeli, one Iranian human rights lawyer, warned that it could amount to “a fresh legal catastrophe.”

Iranian state news agency IRNA reported earlier this month that politicians were split over bill. Before the parliament vote this month, Ebrahim Azizi, chairman of Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said he believed the bill was aimed at creating “transparency in channels of communication with foreigners.”

But others said the bill would not solve the problem of foreign interference. Gholamhossein Karbaschi, a reformist political figure, said: “The problem begins when we assume that the main route of infiltration is simply journalists, interviews or foreign media, and that restricting these areas can solve a significant part of the problem.”

Iran has, however, proceeded to prosecute individuals who were in contact with foreign media under other national security and espionage laws, raising questions about what legal gap the new bill is intended to fill.

Iranian photojournalist Yalda Moaiery, whose stories and photographs have appeared around the world, has herself become a target. She was sentenced to 15 years in prison earlier this month by an Iranian court with “activities in furtherance of the interest of the Zionist regime against national security.” She hopes to appeal the decision.

Moaiery appeared on CNN in February and this month. She provided a rare eyewitness account from inside Iran, even as the regime attempted to block communications with the outside world.

World.title: Netanyahu says US economic measures “tighten the siege on Iran”
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has praised the latest US economic measures against Iran, saying they would “tighten the siege” by targeting countries that do business with Tehran.

In a speech at the Binyamin Regional Council in the occupied West Bank, Netanyahu acknowledged that the Trump administration did not take significant steps against Iran itself, but rather against the country’s allies.

“What President Trump did yesterday was tighten the siege on Iran. Not by tightening the siege on Iran directly, but by tightening the siege on those who help this regime, this terrible dictatorship. This is a very important thing,” Netanyahu said.

When Netanyahu last visited Washington in late-July – his first meeting with President Donald Trump since before the start of the war in February – he said he laid out three options for the US: reaching an agreement, a renewed military campaign, or economic pressure.

Choosing to return to sanctions and economic pressure, Netanyahu said that Trump “reaffirmed that decision in a very, very, very strong way” with the latest measures. On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened new sanctions on countries refusing to cut economic ties with Iran but stopped short of imposing major new penalties.

Netanyahu added that “the challenge of Iran has not yet ended” and that he is “determined” to ensure Iran posed no threat.

World.title: ‘No one can understand the pain:’ Fire in maternity ward kills at least 14 newborn babies in Pakistan’s capital
World.content:
Islamabad, Pakistan — At least 14 newborn babies died Wednesday morning in one of Pakistan’s deadliest hospital fires in recent decades.

The fire broke out inside the maternity ward at the government-run Pakistan Institute for Medical Sciences (PIMS), the largest hospital in Pakistan’s capital Islamabad, around seven am local time.

The blaze appears to have been triggered by an air conditioning compressor explosion inside the nursery where the newborn babies were being cared for, rescue sources told CNN.

Hospital workers were able to rescue one child, the sources said.

Outside the hospital, a grieving father told reporters his three-day-old baby had been killed in the fire.

“No one can understand the pain I’m going through,” he said.

A woman named Muneeba who was visiting family in the hospital described narrowly escaping with her nephew and sister-in-law as the fire began to spread.

“Thank God our baby is safe,” she told CNN.

Multiple people reported encountering locked doors in the ward.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said he is “deeply saddened by this tragic incident” and ordered an immediate investigation into the fire, according to statement from his office.

He promised “strict action against anyone found responsible.”

A worker removes broken pieces of a glass window after a fire broke out at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, August 26, 2026. Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

Health care in Pakistan is delivered through both private and public providers. Government-run facilities are chronically underfunded and short-staffed, and have faced criticism for aging infrastructure and lack of emergency preparedness.

Sharmila Sahibah Faruqui, a member of Pakistan’s national assembly, called the tragedy “shameful and unforgivable” in a post to X.

“Heads must roll. Please do not hide behind another inquiry committee,” she wrote. “Those responsible must be taken to task.”

Islamabad is home to Pakistan’s political and military elite and its facilities are generally of a higher standard than those found in other towns and cities in the country.

A woman carrying an infant moves past police officers as she leaves a ward following the deadly hospital fire in Islamabad, Pakistan, August 26, 2026. Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

The PIMS facility is located on a sprawling site in the capital.

According to its website, its mission is “to be a premier research-intensive medical university that will educate medical students, paramedics, and postdoctoral fellows in accordance with international professional standards.”

Pakistan has experienced several major fires in recent years, including in hospitals, which often run on outdated electrical systems.

Earlier this year, a massive blaze at a shopping center in Karachi killed at least 67 people.

In June 2022, a fire broke out at a children’s hospital in Lahore and destroyed thousands of dollars worth of medicine, local media reported.

World.title: Electricity minister discusses Dabaa plant, SMRs with Rosatom in Russia
World.content:
Minister of Electricity and Renewable Energy Mahmoud Esmat on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, met with Rosatom Director General Alexei Likhachev in Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, to review progress on the al-Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant and explore cooperation on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).

During the meeting, both sides assessed ongoing construction timelines and target schedules, emphasizing coordination between Egyptian and Russian teams to maintain safety and quality standards. Esmat highlighted the strategic importance of the al-Dabaa project in diversifying Egypt’s energy mix, noting steady progress on-site.

Likhachev reaffirmed Rosatom’s commitment to delivering the plant on schedule while emphasizing broader cooperation in technology transfer and training Egyptian personnel to operate nuclear facilities.

Esmat also met with executives from a Rosatom subsidiary specializing in SMR technology to evaluate its application for industrial sectors, remote areas, and future power grids. He underscored Egypt’s interest in integrating SMRs into its long-term energy strategy subject to economic and safety evaluations.

World.title: Egypt, Italian firms discuss $278M bioethanol production project
World.content:
Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid held talks with representatives of Italian companies Proger and Draxil on the latest developments in an investment project to produce second-generation bioethanol using bagasse generated from sugarcane processing, with targeted investments of around $278 million.

The meeting reviewed the latest technical and implementation developments of the project, which aims to utilize agricultural and industrial waste and convert it into a value-added, exportable product, supporting Egypt’s drive toward a green economy, sustainable industries and deeper local manufacturing.

Farid affirmed that the ministry is working to facilitate procedures for investors and improve the efficiency of services needed to attract further investment, noting that priority is given to projects that contribute to increasing Egypt’s production and export capacities, supporting economic growth and creating jobs.

He said green economy and biofuel projects represent promising areas for attracting investment and opening new export markets, stressing that the project combines the utilization of local resources, deeper manufacturing, value creation and export opportunities.

The minister said the ministry would provide the necessary support to expedite the completion of the project’s requirements, enabling it to move from the study phase to implementation, production, operation and export, while benefiting from the availability of raw materials and other prerequisites for establishing the project in Egypt.

The two sides also discussed opportunities to export a substantial portion of the project’s output to European markets, enhancing its access to foreign markets and generating sustainable export revenues.

Representatives of the Italian companies outlined their vision for implementing the project, stressing that the availability of sugarcane bagasse in Egypt presents an opportunity to establish an integrated industrial project for producing second-generation biofuel, with the potential to direct a significant share of production to European markets.

The meeting also reviewed the results of technical tests conducted on bagasse samples and studies related to bioethanol production, as well as efforts to update the feasibility study ahead of completing the final study and determining the project’s investment and financing structure.

The meeting followed talks between representatives of the two companies and Minister of Supply and Internal Trade Sherif Farouk on the project’s technical and implementation developments, completed tests and studies, proposed partnership structures and steps toward implementation.

World.title: Egyptian Red Crescent receives 79th group of injured, sick Palestinians at Rafah crossing
World.content:
Teams from the Egyptian Red Crescent received the 79th group of injured and sick Palestinians arriving in Egypt through the Rafah crossing to receive medical treatment.

The teams also accompanied recovered patients as they left after completing their treatment, in coordination with the ministries of health and population and social solidarity.

The response included psychological support, particularly for children, as well as family-reunification services and the distribution of meals, drinks, clothing and personal-care supplies to meet the needs of injured and sick Palestinians during the crossing process.

The Egyptian Red Crescent continues its humanitarian work at the Rafah crossing around the clock, providing humanitarian and relief assistance to Palestinians and supporting Egyptian efforts to ease their suffering amid difficult humanitarian conditions.

World.title: FM affirms Egypt’s pride in historical ties with Chad
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty emphasized Egypt’s pride in historical, fraternal ties with Chad, stressing Cairo’s keenness to advance cooperation across various fields under directives from President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Chadian President Field Marshal Mahamat Idriss Déby to serve both nations’ mutual interests.

The remarks came during a phone call on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, between Abdelatty and Chadian Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdoulaye Saber Fadoul to discuss bilateral relations, cooperation tracks, and regional issues of mutual concern.

The ministers followed up on implementing the outcomes of the fourth session of the Egypt-Chad Joint Committee, including agreed cooperation projects, agreements and memoranda of understanding.

Both sides exchanged views on Sudan, with Abdelatty reaffirming Egypt’s steadfast support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity and national institutions while rejecting parallel entities. He underscored the need for a Sudanese-owned, comprehensive political settlement that restores security, stability and development.

The two top diplomats also reviewed Libyan developments, as Abdelatty reiterated Egypt’s firm support for Libya’s unity, sovereignty and state institutions, emphasizing the necessity of a Libyan-Libyan political solution leading to simultaneous presidential and parliamentary elections as soon as possible.

World.title: Liberia: Sen. Kogar Blasts Howard-Taylor’s Detention, Demands Police IG’s Resignation, Calls for Probe into Joe Boakai Jr. Over Drug Saga
World.content:
Monrovia — Nimba County Senator Samuel Kogar has sharply criticized the government’s handling of former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor’s arrest, describing the manner in which she was taken into custody as humiliating and traumatic, while calling for the resignation of Liberia National Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman over what he described as an alleged conflict of interest.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Kogar also called for an investigation into Joseph N. Boakai Jr., son of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, amid continuing questions surrounding Liberia’s multimillion-dollar cocaine investigation.

The senator made the remarks Wednesday when he appeared at the Center for Intellectual Exchange in downtown Monrovia.

Kogar: Howard Taylor Was Unfairly Treated

Kogar, citing his professional background in security, argued that authorities could have handled Howard Taylor’s detention differently, particularly given her public profile, reported health condition and longstanding ties to Liberia.

“They sensationalize the whole arrest,” Kogar said, arguing that authorities had other options, including notifying immigration authorities to prevent the former vice president from leaving the country while investigators completed their work.

Howard Taylor, facing charges including drug trafficking and money laundering, was jailed at the Monrovia Central Prison on Tuesday after the Monrovia City Court denied her lawyers’ request to allow her to remain at a medical facility of her choice while receiving treatment.

During Tuesday’s proceedings, Taylor, through her lawyers, requested a preliminary examination and subsequently asked the court to permit her to remain in compassionate detention at the medical facility where she had been receiving treatment.

Her lawyers argued that her medical condition was potentially life-threatening and that she could lose her life if denied treatment by her doctor of choice.

The court, however, denied the request, ruling that it lacked jurisdiction to grant compassionate leave. According to the court, such authority rests with the Executive Branch through the Ministry of Justice.

The court cited Chapter 34, Section 34.20.1 of the relevant law, which provides that the Attorney General shall formulate rules and regulations governing compassionate leave and, under those rules, may permit a prisoner to leave an institution for a short period for compelling reasons.

The court therefore held that the authority to grant formal compassionate leave rests with the Ministry of Justice, not the Judiciary.

The court also referenced a medical report presented during the proceedings, which recommended hospital admission because of fluctuations in Taylor’s blood pressure and anxiety associated with a stressful environment. The court noted, however, that the recommended 48-hour admission period had expired and that the report indicated she was in a stable condition.

The court further noted that some of the offenses with which Taylor is charged are non-bailable.

Kogar said the former vice president should instead have been placed under house arrest while investigators completed their work.

“Due to my professional background in security, JHT should have been put under house arrest,” he said. “When you finish and gather everything, you take her to court.”

He described the current approach as resembling “custodial interrogation” and urged authorities to exercise caution in sensitive criminal investigations involving prominent individuals.

While acknowledging that drug-related offenses may carry strict bail restrictions, Kogar said investigators should also consider the circumstances of suspects, particularly individuals with established residences and property in Liberia.

“Granted, drugs are non-bailable, but we have to be careful when we are dealing with sensitive cases,” he said. “She has properties all around this country. We all know her health condition. It is not a secret here.”

Kogar warned that the manner in which Howard Taylor was arrested could generate unnecessary political and social tensions among her supporters.

“She is from a county. She has her people. They might be feeling bad,” he said.

He drew a comparison with the 2006 arrest and transfer of former President Charles Taylor, arguing that authorities at the time took steps to avoid a potentially destabilizing situation.

He argued that the handling of Charles Taylor’s arrest and subsequent transfer to the Special Court for Sierra Leone was designed to minimize potential unrest.

“Liberia is not moving in the rightful trajectory,” Kogar added.

Kogar Calls for Police IG Coleman to Resign

Kogar’s strongest criticism was directed at Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman, whom he accused of creating the appearance of a conflict of interest in the ongoing cocaine investigation.

The senator referred to previous public comments by Coleman indicating that current and former government officials were allegedly connected to the drug investigation.

Kogar questioned why those officials had not been publicly identified or arrested if investigators possessed evidence linking them to the alleged drug network.

“The police director openly said there are past and current government officials that are connected to this drug saga,” Kogar said. “Without naming them, without charges. Why has he not named them or arrested them, but [is] going after former government officials?”

He argued that the alleged discrepancy raises questions about the impartiality of the investigation.

“That’s a conflict of interest. He needs to be removed,” Kogar said, calling for Coleman’s resignation.

Coleman has previously denied allegations by activist Martin Kollie that he received money as a gift to facilitate the purchase of a fleet of police vehicles.

Coleman has maintained his innocence and said he is guided by high ethical standards. He has also stated that if he ever believes his integrity has been compromised, he would resign rather than wait to be removed.

Senator Wants Joe Boakai Jr. Investigated

Kogar also called for an investigation into Joseph N. Boakai Jr., son of President Boakai, over allegations that surfaced earlier this year linking him to international narcotics trafficking.

Boakai Jr. has denied the allegations, insisting that he has never participated in illegal drug activities or used his relationship with the Presidency to influence government decisions.

The allegations emerged after a video circulated on social media, purportedly released by individuals claiming to be members of a Colombian drug cartel. The video accused Boakai Jr. of having ties to an international drug-trafficking network and displayed what it claimed were his WhatsApp profile picture, telephone number and messages exchanged with a Colombian contact.

Boakai Jr. strongly rejected the allegations, describing narcotics trafficking as a serious threat to Liberia.

“I have never participated in discussions involving narcotics trafficking. I have never facilitated illegal drug activity. I have never accepted money in exchange for influence. I have never used my relationship to the Presidency to shield anyone from accountability,” he said in his earlier response.

According to Boakai Jr., the controversy began after he received a threatening WhatsApp message at about 3 a.m. from a number he said was identified as originating from Colombia.

He said the sender accused him of involvement in drug trafficking, prompting him to reject the allegations, block the sender, and report the incident to the Liberia National Police and the National Security Agency.

Boakai Jr. also alleged that the video later circulated online omitted his response denying the accusations, creating what he described as a false impression of his involvement.

Kogar, however, argued that Boakai Jr. should be questioned as part of a formal investigation.

He said if Boakai Jr. acknowledged communicating with a person alleged to be connected to a drug cartel, investigators should establish the nature of that communication and determine whether his account is accurate.

Kogar said investigators must apply the same standards to Liberian and foreign nationals and should not selectively pursue suspects based on political status or nationality.

Kogar Challenges Government’s Deportee Arrangement

Kogar also questioned the legality and constitutional implications of Liberia’s decision to receive deportees from the United States, arguing that the arrangement raises questions about the extent of executive authority.

He cited Article 57 of the 1986 Liberian Constitution, which gives the President authority over the foreign affairs of the Republic, while noting that certain international agreements require legislative concurrence.

Kogar rejected comparisons between the deportee arrangement and conventional extradition proceedings.

“One of my colleagues said I was in error and cited the extradition treaty,” he said. “The refugee situation is not extradition.”

He explained that extradition generally involves one country requesting another country to surrender an individual accused or convicted of a crime who has fled abroad.

“Extradition is when a country requests a foreign country to turn over its citizens who committed crimes at home and fled to that country for safety,” he said.

Kogar maintained that although the Constitution grants the President broad executive powers, those powers are subject to constitutional limitations.

“The Constitution outlines several provisions that give the President certain executive powers and also limit that power,” he said.

He questioned the government’s decision to receive foreign nationals whose legal status in Liberia, he argued, requires greater clarification.

“But you brought them here; why did you bring them? We have not approved their coming. Where are they going to be lodged?” he asked.

Kogar also warned that fear of possible retaliation could discourage Liberians from publicly questioning the arrangement.

“Some people will be afraid not to talk because of fear of retaliation,” he said, adding that he was prepared to speak regardless of the consequences.

“I don’t care. We are here for history,” Kogar said.

Invoking the legacies of Nelson Mandela and Mahatma Gandhi, the senator said public officials should consider how their decisions will be judged by future generations.

“Nelson Mandela is dead, but today he is respected. Mahatma Gandhi is dead and gone, but still respected,” he said.

World.title: Liberia: Senator Konneh Urges Justice Ministry to Publish Documents Behind Police Vehicle Procurement Amid Drug Allegations
World.content:
Monrovia — Gbarpolu County Senator Amara Konneh has urged the Ministry of Justice and security authorities to publicly release documentary evidence surrounding the procurement and assignment of a fleet of vehicles to the Liberia National Police, warning that transparency is essential to protecting the government’s credibility amid allegations linked to Liberia’s ongoing drug investigation.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Senator Konneh, Chairman of the Senate Public Accounts Committee, said authorities should not rely solely on verbal denials to counter allegations made by activist Martin K. N. Kollie concerning the source of vehicles being used by senior security and government officials.

Instead, he called for the publication of the complete “paper trails” showing how the vehicles were procured, paid for, registered and assigned.

The senator made the remarks at the Edward Wilmot Blyden Intellectual Forum, organized by the Press Union of Liberia, where he addressed emerging public financial-management concerns and the broader implications of the country’s escalating drug-trafficking investigation.

Kollie recently alleged that Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman received money from drug cartels and used the funds to procure vehicles for the police, including a vehicle allegedly given to Justice Minister Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh.

The Ministry of Justice has categorically rejected the allegation, describing it as false and unsupported by facts.

According to the ministry, it formally requested a suitable official vehicle for the Justice Minister from the Inspector General of Police on November 10, 2025, because the ministry had no budgetary allocation at the time to purchase a new vehicle.

The ministry said the Liberia National Police subsequently assigned a white Toyota Land Cruiser Prado, identified as GSA-LNP-03-14, from a fleet procured by the Government of Liberia from Dutch Health BV for the police.

The ministry said the broader procurement, valued at approximately US$1.5 million, included pickups, jeeps, motorcycles and ambulances, with ten Toyota Land Cruiser Prado vehicles among the jeeps.

It maintained that the vehicle assigned to Minister Tweh is government property, purchased with government funds and assigned for official use—not a personal gift from the Inspector General, a drug cartel, a private individual or a criminal suspect.

But Senator Konneh said the government could easily settle the controversy by producing the records supporting its explanation.

“The one good solution in this matter is for the task force to publish in one press package” the relevant procurement and financial documents, he said.

He specifically pointed to the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) approval process, General Services Agency (GSA) asset-registration records and Ministry of Finance voucher-payment records as documents that could establish the origin and ownership of the vehicles.

Konneh also referenced Section 40 of Liberia’s Public Financial Management Law, which requires government agencies to submit annual procurement plans and subject procurement activities to the applicable approval process.

As Chairman of the Senate Public Accounts Committee, he said security officials facing allegations should voluntarily make the records available as a means of putting the controversy beyond dispute.

“I encourage our colleagues in the security sector who have been accused to show these documents as a bulletproof,” Konneh said.

The senator emphasized that he was not declaring the allegations against the police or government officials to be true, stressing that the claims “may be false.”

But he warned that in a high-profile drug case, perception itself can undermine the government’s position, particularly when the country is under scrutiny over its handling of allegations of transnational narcotics trafficking.

“In a drug case such as this, perception is dangerous for a successful outcome,” Konneh cautioned.

He said authorities should understand that information appearing in local and social media can eventually become part of the evidentiary trail used by foreign governments and international institutions when assessing cases, sanctions or broader security concerns.

“Most of the evidence comes from the local media and social media that people go there and gather their evidence,” he said.

For Konneh, therefore, dismissing the controversy as a minor social-media dispute could prove costly.

“You may be investigating and thinking that this is a minor issue,” he warned, “but this issue, if we don’t confront it right now and be brave and publish any documents that we have relating to these police vehicles, it will be a problem for us.”

Konneh’s intervention comes as the Liberian government faces mounting scrutiny over the investigation into massive cocaine seizures and allegations of possible links between narcotics networks and individuals within or around the country’s security and political establishment.

The Ministry of Justice has defended its handling of the investigation and said its focus remains on combating illicit drugs and dismantling criminal networks operating in Liberia.

The ministry has also urged the public to exercise caution in treating social-media allegations as established facts, arguing that information from unnamed sources may be incomplete, inaccurate or deliberately misleading.

But Senator Konneh’s position is that documentary transparency can resolve the dispute more effectively than competing public statements.

He said releasing the procurement records would help authorities “bulletproof” their position and demonstrate that public resources, rather than illicit funds, were used to acquire the vehicles.

“We want our government to win this case,” Konneh said.

For the senator, the issue is bigger than the ownership of a single official vehicle. He argues that producing the procurement and financial records now could help protect Liberia’s credibility, strengthen the government’s drug-trafficking case and prevent questions over the vehicles from becoming a vulnerability in future legal or international proceedings

World.title: The Ship We Couldn’t Catch Was Never Just About A Ship
World.content:
Part One of this newspaper’s series on Liberia’s cocaine reckoning was not really a story about a vessel, a stash house, or even a former Vice President. It was a story about how many different ways this country’s institutions found to look away, and how little it has cost anyone, so far, to have looked away.

READ PART ONE OF OUR SERIES, Inside Liberia’s Cocaine Reckoning”, in full and one image outlasts all the others: a Liberian patrol boat, sent to intercept a vessel loitering off the country’s own coast, that simply was not big enough or fast enough to catch it.

THE IB ATLANTIC IV SAT IN LIBERIAN WATERS for the better part of a week before anyone acted decisively, and when the Armed Forces of Liberia finally did, the ship reached open water anyway. Nobody needs a law degree or a finance background to understand what that image means. It means that for one uncomfortable week this summer, a foreign vessel suspected of ferrying narcotics understood the limits of Liberia’s maritime security better than Liberia’s own government seemed to.

That single image would be damning enough on its own.

WHAT PART ONE ACTUALLY documents is that it was never isolated. A letter vouching for that “distressed” ship carried the signature of a senior airport official who kept his job for weeks afterward. A drug enforcement chief recused himself over a vehicle he could not adequately explain, and two months later, Liberians still have no public resolution of that recusal. A police inspector general told this newspaper trafficking had been “sanctioned at very, very senior level” and, months on, has still not named a single person.

A SECURITY OFFICER MOONLIT as a personal driver for the very agency meant to be investigating him. None of these, alone, proves a conspiracy. Together, read the way Part One lays them out, they describe something more damning than a conspiracy: an institutional culture so accustomed to looking away that it took a US$317 million stash house, not the mystery ship, the recusal, or the unnamed claim, to finally force the country to look directly at what had been building under its own roof.

WE DO NOT SAY THIS TO RELITIGATE a single seizure or a single dismissal. We say it because the danger in a story this large is that it gets remembered as a story about individuals — a former Vice President, a fired airport official, a police chief under pressure — when the more urgent lesson sitting underneath Part One is institutional. Liberia did not fail to catch a drug network because its people were unusually careless. It failed because its ports operate without unified command, its maritime patrol vessels cannot outrun the ships they are meant to intercept, its agencies recuse and dismiss without ever quite explaining why, and its most senior investigator can make an explosive public claim without ever being required to finish the sentence.

THOSE ARE NOT THE FAILURES of any one administration. They are structural gaps that will keep producing summers like this one until someone actually closes them.

President Boakai has pledged “no sacred cows,” and this newspaper has taken that pledge seriously enough to hold him to it, arrest by arrest, in the reporting that follows in Part Two. But no sacred cows, applied only to people, will not fix a patrol boat too small to do its job. It will not give the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency a recusal process that actually resolves instead of just pausing.

IT WILL NOT PUT A NAME to the “senior level” Coleman himself raised and then left hanging. The individual prosecutions matter, and Liberians are right to watch them closely. But Part One of this series was, at its core, a portrait of a country that got lucky enough to catch a US$317 million shipment while still operating with the same institutional blind spots that let a suspicious vessel sit off its coast for a week, first. Luck is not a strategy. It is well past time Liberia stopped treating it like one.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court To Decide Fate Of Ex-Speaker Koffa, Others In Capitol Arson Case
World.content:
Court to also rule on FDA officials’ $6M forestry fraud appeal as it clears 55 cases before term’s end. The Supreme Court will this week rule on a bid by former House Speaker J. Fonati Koffa and three sitting lawmakers to overturn a judge’s decision to disband the jury in the Capitol Building arson case, one of 55 judgments the Court is set to deliver as it winds down its term.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — The Supreme Court of Liberia is set to render final judgments this week in several high-profile criminal cases involving past and present government officials, in what promises to be one of the most consequential weeks for the nation’s judiciary this term.

Chief among them is the long-running Capitol Building arson case, in which former House Speaker Cllr. J. Fonati Koffa and Representatives Dixon W. Seboe, Abu B. Kamara, and K. Jacob C. B. Debee stand accused. Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, Sr. is expected to deliver the ruling on Friday, August 28, at 11:00 a.m.

At issue is a petition for a writ of prohibition filed by defense lawyers challenging a decision by Criminal Court “A” Judge Roosevelt Willie to disband the jury panel empaneled to hear the case. The defense argues the move was unlawful and prejudicial to their clients’ constitutional rights, and is asking the Supreme Court to block the case from proceeding under a newly constituted jury.

A Case Nearly Two Years In The Making

The arson case stems from the December 18, 2024, fire that gutted key sections of the Capitol Building, including the joint chambers, the legislative archives, and electoral infrastructure, causing damage estimated at $8.6 million. A Special Grand Jury for Montserrado County later indicted Koffa alongside more than a dozen others, including sitting Representatives Seboe, Kamara, and Debee, as well as several former staffers of the Speaker’s office, on a sweeping list of charges that includes arson, criminal conspiracy, attempted murder, criminal solicitation, facilitation, and the release of destructive forces.

Koffa has consistently denied any wrongdoing, describing the case as a politically motivated attempt to damage his reputation. His attorneys have argued that the state’s case against him rests on circumstantial evidence, including phone recordings and messages allegedly showing that a co-defendant was instructed to report to Koffa’s residence shortly after the fire was set, and that two of his former staffers took part in a chat exchange discussing the incident.

The case has moved through a lengthy and, at times, contentious pretrial process. Koffa and his co-defendants spent time in detention last year over a bond dispute before being released, and the Supreme Court separately heard — and in October reserved a decision on — a defense challenge seeking to exclude key evidence, including an alleged confession and forensic data extracted from mobile phones. Friday’s ruling on the jury dispute will mark the latest, and potentially most consequential, intervention yet by the high court in the case.

FDA Officials Await Ruling On $6M Forestry Fraud Appeal

A day earlier, on Thursday, August 27, at 11:00 a.m., Associate Justice Boakai N. Kanneh will deliver judgment in a separate but equally closely watched appeal brought by former Forestry Development Authority (FDA) Managing Director Moses Wogbeh, former Technical Manager John Kanto, former Commercial Forestry Manager Janger Kamara, former Grand Bassa County Surveyor David Blayee, and former Ministry of Lands, Mines & Energy Director of Cartography Maxwell Gwee.

The five were convicted in 2015 by Criminal Court “C” Judge Peter W. Gbenewelleh on charges of economic sabotage, forgery, criminal conspiracy, and obstruction of government functions, after being found to have defrauded the Liberian government of $6 million through illegal forestry permits. They have since appealed to the Supreme Court, seeking to overturn or modify the lower court’s judgment.

A Term-Ending Docket Of 55 Cases

The two rulings are part of a packed closing docket for the Court. Between Thursday and Friday, the Supreme Court is expected to hand down a total of 55 judgments — 30 on Thursday and 25 on Friday — in cases ranging from murder to ejectment actions and debt disputes, underscoring the scale of the caseload the Court is clearing as it concludes its current judicial term.

World.title: Liberia: Drug Fight Faces Credibility Crisis as Experts Demand Independent Probe; Justice Minister Pushes On
World.content:
Monrovia — Calls for an independent investigation into Liberia’s escalating illicit drug crisis intensified Wednesday as leading experts warned that ongoing investigations could suffer a serious credibility deficit if state institutions and individuals allegedly connected to the drug network are perceived to be investigating themselves.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The call came during the relaunch of the Edward Wilmot Blyden Intellectual Discourse of the Press Union of Liberia (PUL), where veteran journalist Aaron Kollie, Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) Executive Director Anderson Miamen, and Gbarpolu County Senator Amara Konneh urged the government to establish an independent panel to investigate the country’s multimillion-dollar drug-trafficking crisis.

Their position, however, was met with a measured disagreement from Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. Oswald Tweh, who said the government does not oppose an independent panel but insisted that the ongoing investigations and prosecutions must continue.

Justice Minister: ‘We Can’t Abandon the Investigation’

Minister Tweh defended the government’s handling of the investigation, pointing to the involvement of international law-enforcement partners, including the United States Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Homeland Security and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

He said the international partners have had access to evidence and investigative leads and have expressed confidence in Liberia’s ongoing processes.

“Independent investigation, yes, that might come later. But right now, we don’t see it,” Tweh said. “Everything was open to our partners — all the evidence, all the leads — and they applauded us.”

The Justice Minister said the government’s response must go beyond arrests and prosecutions to identifying and correcting institutional weaknesses that allow illicit drugs to enter or move through Liberia.

“If narcotics can move through a chain of handling, screening or transportation, then that chain must be examined and strengthened,” Tweh said.

He argued that authorities must investigate possible facilitation and corruption, strengthen screening and intelligence capabilities, improve coordination among law-enforcement agencies and ensure that criminal networks are dismantled rather than temporarily disrupted.

“Strong institutions are not institutions that claim perfection,” he said. “Strong institutions are institutions that can detect failure, correct it, investigate wrongdoing and continue to improve.”

Konneh: ‘Selective Justice Kills Trust’

Senator Amara Konneh called for an approach that he said would produce a “win-win” outcome for the country, arguing that public confidence depends on the equal application of justice.

“I want to focus on win-win. I really want our country to win. I want everybody to win,” Konneh said.

He warned that selective enforcement could undermine confidence in the justice system.

“Selective justice kills trust. Full, equal justice for everyone builds trust,” he said.

Konneh urged the government to prosecute cases swiftly, proposing a 90-day target for bringing cases to trial where legally and practically possible.

He also called for additional resources to help the Justice Ministry handle what he described as an exceptional national case.

“If you were to, through the President’s request, [seek] special financing to help you prosecute this case quickly, you will have the full support of the Legislature,” he said.

Konneh also focused on the need to restore public confidence in Liberia’s security institutions.

“A swift public trial clears innocent officers and permanently removes compromised ones,” he said. “It tells the honest police officers the system will protect you.”

He urged authorities to make investigators more credible than those they are investigating.

“Make the investigators more credible than the suspect,” Konneh said.

Bar Association Calls for Stronger Institutions

Cllr. Juah Lawson, President of the Liberia National Bar Association, said Liberia’s response to drug trafficking must be firm, coordinated, evidence-based, sustained and grounded in the law.

She called for the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, Liberia National Police, Ministry of Justice, Financial Intelligence Agency, Customs and Immigration authorities, as well as the Judiciary, to be adequately resourced and professionally staffed.

She also emphasized institutional independence and coordination.

“Drug trafficking thrives where institutions are weak, investigations are compromised, borders are porous, evidence disappears, prosecution fail, and criminal networks are able to purchase influence,” Lawson said.

She argued that strengthening Liberia’s anti-narcotics response requires more than arrests, saying the institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting drug crimes must themselves be capable of resisting corruption and political interference.

CENTAL Wants LDEA Recruitment Reformed

Anderson Miamen of CENTAL said Liberia must move beyond providing security institutions with vehicles and other logistical support and undertake deeper institutional reforms.

He called for additional resources, technology and logistics for security agencies while urging greater transparency and public participation in institutional reforms.

“The process has to open up,” Miamen said.

He called for reforms to the law establishing the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, particularly provisions governing the recruitment and selection of personnel.

Miamen said recruitment into the agency should be transparent, inclusive and participatory, with independent oversight similar to approaches used for other integrity-focused institutions.

He argued that strengthening the drug enforcement agency must include vetting personnel to ensure that individuals entrusted with fighting narcotics trafficking are themselves properly screened.

Journalist Calls for Rehabilitation Center

Veteran journalist Aaron Kollie warned that Liberia’s fight against illicit drugs must address the social consequences of addiction, particularly among young people.

“You can construct all the roads, all the market buildings, and all the political projects,” Kollie said. “If you do not address the fundamental problem and the root cause of the drugs problem affecting the foundation of our country, the young people, it will all be meaningless.”

Kollie called for serious consideration of the construction or rehabilitation of a national drug rehabilitation center.

He also urged the government to properly resource the LDEA and other institutions involved in the fight against drugs while strengthening the vetting of personnel.

He said security officials must be adequately supported and incentivized to prevent corruption and protect Liberia’s national and international reputation.

PUL Relaunches Blyden Intellectual Forum

The discussions formed part of the formal relaunch of the Edward Wilmot Blyden Intellectual Discourse, the flagship intellectual forum of the Press Union of Liberia.

The forum was relaunched by former PUL President Gabriel Williams, who called for a collective national response to Liberia’s growing illicit drug problem.

PUL President Julius Kanubah commended the panelists for what he described as expert and factual contributions to the national debate.

Kanubah said the discussion would help deepen public understanding while advancing transparency, accountability and institutional reform in Liberia’s campaign against illicit drugs.

The debate comes amid heightened public scrutiny of Liberia’s handling of major cocaine seizures, arrests of prominent individuals and allegations of possible links between drug trafficking networks and elements within or around state institutions.

While government officials maintain that the ongoing investigations are being conducted professionally with the support of international partners, calls for an independent mechanism to examine the broader drug-trafficking crisis are gaining momentum.

The central question emerging from Wednesday’s forum is whether Liberia can simultaneously pursue criminal prosecutions and establish an independent process capable of examining the institutional failures, corruption allegations and possible official complicity that may have allowed the drug trade to flourish.

World.title: ‘A Dream Team’: Liberian Delegation in Rwanda, South Africa to Study Memorials For Proposed Peace Museum
World.content:
Monrovia – Liberians are celebrating this week as a high-powered government delegation arrives in Rwanda and South Africa.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The mission is to gather lessons for a proposed national museum aimed at transforming the country’s civil war legacy into a monument of peace and unity.

The mission, backed by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, seeks a “world-class blueprint” for the planned Liberia Peace, Reconciliation, and Memorial Museum. If constructed, the project will elevate Liberian heritage, arts, and culture while serving as a tool for conflict prevention and national healing.

“This is not just about erecting a building,” said Liberia’s Arts and Culture Ambassador Kekura M. Kamara, alias Malawala Balawala.

“Culture is not merely the clothes we wear, the songs we sing, or the drums we beat. It is our identity. A nation that respects its culture will never lose its soul. When we tell our story through music, art, and film, we celebrate who we are and invite the world to know us better,”Kamara furthers.

A ‘Dream Team’ On the Ground

Led by Minister of State without Portfolio Hadja Mamaka Bility, the delegation includes Assistant Minister Varfin Vamuen Donzo, Peace and Security Advisor Emmanuel Bawoh, Audio/Visual Supervisor Varney Shakeh Kamara, and Arts and Culture Ambassador Kamara.

They are joined by key development partners including UNDP Liberia Resident Representative Ambassador Aliou Mamadou Dia and UNDP Governance Team Lead Stanley Kamara.

Learning from Rwanda and South Africa

With support from UNDP, the team is touring sites that have turned painful histories into platforms for reconciliation.

In Rwanda, the delegation is visiting the Kigali Genocide Memorial to study how the country converted national memory into community reconciliation and atrocity prevention programs.

In South Africa, the team will tour Freedom Park, Constitution Hill, the Apartheid Museum, and Robben Island to learn how oral histories were preserved and how educational programs were built in the post-apartheid era.

A major focus of the trip is also digital preservation.

The team is also gathering modern strategies to digitize Liberia’s stories, community narratives, and historical records before they are lost to time.

Why the Excitement

The proposed museum will be integrated with the National Museum of Liberia and designed as a living institution for research, digital innovation, and historical education, according to the delegation.

For many citizens across Bomi, Monrovia, and beyond, the mission represents long-awaited recognition of Liberia’s music, storytelling, arts, and traditional history.

“By investing in this mission, the government isn’t just preserving memory,” the statement indicates.

“It is investing in conflict prevention, national pride, and a dynamic cultural renaissance that proves Liberia is indeed rich beyond measure.”

Meanwhile, no timeline has yet been announced for construction of the museum.

World.title: Justice Minister Tweh: Liberia Will Not Surrender to Drug Traffickers
World.content:
MONROVIA— Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh has vowed that the Government of Liberia will intensify its fight against drug trafficking, warning that criminal networks seeking to profit from narcotics will not defeat the Liberian State.

By J.H. Webster [email protected]

Speaking Wednesday, August 26 at the re launch of the Edward Wilmot Blyden Intellectual Discourse at the Press Union of Liberia (PUL) Headquarters in Sinkor, Monrovia, Minister Tweh said Liberia’s response to drug trafficking must be anchored in strong institutions, accountability, credible evidence and respect for the rule of law.

The discourse was held under the theme: “Confronting Drug Trafficking: Strengthening Institutions, Advancing Accountability and Safeguarding the Rule of Law.”

Minister Tweh commended the PUL for reviving the intellectual discourse and said the choice of Edward Wilmot Blyden’s name was particularly appropriate because of Blyden’s contributions to Liberia’s intellectual, political and institutional development.

He described Blyden as a scholar, Pan-Africanist, diplomat, educator, journalist and public servant who used scholarship, public service and the press to challenge systems that sought to undermine the dignity and independence of African people.

According to Minister Tweh, the fight against drugs is similarly a fight for Liberia’s freedom and future because narcotics destroy young lives, weaken families, corrupt institutions and finance criminal networks.

“A country that allows drugs and drug money to capture its communities and institutions cannot claim to be fully free,” he said.

The Justice Minister also praised the Liberian media for reporting drug seizures, raising public concerns and sustaining national discussions about the country’s growing narcotics problem.

He stressed, however, that journalism must be accompanied by responsibility, noting that information should enlighten rather than inflame public sentiment.

Minister Tweh said journalists have the right and duty to ask difficult questions, while government has a corresponding responsibility to provide honest answers and accept public scrutiny.

Gov’t Highlights Major Drug Seizures

The Justice Minister cited several major drug enforcement operations as evidence of the government’s ongoing efforts to combat narcotics trafficking. He said the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) seized more than 400 kilograms of illegal narcotics and arrested over 200 suspects during the first quarter of 2026.

He further disclosed that approximately 237 kilograms of cocaine were intercepted at Roberts International Airport in June, followed by the discovery of nearly four tons of cocaine in Duazon.

According to him, the Duazon seizure represented the largest narcotics seizure in Liberia’s history. He noted that more than US$336 million worth of the seized cocaine was destroyed in Margibi County at the end of July in full public view.

“These are not slogans. These are concrete actions,” Minister Tweh declared.

He attributed the operations to coordinated efforts involving the LDEA, Liberia National Police, Ministry of Justice prosecutors, investigators, security personnel and other national security institutions.

Minister Tweh said the government has drawn a clear line between the Liberian State and drug cartels, insisting that there will be “no accommodation with criminality.”

“Drug traffickers may challenge the authority of the State, but they will not defeat it. The Republic of Liberia will prevail, not through vengeance or political persecution, but through strong institutions, credible evidence, due process, and the unwavering enforcement of the law,” he intimated.

‘No One Will Be Protected’

The Justice Minister stressed that the government’s responsibility extends beyond the seizure of narcotics and arrest of suspected couriers and low-level dealers.

He said investigations must identify the financiers, facilitators and other powerful actors who enable drug trafficking networks to operate.

“If the evidence leads to a customs officer, a security officer, a businessman, a politician or any other person, the law must be allowed to take its course,” Minister Tweh said.

He assured that no individual would be protected because of influence, friendship, wealth or political connections.

At the same time, Minister Tweh cautioned against convicting individuals in the court of public opinion based solely on allegations circulating on radio, social media or political platforms.

“The Government will not fight lawlessness by abandoning the law. Our cases must be built on evidence, tested in court and determined through due process,” he emphasized.

Rejects Political Criticism

Minister Tweh also criticized what he described as attempts by some critics to view every government action through a political lens.

He argued that while the government welcomes criticism, criticism should not become an unwillingness to acknowledge concrete progress.

He maintained that Liberia’s drug problem did not begin with the current administration and would not disappear overnight, but said the historical record would show whether the government confronted the crisis or ignored it.

According to him, the recent seizures, arrests, investigations and coordinated law enforcement operations demonstrate that the government is taking action.

However, the Justice Minister acknowledged that major drug seizures also expose vulnerabilities within Liberia’s institutions.

He pointed out that the government must investigate how narcotics move through handling, screening and transportation processes and identify possible cases of corruption or facilitation.

He called for stronger screening systems, improved intelligence gathering, enhanced coordination among law enforcement agencies and investigations aimed at dismantling criminal networks rather than merely interrupting their operations.

‘Rule of Law Cuts in Every Direction’

The Justice Minister emphasized that the rule of law must protect both the authority of the State and the rights of individuals accused of wrongdoing.

“The rule of law cuts in every direction,” he averred, explaining that it gives the State the authority to investigate and prosecute while protecting accused persons from arbitrary action.

He indicated that the same principle protects journalists who question government and citizens who demand accountability.

“If we weaken due process in the name of fighting drugs, we weaken the very Republic we claim to defend,” Minister Tweh warned.

He said Liberia’s response must therefore be effective, lawful, fair and unwavering.

Reflecting on Blyden’s legacy, Minister Tweh noted that nations are not strengthened by rhetoric alone but through courageous citizens who build institutions, discipline public power, educate the public and protect the country’s future.

He identified drug trafficking, corruption, institutional weakness, indifference and deliberate distortion of facts as threats to Liberia’s future.

Minister Tweh concluded by reaffirming the government’s commitment to confronting drug trafficking and strengthening Liberia’s justice and law enforcement institutions.

“We did not choose this threat. But we must choose our response,” he said.

“Liberia will confront drug trafficking, strengthen its institutions, advance accountability and safeguard the rule of law,” he added.

World.title: Ex-PUL President Coffey Urges Calm, Patriotism and Respect For Rule of Law In Drug Prosecution
World.content:
EX-PUL President Charles B. Coffey Jr.

MONROVIA – Former President of the Press Union of Liberia, Charles B. Coffey Jr., has called on Liberians, including political institutions and actors expressing divergent views on the Government’s fight against harmful drugs and the prosecution of alleged drug traffickers to remain peaceful, patriotic and respectful of the rule of law.

By Augustus D.R [email protected]

Coffey said the ongoing national campaign against harmful drugs is a matter of serious national concern that requires collective responsibility, unity and support for lawful institutions rather than political confrontation, public pressure or prejudgment of cases before the courts.

He urged all parties with differing opinions on drug-related prosecutions to allow the courts and other competent institutions of the justice system to perform their constitutional responsibilities without interference.

“We must allow the rule of law to prevail. Allegations of criminal conduct must be determined through due process, and no individual should be convicted in the court of public opinion before the competent court has spoken,” Coffey emphasized.

The former media leader, who is currently studying law at the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law, University of Liberia, expressed optimism that justice will ultimately be served through the established legal process.

He described Liberia’s judicial system as an important pillar of the Republic and expressed confidence in the ability of the courts to administer justice impartially and independently.

According to Coffey, Liberia’s constitutional and judicial framework places a compelling responsibility on judges, lawyers and other legal practitioners to uphold the principles of fairness, impartiality, professional integrity and ethical conduct in the administration of justice.

He stressed that the 1986 Constitution of Liberia provides fundamental safeguards for due process and the protection of individual rights, making it imperative for legal practitioners and judicial actors to conduct themselves in accordance with constitutional principles and established ethical standards.

Coffey further cautioned against attempts by political actors, commentators or other influential individuals to undermine public confidence in the judiciary through inflammatory statements or premature conclusions concerning matters pending before the courts.

He stated that disagreements over government policy or criminal prosecutions are legitimate in a democratic society, but such disagreements must be expressed peacefully and within the bounds of law.

“Patriotism does not mean that we must all hold the same opinion. It means that, even when we disagree, we must protect the peace, respect our institutions and allow the law to take its course,” he pointed out.

He, therefore, encouraged Liberians to support legitimate efforts by the Government and security institutions to combat the harmful drugs crisis while simultaneously respecting the constitutional rights of persons accused of drug-related offenses.

Coffey maintained that the fight against harmful drugs should not become a source of political division, but rather a national cause requiring cooperation among the Government, political institutions, civil society, the media, religious leaders, traditional authorities and ordinary citizens.

He concluded by urging all Liberians to remain calm and allow the courts to independently determine the facts and law in cases before them, stressing that justice is best served when the rule of law, rather than public pressure, determines the outcome of criminal proceedings.

World.title: Mo Ibrahim Warns Hichilema Against Wasting Zambia’s Democratic Legacy
World.content:
Mo Ibrahim, the Sudanese-British telecoms billionaire and founder of the Mo Ibrahim Foundation, has issued a public statement expressing deep concern over developments in Zambia following the general election, warning President Hakainde Hichilema against squandering the progress made during his first term in office. The statement, dated 26 August, was published on the foundation’s website.

“Mr President, your first mandate was defined by progress. Do not waste what you have achieved,” it reads.

Ibrahim said his foundation was watching post-election developments in Zambia closely, arguing that elections test democracy well beyond what happens at the ballot box. He pointed to the arbitrary arrest of opposition members, the killing of a former minister, and the suspension of vote counting as developments he said should never occur in a genuine democracy.

“The arbitrary arrest of opposition members; the killing of a former minister; and the suspension of vote counting: these should never happen in a true democracy,” he said.

He also raised the closure of Zambia’s top courts, including the Constitutional Court, ahead of the deadline for challenging the election result, describing it as adding to the country’s difficulties. Ibrahim said Zambia had built a reputation over decades for competitive elections, peaceful transfers of power and respect for constitutional processes, a legacy he said had been held up internationally as a model for other nations to follow.

“Mr President: Your own legacy could be just as strong,” he said, adding that no legacy could be taken for granted and must be protected and strengthened from one mandate to the next.

Ibrahim closed with a direct warning to the Head of State.

“It would be a waste and a shame for it all to crumble now,” he said.

There was no immediate response from State House or the Zambian government to the foundation’s remarks. Ibrahim’s organisation is known across the continent for its annual index measuring governance quality in African states and for a leadership prize awarded to democratically elected leaders who transfer power at the end of their term, giving the intervention added diplomatic weight.

The statement adds an international voice to the domestic dispute over the vote, which has centred on the constitutional petition window, the closure of the courts, and the death of former MP Mutotwe Kafwaya. Civil society groups in Zambia have separately raised concerns over the handling of the vote count and the timing of the court closures relative to the petition deadline, and Ibrahim’s statement is among the most prominent international responses to the post-election dispute to date.
