World.title: BEL explains why Belize went dark Tuesday night
World.content:
BEL explains why Belize went dark Tuesday night

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Electricity Limited says an unplanned system collapse caused Tuesday night’s countrywide power outage.

According to BEL, the collapse occurred at 7:28pm following a temporary loss of power from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad, due to issues on the Mexican power system.

At the time, available in country generation stood at approximately 103 megawatts while evening peak demand reached 122 megawatts, leaving a shortage of about 19 megawatts.

The sudden loss of a significant portion of supply activated BEL’s grid protection system, which shed load across various parts of the national grid to restore balance. That produced outages in several service areas countrywide until CFE supply was restored at 10:54pm.

BEL says in country generation remains constrained. Certain renewable sources are unavailable due to seasonal conditions, some generating units are out of service for maintenance, and others are operating at reduced capacity.

The company says teams continue to monitor generation and grid conditions.

Updates will be shared through the BEL 24-7 app. Customers can call toll free at 0-800-235-2273.

World.title: UDP Leader Tracy Panton downplays high profile resignations, says Thimbriel and Wallace remain part of rebuilding effort
World.content:
UDP Leader Tracy Panton downplays high profile resignations, says Thimbriel and Wallace remain part of rebuilding effort

By Breaking Belize News Staff: UDP Leader Tracy Taegar-Panton says the recent resignations of Juliet Thimbriel and Audrey Wallace from senior party positions should not be interpreted as a split within the Opposition.

Panton confirmed Wednesday that Thimbriel stepped aside as National Campaign Manager while Wallace relinquished her role as chair of the UDP’s Public Relations Committee. She said both cited personal and professional reasons that prevented them from continuing in those substantive positions.

Panton stressed, however, that both women remain members of the UDP and continue working closely with the leadership team. She specifically said Thimbriel continues investigative and political work through Wave Radio and Television.

7News reported Tuesday that Thimbriel and Wallace had resigned within roughly two weeks of each other ahead of the March 2027 municipal elections. The report cited sources suggesting candidate-vetting disagreements in Thimbriel’s case and party advertising finances in Wallace’s case. Those accounts were not confirmed by Panton, who attributed the departures to personal and professional circumstances. (7 News Belize)

Asked whether the party has sufficient financing for municipal campaigns, Panton dismissed continuing speculation about the UDP’s finances and insisted the party would field slates and compete in the March 2027 elections.

World.title: Archaeologists uncover classrooms for young Maya boys at Xunantunich
World.content:
Archaeologists uncover classrooms for young Maya boys at Xunantunich

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Archaeologists working at Xunantunich have identified what they believe was a school for young Maya boys in the late seventh and eighth centuries.

The complex, excavated on a ridge above the Mopan River, includes student housing with a large sweat bath, gaming boards, and rooms with benches for sitting or sleeping.

Inside El Castillo, the site’s central pyramid, researchers found two rooms whose walls contain around 400 drawings. These include a headdress wearing sage, calendar dates, hieroglyphs, and multiple monkeys sketched by different hands.

The skill levels vary widely. One monkey is expertly rendered. Others are clearly the work of beginners.

“We have lots of images that look like someone just learning to draw,” said archaeologist Kathryn Brown of the University of Texas at San Antonio. “It’s almost as if somebody was saying, OK, this is how you draw a monkey. Now you try, you try, you try.”

Before this discovery, archaeologists had little evidence of where and how Maya children were educated.

The work was carried out by Brown alongside Jason Yaeger, Lauren Nowakowski and Whitney Lytle.

World.title: Di same knife weh stick goat stick sheep, the proverb Belize keeps forgetting
World.content:
Di same knife weh stick goat stick sheep, the proverb Belize keeps forgetting

By Horace Palacio:

Our grandmothers kept a proverb sharp enough to draw blood.

Di same knife weh stick goat, stick sheep.

Say it slowly and picture the butcher’s yard. The goat goes first, and nobody mourns the goat. The goat was trouble. He climbed the fence, ate the garden, butted the children. When the knife came for him, the yard nodded. He had it coming.

But watch what happens next, because this is the whole proverb. The knife does not retire after the goat. The knife gets wiped, sharpened, and returned to the shelf. And the knife has no memory, no loyalty, and no conscience. The next time it comes down from that shelf, it does not check the species of the neck beneath it. The gentle sheep, the favored one, the innocent one, bleeds on the same blade, in the same yard, held by the same hand or the next hand after it.

Our grandmothers were not teaching butchery. They were teaching politics, and power, and the most expensive mistake a citizen can make. Today, let me make the full case for their wisdom, because Belize is a yard full of knives right now, and too many of us are cheering them because of who they are pointed at.

Here is the principle in one sentence. Never judge a power by its first target. Judge it by its permanence.

Because targets change and tools remain. Intentions die with the men who held them, but instruments get inherited. Every dangerous power in history was introduced the same way, aimed at a goat nobody would defend. That is the sales technique. Pick a first victim the crowd dislikes, and the crowd will approve the blade itself. Then wait. The blade always finds new necks.

History signs this proverb in blood. In revolutionary France, Robespierre fed his enemies to the guillotine and the crowds roared, until the morning in 1794 when the cart came for Robespierre himself, and the machine he had sharpened took his own head without a flicker of gratitude. And readers of this column will remember our Sunday on the Council of Nicaea, where an emperor’s power of exile was first used to banish the loser of a church dispute, and everyone approved. Within years, that same instrument banished Athanasius, the winner’s own champion, five separate times as the winds shifted. The knife that stuck Arius stuck Athanasius. It always does.

Now walk our own Belizean yard with me, and count the blades.

Start with one this column dissected months ago, the CEO system. In 2000, one party forged a knife that let the government of the day install its loyalists atop every ministry. Its makers surely imagined it serving their good intentions forever. Then 2008 came, the other party won, and picked up the exact same knife with delight. Twelve years later it changed hands again. Three governments, one blade, and the same victim every single time, the professional public service of Belize. Both tribes cheered when their hand held the handle. Both tribes bled when it passed. Di same knife.

Look at the calls, every time crime surges, for detention without trial, for the strongman’s methods, aimed at the gang boys today. I asked the question once and I ask it again. That knife, once forged, sits on the shelf for whoever wins the next election. Would you trust it in the hands of the party you despise, pointed at a son you love? Because that is precisely where inherited knives end up.

Look at the proposed broadcasting licence for online voices. Some Belizeans quietly cheer it, imagining it muzzling the pages they hate. Understand what you are cheering. A licence that can be denied can be dangled, and the clause does not know your politics. The government that can silence the commentator you despise holds the identical power over the one you trust. You are not approving a target. You are approving a blade.

Look at the whistleblower question. If the officers who leaked the SmartStream records are hunted for embarrassing this administration, the precedent does not expire with this administration. It waits, oiled and ready, for the honest officer who will one day try to expose the next government, perhaps one you oppose with all your heart. Hunt today’s truth-tellers and you have pre-silenced tomorrow’s.

And look at the smallest knife of all, the one in our own hands, the mob. When the pile-on forms against someone you dislike, and you add your stone because this goat deserves it, remember that a mob is a knife with no owner at all. It does not disband after your enemy. It scrolls onward, hungry, and one day it finds a name you love. Perhaps yours.

Why do we keep falling for it? Because tribalism blinds us to tools. We see only targets. Red cheers the knife in red’s hand, blue cheers it in blue’s, and the knife, patient beyond both, simply waits its turn to be inherited. The goat always deserves it. That is what makes the goat useful to the people selling the knife.

So here is the test I ask every Belizean to carry from today, and it takes ten seconds. Before you cheer any new power, any law, any precedent, any crackdown, any mob, perform the knife test. Place the instrument, in your imagination, into the hands of the person or party you most distrust in this world, and aim it at someone you love. If it frightens you then, oppose it now, while it is still pointed at the goat. Because the only moment a knife can be stopped is before it becomes tradition.

Let me be fair before I close, because this is not an argument against all knives. A nation needs blades. Laws, police, courts, these are edged tools, and a country without them is eaten alive. The question is never whether knives exist. It is how they are kept. A good law is a knife in a locked case, with a judge holding the key, due process guarding the lid, and daylight shining on every use. A bad law is a knife left loose on the kitchen table of whoever wins the next election. Everything this column demands, the courts, the transparency, the entrenchment, the oversight, is really just one demand. Lock the cases.

The goat and the sheep in Belize are not strangers, my friends. They are neighbors. They wear red and blue. They swap places every five years. Today’s cheering crowd is tomorrow’s trembling flock, in the same yard, under the same shelf.

Our grandmothers knew it and folded it into seven words of Kriol so we could never claim we were not warned.

Di same knife weh stick goat, stick sheep.

Protect the goat you despise, Belize. His neck and yours share a yard.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: UDP raises alarm over possible changes to public officers’ retirement age and pensions
World.content:
UDP raises alarm over possible changes to public officers’ retirement age and pensions

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The United Democratic Party is urging public officers to closely monitor discussions surrounding pension reform amid suggestions that the retirement age could eventually be increased and pension benefits adjusted.

During Wednesday’s press conference, UDP Chairman Senator Sheena Pitts said she had heard discussion of increasing the public service retirement age from 55 to 60 as part of efforts to control Government’s wage and pension bill. Pitts also warned of the possibility that future reforms could reduce the proportion of salary paid as a Government pension.

The comments were framed as a warning about proposals being considered rather than an announcement of an approved Government policy. No formal Cabinet decision implementing the specific changes outlined by Pitts was identified in current public reporting.

The issue nevertheless has a substantial policy history. Belize’s Government pension scheme generally has a normal retirement age of 55, creating a gap before Social Security retirement benefits become available from age 60. The Social Security Board’s latest actuarial review has recommended that Government increase its normal retirement age for new hires to 65, while earlier IMF analysis also examined raising the retirement age and reducing future pension replacement rates as possible long-term reforms.

Government’s 2026/27 budget also identifies pension sustainability and management of the public-sector wage bill as areas requiring reform.

World.title: Unhealthy trend: Student obesity surges to 15.3%
World.content:
The Global School-based Health Survey confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight. (Photo: Adobe stock)

MORE than three in every 10 students captured in a recent survey by the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) were overweight while 15.3 per cent of them were obese.

The Global School-based Health Survey (GSHS), which was conducted between January and March this year, had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools.

It confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight, while underweight remains a concern.

According to the survey, obesity moved from six per cent in 2010 to 15.3 per cent in 2026, while the number of overweight students jumped from 21.7 per cent in 2010 to 31.7 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, there was an uptick in underweight students, from 2.1 per cent in 2010 to 3.4 per cent in 2026.

The survey also found a dip in physical activity from 23.2 per cent in 2017 to 19.6 per cent in 2026, while 70.2 per cent reported less than eight hours of sleep, which can be attributed to the long hours students spend on the Internet as sedentary behaviour — sitting down for more than three hours per day increased from 56.4 per cent in 2017 to 68 per cent in 2026.

“Students [who are] less active, more sedentary, and many not getting enough sleep means that there is an increased risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems,” said the NCDA.

It called for more physical activity, greater promotion of recreation and sports, and encouragement for students to adopt healthy sleep habits.

The NCDA blamed unhealthy eating patterns for the rise in obesity among students, and recommended the promotion of healthy school food environment, expansion of nutrition education, and promotion of balanced diets.

But despite the increase in obesity and overweight, the survey found that in the 30 days before it was conducted there was a drop in consumption of one or more sodas per day by students.

In 2010 the NCDA found that 72.5 per cent on the respondents had consumed one or more sodas in the 30 days before the survey, while this year only 49.7 per cent of the respondents said they had done so in the past seven days.

The survey said underweight was highest among grade nine boys, 6.4 per cent, and grade 11 girls, 4.8 per cent.

Meanwhile, the highest rate of obesity was among grade seven girls, 43.2 per cent, and grade seven boys, 40.5 per cent.

The Global School-based Health Survey, noted the NCDA, provides high-quality data to inform decision-making and action for school and youth health.

In his reaction to the survey findings, Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton urged parents and guardians to ensure their children eat healthy foods at home and school.

He said it is always a better choice to take a meal from home to school if the school does not have facilities for the preparation of hot meals.

Tufton also urged parents and guardians to encourage their children to participate in more physical activities if they want to ensure that they do not fall victim to diabetes, heart disease, and other non-communicable diseases.

“Parents and guardians must insist that their children become more health conscious. Fast food and sugary beverages are not healthy, and I want to remind you parents that, should these young ones get diagnosed with a non-communicable disease, it will follow them into adulthood and put more stress on your resources as well as the health system,” said Tufton.

The NCDA said the survey has shown that healthy eating, regular physical activities, and adequate sleep are essential for the well-being, learning, and long-term health of Jamaica’s children and adolescents.

It added that the lack of physical activity increases the risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID); and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: A different route for boys
World.content:
In this video grab Seargeant Kevin Wallace, dean of discipline and drill instructor at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Cadet Academy, inspects trainees during muster.Video: Jamaica Constabulary Force

As Jamaica continues to grapple with the persistent underperformance of boys in school, the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) is offering an alternative path that combines academics, discipline, and mentorship to help young men find their footing.

The JCF Cadet Academy, established in September 2021, was born out of the police force’s experience working with young people through its Safe Schools Programme and other youth initiatives where cops observed particular challenges among boys, including truancy.

Speaking on the JCF’s Force4Good podcast, principal of the academy Deputy Superintendent of Police Tanecia Johnson said the force recognised the need for a setting where it could provide more focused support to young men.

“When those reports come in, it’s always about the boys outnumbering the girls in terms of truancy and so on, and so as a force… we decided that something must be done in terms of having a better structure to have these boys in an area where we can have that direct concentration,” she said.

The academy now combines traditional schooling with a highly structured boarding environment, with police, trained teachers, guidance counsellors, and other staff working closely with the students.

Johnson said the academy’s approach is based on more than discipline, with staff seeking to understand the circumstances affecting each student and build relationships that encourage them to open up.

“Oftentimes in the schools the students will tell us as the police, as their mentors, as their motivators, things that they will not tell a school principal, things that they will not tell their parents,” she revealed.

Those conversations, Johnson said, allow the academy to address issues such as anger, identity, purpose, attitude and a student’s plans for the future.

The approach is producing encouraging academic results.

This year’s Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) performance included a 100 per cent pass rate in information technology and physical education and sports, while human and social biology recorded 98 per cent, English A 92 per cent, and office administration 90 per cent. Mathematics recorded a 75 per cent pass rate.

At the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) level, communication studies recorded an 88 per cent pass rate, information technology 93 per cent, law – unit one 84 per cent, and law – unit two 75 per cent. Johnson said the results represent the academy’s best academic performance since it was established.

For Johnson, however, the results are only part of what the academy is trying to achieve.

She recalled the experience of a 17-year-old student who arrived after struggling to gain CSEC passes. When staff spoke with him about his experience they discovered that his academic difficulties did not necessarily reflect his ability.

“Sometimes all it takes is a change of environment for these youngsters, and at the Cadet Academy we’re thriving because, first and foremost, we have educators, we have our teachers, but love is central to what we do,” she said.

Johnson said that philosophy extends to how students are treated when they make mistakes. Rather than focusing on punishment, staff speak of corrective measures and ensure students have immediate access to adults when problems arise.

According to Johnson, the academy normally takes about 80 students in an intake and has approximately 10 resident facilitators and 15 external teachers, in addition to administrators, guidance counsellors, and access to the JCF’s medical services. It currently offers seven CSEC and four CAPE subjects.

The academy also serves as a potential pathway into the JCF, although Johnson stressed that becoming a cop is not compulsory and admission to the academy does not guarantee recruitment.

Students who want to join the force must still meet the requirements, sit the JCF entrance examination, and undergo further background checks.

Of the 35 students who graduated on June 25 this year, 34 were awaiting the next intake to join the JCF, while one planned to attend university first.

Johnson said that, overall, 99.9 per cent of students who choose to pursue policing after completing the programme progress towards the JCF, with more than 175 former cadets now serving in the organisation.

But the academy’s purpose is not simply to produce police personnel.

Johnson said students are encouraged to pursue tertiary education or other careers if that is the path they choose, while the JCF hopes the education and personal development they receive will prepare them for life beyond the academy.

The academy’s model comes against a separate national conversation about the performance of boys in Jamaica’s education system, where they continue to face challenges in areas such as engagement, attendance, and academic achievement.

That wider concern provides an important backdrop to the academy’s results, but Johnson said the programme itself grew from the JCF’s direct experience with young people and its decision to create a more concentrated intervention.

World.title: Kabaka Pyramid’s Rebel Music gets new life
World.content:
Kabaka Pyramid .

Fifteen years can change a lot in music. Trends come and go, audiences shift, and artistes inevitably evolve. But for Kabaka Pyramid, the years since his breakthrough Rebel Music EP have not meant abandoning the foundation on which his career was built. Instead, the Grammy Award-winning reggae artiste is returning to it.

On August 28, Kabaka will release Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape, a 10-track project marking the 15th anniversary of the EP that helped introduce him to a wider audience and establish his reputation as one of Jamaica’s more lyrically conscious voices.

But the project is less about recreating 2011 and more about examining what has endured since then. Since his breakout year in music, he has moved from emerging artiste to international stages and even Grammy success with The Kalling.

Through it all, his ability to move between reggae, dancehall, and hip hop while maintaining an unmistakably Jamaican perspective has remained a defining feature of his music.

That musical identity is again at the centre of Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape. Three songs already released from the project — Rotation, From Weh Day and We Dem Wah — offer a glimpse into the different influences that have shaped the artiste.

“There is so much going on in the world, and I really believe if we played more reggae we would be better off,” Kabaka Pyramid said. “Reggae has a healing nature. The music has always been able to uplift people, bring people together and give us something positive to hold on to.”

With that said, he is encouraging DJs, selectors, and veteran artistes to invest in younger talent, a plight that makes the anniversary project about more than Kabaka’s own journey.

Fifteen years after Rebel Music helped him find his audience, he is using that milestone to question whether emerging reggae acts are being given similar opportunities to find theirs.

Across its 10 tracks, the project moves through cultural commentary, reflection, reggae consciousness, dancehall energy, and lyrical competition. In doing so it connects the artiste he was becoming 15 years ago with the one he is today.

For an artiste, longevity is not simply measured by how long one manages to remain visible. Sometimes it is also measured by whether the things that mattered at the beginning still matter after the success arrives. Fifteen years later, Kabaka Pyramid appears to be making his answer clear: The music may evolve, but the foundation remains.

Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape will be available on all major digital streaming platforms.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: HARD ROCK CLEARS CABINET HURDLE
World.content:
Hard Rock International has received Cabinet approval for a proposed integrated resort development in Montego Bay, but separate regulatory approval is required before casino gaming can begin..

HARD ROCK International has received Cabinet approval for a proposed integrated resort development in Montego Bay, clearing a key government hurdle for a planned hotel and casino within a wider three-phase development, with projected investment of US$756.9 million.

The approval was disclosed to the Jamaica Observer last Monday by a person familiar with the process who asked not to be identified because the decision had not yet been publicly announced.

Hard Rock subsequently confirmed the approval in written responses to Business Observer queries.

“Hard Rock International is pleased to confirm that we have been granted a provisional casino licence for an integrated resort in Montego Bay,” the company said on Friday.

“We are honoured by this opportunity and look forward to bringing our distinctive blend of world-class hospitality, entertainment, and exceptional guest experiences to Jamaica.”

Hard Rock did not identify the government authority that issued the approval, the legal entity that received it, or any conditions attached.

The approval moves the project forward but it does not by itself permit Hard Rock or an affiliated company to operate a casino in Jamaica.

Casino Gaming Commission Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen, responding to questions from the Business Observer, said Jamaica’s regulatory framework requires separate approvals for an integrated resort development and the operation of a casino.

At the first stage, a developer must secure approval from the minister responsible for finance through an Approved Integrated Resort Development (AIRD) Order under Section 9 of the Casino Gaming Act.

“The making of an AIRD Order does not, by itself, authorise casino gaming,” Allen said. “Rather, it establishes the developer’s eligibility to proceed to the second stage by applying to the Casino Gaming Commission for a casino gaming licence.”

Allen did not say whether an AIRD Order has been formally issued for the Hard Rock development or whether Hard Rock or an affiliated Jamaican company has applied to the commission for a casino gaming licence.

Jamaica allows casinos only as part of larger tourism developments offering hotel accommodation, entertainment, sporting facilities, and other visitor services.

Government filings place the proposed Hard Rock hotel and casino within a three-phase development on the same property in Montego Bay.

A table prepared by Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro), and included in the Government of Jamaica’s annual report for the 2025/26 financial year, identifies UNICO Resort as the first phase of the Hard Rock Hotel development.

The 451-room UNICO is under construction. Work began in October 2023 and completion is expected by the end of 2026, according to the report. Jampro placed the projected capital expenditure at US$250.2 million and estimated that the development would generate 1,000 temporary and 1,000 permanent jobs.

The second phase, identified as Hard Rock Hotel – Phase 2 – RCD Hotel Group, is projected to have 1,100 rooms and require US$373.3 million in capital expenditure.

Jampro said land clearing and preliminary groundwork had started on that phase, which will be built on the same Montego Bay property adjacent to UNICO. It projected 1,300 temporary jobs during development and 1,200 permanent positions.

DOMA Residences, the third phase, is planned as a 250-room development valued at US$133.4 million. The government report said construction was estimated to begin in 2026 on the same property, beside UNICO and the Hard Rock hotel.

Together, the three phases account for a projected 1,801 rooms, US$756.9 million in capital expenditure, 3,300 temporary jobs and 3,200 permanent positions, based on the figures supplied to Jampro.

The government filing does not specify whether Cabinet’s integrated resort approval covers all three phases or only the proposed hotel and casino component.

Hard Rock International is owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, which acquired the brand in 2007. The company says its network comprises more than 300 hotels, casinos, cafes, entertainment venues and retail locations across more than 80 countries.

The process followed by Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover, illustrates the distinction between approval of an integrated resort and the licensing of its casino.

Allen said an AIRD Order for the Princess Integrated Resort Development was issued in August 2023. The resort opened in December 2024, and an application for a casino gaming licence was submitted in August 2025.

The commission approved the application in July 2026 after completing its assessment and due diligence. It was the first casino operator’s licence granted under Jamaica’s regulatory framework.

The licence was issued to Adamas Grand Casino Limited, which will operate the proposed casino at Princess Grand under a management agreement with Grupo Orenes, a Spanish gaming and hospitality company.

The licence does not allow the casino to open immediately. Adamas must first meet the commission’s pre-operational requirements and receive clearance to begin operating.

World.title: ‘RAIN DELAY’ FOR JCA AGM
World.content:
A view of Sabina Park, headquarters of the Jamaica Cricket Association, during a rain delay in a West Indies versus Sri Lanka One-Day International game in June.garfield Robinson

JAMAICA Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says the voting annual general meeting (AGM) is likely to be held in October, after it was previously postponed.

The JCA annual meeting and election were to have been held in May but were pushed back pending ratification of proposed governance changes to its constitution.

Bennett told the Jamaica Observer that the board will get the opportunity to ratify the changes in just over two weeks.

“We will have a special meeting in September to deal with matters that we have had hanging around for years. Immediately after that September 10 meeting we will set a date for the AGM. I imagine that we will have the voting AGM in October,” he said.

Bennett, who had previously served as JCA vice-president, swept to power in April 2024 when he defeated the incumbent President Wilford “Billy” Heaven.

He admitted that, ideally, he had wanted the elections to be held months ago, but those plans had to be put aside.

“I would have preferred to have had the AGM exactly after two years — which would have been about March/April — but it didn’t happen.

“The AGM is not constitutionally due until December but… we don’t want to take it down to the last,” he said.

Though choosing to not outline granular details, Bennett insisted the constitutional changes are important for the greater good of cricket in Jamaica.

“It’s a matter of our constitution and [about] what we have and what we need to have,” he said, noting there are current glaring governance loopholes in how the JCA can regulate clubs and parish associations.

The JCA president said he is eager to be given a fresh mandate in his bid to improve the struggling sport in the country, and by extension the region.

“I get the impression there are some positive movements in the game, so I’m just hoping we can accelerate that process because we really want to get back to the top as soon as possible. It’s very important for West Indies cricket that Jamaica does well. Jamaica has the largest economy and the largest population so it stands to reason that if Jamaica does well then West indies cricket will do well,” he argued.

While Bennett is likely to return to the top post unopposed, there is intrigue surrounding the first vice-president job. Both the incumbent Fritz Harris, the Clarendon Cricket Association president, and Nehemiah Perry, former West Indies off spinner and current head of Kingston Cricket Club, were previously nominated.

However, Bennett confirmed that the nomination process will be redone ahead of the rescheduled elections.

— Sanjay Myers

World.title: Atlantic Hardware turns to e-commerce as profit triples
World.content:
For both its three-month an half-year results, Atlantic posted record revenues and profits.

ATLANTIC Hardware & Plumbing Company Limited is preparing to introduce e-commerce and expand its product portfolio after revenue jumped 69 per cent and profit more than tripled during the first half of 2026.

Managing Director Deanall Barnes told the Jamaica Observer on Monday that the hardware distributor had begun discussions on establishing an e-commerce platform as part of a wider effort to strengthen its digital footprint and use technology to improve its operations.

“On the technology front, we have commenced discussions on introducing an e-commerce platform, alongside broader consideration of how technology can be used to enhance the business — from inventory management to customer service — ultimately with a view of continuing to improve our bottom line,” he said to the Business Observer.

The digital push follows a sharp increase in sales at the company, which listed on the Junior Market of the Jamaica Stock Exchange in April 2025.

For the three months ended June 30, Atlantic reported record revenue of $776.4 million, up 92 per cent from $404.8 million in the corresponding quarter last year. Net profit rose 140 per cent to $42 million from $17.5 million.

Revenue for the six-month period increased 69 per cent year-on-year to $1.46 billion, while net profit more than tripled to $116.3 million from $33.9 million.

The company’s balance sheet also strengthened, as shareholders’ equity rose to $596.3 million and cash and cash equivalents more than doubled year-on-year to $255 million. Total assets on the other hand stood at $1.6 billion at the end of June.

Atlantic, which has operated since 1994 and distributes more than 2,400 hardware and building products from leading global brands, including Stanley, DeWalt, Black & Decker, Bosch and WD-40.

For its 2025 financial year, the company recorded revenue of $1.8 billion and net profit of $68.9 million.

Barnes said Atlantic’s new agricultural distribution division had become a significant contributor to revenue and was expected to support further growth as the company added products.

Launched earlier this year, the division has distribution rights for brands, including Bonanza seeds, Nutramix feed, and Bellota machetes. It generated approximately $300 million in revenue during the first half of 2026.

“We continue to expand within that category and will shortly be introducing a wider variety of seeds and pesticides — these products have already been tested by our suppliers, orders have been placed, and we anticipate arrival by mid-third quarter,” Barnes said.

He said Atlantic also sees opportunities to expand the division into fertilisers, veterinary products, and home and garden lines while assessing other categories that complement its existing distribution infrastructure and broad customer base.

As the company adjusts its procurement strategy in response to disruptions to global shipping, Barnes said it continues to deepen relationships with local and regional suppliers to reduce the risk of stock-outs as it manages its expanded portfolio.

The strategy has become increasingly important as Atlantic continues to widen its product offerings while seeking to maintain reliable supplies for customers.

Despite potentially subdued macroeconomic conditions, Barnes said management remains cautiously optimistic about the company’s prospects for the remainder of the financial year.

As the company plans to continue growing market share by widening its range of traditional hardware and building products alongside increasing its participation in government projects, the managing director said it will also tighten partnerships with suppliers to target major hotel developments.

“Disciplined capital allocation and continued balance sheet strength remain central to funding this growth,” Barnes said.

World.title: ‘Baddies build furniture too’
World.content:
Carpenter Sydonie Miller at her shop in DunKirk, Kingston (Photo: Garfield Robinson).

With work hard to find and financial constraints mounting during the coronavirus pandemic, one Jamaican woman discovered a hidden talent that opened an unexpected livelihood for her in a labour-intensive trade not often pursued by local females – carpentry.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sydonie Miller had been finding it difficult to secure a job in 2020, during the heights of COVID-19, despite having a bachelor’s degree in business management and secretarial skills.

Miller, who was a new mother at the time, said her husband, a taxi operator, was the only one working and she was determined to find a way to contribute to her family.

Her journey to carpentry began with a desire to own a padded bedhead and being quoted what she considered an exorbitant price to have one made.

“At the time, it was padded bed did run the place. When I go to ask the price, them a give me an arm and a leg for it. Me say me nah pay that,” Miller told Observer Online.

So, she decided to build it herself.

Seeking the guidance of a carpenter friend on Charles Street and gathering the necessary materials, Miller went on to make her first bedhead.

After completing the project, Miller’s curiosity and determination pushed her to learn more. She eventually made her way to Oxford Street, where veteran carpenters such as Chucky, Paul, Max, Abi Doll and Warren took her under their wings and taught her how to build a wider range of furniture, including dressers, chests of drawers and beds.

But for Miller, learning the trade was not difficult because she has always been a practical learner. She quickly grasped the skills being taught to her.

“If you’re going to do something, I see what you’re doing. If you show me one time, you don’t have to show me again. Just the one time, I know what to do,” she explained.

But the mother of three said her entry into carpentry was about more than simply learning how to build furniture. She believes the skill was placed in her path for a reason.

“At the time, I was at work and I can’t forget the day. The almighty say I give you a skill, go and use it. I have business management, secretarial skills. I thought it was that skill but I never knew it was this skill. So when him say I give you a skill, go and use it, me just say alright me ago just go deal with the bed head. Me see say me can build dresser and me just a build. Me go under the wings of the veterans,” she said.

Miller, who now owns her very own furniture business, Luxurious Furnitures by Syd, said her client base now ranges from individual customers to stores in the downtown Kingston area.

When Observer Online visited her shop on Banana Street in the McIntyre Villa community of East Kingston, Miller was seen working on a bedhead and bed bottom for one of her customers.

While her skills have helped her build a business, Miller said being a woman in a male-dominated trade has presented its own challenges.

“Some of them, when them see a woman come and say you know say me build this, them don’t believe it” she explained.

Miller said some customers only become convinced that she builds the furniture herself after seeing a male carpenter deliver one of her pieces.

Despite the doubters, Miller said she has also encountered customers who appreciate the fact that she is a woman in the trade and are willing to give her the time needed to complete their furniture.

“To be honest, it’s a bittersweet moment, but at the end of the day there are some people that really love me, who are really happy that I’m a woman and I do this. You have some patient ones, big up on unu self. Them say alright then, I’ll give you time,” she added.

The carpenter said each piece of furniture requires patience and attention to detail, with the process involving several stages before a finished product is ready.

“For me its patience, to really put in the work, because remember, furniture building takes time. It has different layers, different processes to build. So to build a bed head like this, it takes time. I have a lot of different grades of sanding to do,” she said.

She further explained: “I have to start the sanding from, like, 80, and I go down to 180. Then I go down to 200. Then I go down to 220. It’s patience. And you have to get all the nooks and crannies. You can’t just sand off just the bigger parts. You have to sand from the corners, from underneath, behind, everything. So it’s just patience.”

Of all the furniture she has made since entering the trade, Miller said one particular piece remains her favourite, a king-size mahogany bed set. She said the piece holds special significance because it challenged her skills when she was still new to furniture building.

Miller is now encouraging other women not to allow traditional perceptions about certain professions to prevent them from pursuing their interests.

“Don’t follow the stigma say a man work. Woman can do it, too. Once you see something that you want to do just do it. Learn the skill, do it, because at the end of the day, it’s not who do it. It’s really how you set your mind to do it or if you have the determination to do it,” Miller said. “So don’t follow them a man work. Baddies build furniture too. Baddies build furniture too.”

World.title: Fewer students drunk or high
World.content:
(Photo: Adobe stock)

THE National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) is reporting that fewer teenagers are using illegal drugs or drinking alcohol across Jamaica, but the numbers remain concerning.

According to the NCDA, its recent Global School-Based Health Survey (GSHS) conducted January to March 2026 — which had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools — showed that the consumption of alcohol by students in grades seven to 11 dropped from 52.5 per cent in 2010 to 38.8 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, the number of children who started consumption of alcohol before age 14 has decreased from 80.2 per cent in 2010 to 71.5 per cent this year. Also, teenagers who get drunk after the consumption of alcoholic beverages dropped from 35.5 per cent in 2010 to 21.5 per cent in 2026.

But 10.3 per cent of adolescents still attend school under the influence of alcohol, and 10.6 per cent are exposed to s about alcohol.

The NCDA — an agency of the Ministry of Health and Wellness — believes the overall message for positive trends has been working; however, it says continued action is needed to strengthen early prevention programmes, enforce underage drinking laws, reduce youth exposure to alcohol marketing, and increase parent and school engagements.

The survey also found that the use of ganja among adolescents declined from 21.5 per cent in 2017 to 15.7 per cent in 2026, a trend welcomed by the NCDA.

However, the organisation says it is concerned that 24.3 per cent of adolescents have easy access to the weed, while it noticed an emergence in the use of ecstasy, also known as molly.

Ecstasy is a synthetic psychoactive drug with both stimulant and psychedelic effects. Teens use it at parties and other gatherings, but it can cause dangerous spikes in body temperature, dehydration, high blood pressure, and heart failure.

With some students still attending school under the influence of substances because of the easy access to ganja and ecstasy, the NCDA says it will be expanding its substance-use prevention programme, aimed at strengthening prevention, delaying initiation, reducing access, and providing timely support for young people.

It also plans to improve the monitoring of emerging drugs.

In the meantime, the GSHS found that physical fights among students declined from 50.1 per cent in 2010 to 27 per cent in 2026, while injuries from fights dropped from 59.6 per cent in 2010 to 49 per cent in 2026.

In addition, the survey says bullying dropped from 40.2 per cent in 2016 to 27 per cent in 2026.

However, the survey found that 15 per cent of teenagers faced cyber bullying in the past year but there was no comparative figure with 2010. Another 16.9 per cent experienced bullying off school compounds.

The NCDA said despite a drop in physical fights among students, it will be strengthening its violence-prevention programme as it seeks to maintain safe school policies.

“Safe environments are essential for academic success and healthy development,” said the NCDA.

“Violence and injuries impact students’ physical and mental health, learning and well-being. Bullying and cyberbullying can lead to anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and social isolation,” the NCDA added.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: Can Canada teach Europe how to stand up to Trump?
World.content:
Canada is taking a much harder line against Donald Trump — and Brussels is watching closely. As the U.S.-Canada trade war escalates, Zoya Sheftalovich and Kathryn Carlson look at Mark Carney’s gamble, his call for the world’s “middle powers” to band together, and whether Europe is ready to follow his lead or would rather keep Washington onside.

Then, France’s 2027 presidential race gets its first major televised debate. The political center goes into it weaker and more divided than ever, while Jean-Luc Mélenchon has managed to put his radical plan for dealing with France’s €3.5 trillion debt right at the heart of the campaign.

And finally, could Brussels make the beautiful booze bottle an endangered species? Europe’s glassmakers fear new anti-waste rules could squeeze out some of the elaborate designs that help make spirits, wine and perfume instantly recognizable — although the reality is rather more nuanced.

World.title: Das neue Machtzentrum der Koalition
World.content:
Die Fraktionsspitzen der großen Koalition suchen in Münster wohl auch sowas wie einen westfälischen Frieden. Maximilian Stascheit blickt auf das mächtige Führungstrio um Thorsten Frei (CDU), Alexander Hoffmann (CSU) und Matthias Miersch (SPD). Sie müssen nun beweisen, dass sie ohne Jens Spahn knappe Mehrheiten organisieren können. Maximilian Stascheit analysiert, welchen neuen Wind sie in die Koalition bringen könnten, welche Altlasten sie mit sich schleppen und wie auf „Love is in the Air“ gehofft wird. Dazu berichtet Rasmus Buchsteiner aus Münster über die neue Rolle für Thorsten Frei, der jetzt von Leisetreter auf Lautsprecher umstellen muss.

Aus der Opposition kommen derweil harte Worte zur Performance der Regierung. Grünen-Chefin Franziska Brantner fordert im Interview ein sofortiges Ende der Streitereien zwischen Union und SPD. Ein rein rhetorisches Klima-Bekenntnis von Kanzler Friedrich Merz reiche angesichts der angespannten Wirtschaftslage nicht aus.

Auf europäischer Ebene geht es zeitgleich um den Konflikt um das EU-Budget. Kanzler Merz schmiedet in Berlin eine Allianz mit den sparsamen Ländern, um den Brüsseler Etat nicht so sehr anwachsen zu lassen, wie es sich die Kommission das wünscht. Hans von der Burchard ordnet ein, wo die Konfliktlinien verlaufen, wenn es um den mehrjährigen Finanzrahmen für 2028 bis 2034 verlaufen, wie dem Kanzler ein Gipfel-Marathon dabei bevorsteht und wie es am Ende – mal wieder – alles kurz vor knapp werden könnte.

World.title: France’s imperiled moderates look weaker than ever ahead of first presidential debate
World.content:
One of Medef’s most pressing concerns is Paris’ inability to rein in a stubbornly high budget deficit and reduce a massive pile of debt worth more than €3.5 trillion — or 117.5 percent of gross domestic product — even before the recent spike in global borrowing costs.

The solution du jour comes from far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is calling for the European Central Bank to waive interest payments on its French bond holdings, a move likely to frighten the investors Paris depends on to purchase French sovereign debt. Mélenchon’s proposal is strongly opposed by centrists and the business community, including MEDEF chief Patrick Martin, yet it dominates the discourse on French public debt.

And it’s the latest sign that as France’s economic outlook deteriorates, anti-establishment candidates are successfully pitching themselves as the ones who can fix France’s finances.

“You’d think that it would be a moment … that would profit those who are credible on economic matters,” said lawmaker Erwan Balanant from the centrist Democratic Movement. “But I don’t know who is credible on the economy anymore.”

Surveys continue to show far-right leader Marine Le Pen dominating the field of presidential hopefuls, and a poll released Monday showed Mélenchon on the rise and in a strong position to advance to the second round. The French presidential election goes to a two-candidate runoff if no one clears 50 percent of the vote — and a Le Pen-Mélenchon showdown would be a nightmare scenario for the European Union given their respective antipathy toward some of the bloc’s key pillars.

But Monday’s poll isn’t triggering calls for unity from ideologically similar centrists like former prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal as well as conservative leader Bruno Retailleau.

World.title: Deal or no deal: Farage faces polling hit from Restore Britain either way
World.content:
Earlier this month, Lowe offered to put his differences with Farage aside to form a pact with Reform, and Reform officials have been taking Lowe’s public offer of a pact seriously.

“They would like to work with us because he [Lowe] needs us to survive in the long run,” as one Farage adviser, granted anonymity to discuss the rift, put it.

But Lowe’s deal comes with conditions — he advocates mass deportations, including of women and children, a ban on halal and kosher slaughter, a referendum on the death penalty, and the exclusion of Conservative ministers from a future Cabinet.

Luke Tryl, U.K. director of More in Common, which conducted polling on right-wing pacts earlier this month, said a deal with Restore would be “more likely to damage than bolster Reform’s fragile voter coalition.”

“Some Reform voters are open to Lowe’s messages, but they risk deterring the wider pool of voters that Reform would need to win an election.

“It seems that a pact with Restore would cross too many lines for Reform’s wavering voters: this group wants to see Farage condemn racist views, retain a distance with figures on the hard-right like Tommy Robinson, and avoid ethnonationalist positions,” he said.

World.title: Trump-aligned Morocco dials up political heat on Spain’s Sánchez
World.content:
Only last week, Spain’s foreign ministry had to push back against a call from Morocco’s Justice Minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, for Madrid and Rabat to discuss the future of the two cities, citing Morocco’s historic and geographical “right” to them.

Facing a general election in the coming months and already floundering under a welter of corruption scandals in his party, Sánchez is desperate to avoid a showdown with Morocco — a country with which Madrid needs to maintain smooth relations because of its vital importance as a partner on trade, migration and fighting drug trafficking.

Since the beginning of the crisis in Ceuta, Sánchez has sought to avoid blaming King Mohammed’s operatives, instead pointing the finger at smuggling networks and misleading social media campaigns for the migrant influx. His Migration Minister Elma Saiz has even hailed Morocco as “a reliable partner, a loyal partner.”

Blaming Morocco

But that diplomatic tone with Rabat is playing badly with the rest of Spain’s parties. Many politicians complain that Rabat withdrew border guards before the surge across the border.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), who is the current favorite to succeed Sánchez as prime minister, said: “It turns out that [Sánchez] behaves more like a subject of Morocco than a prime minister of Spain.”

He then insisted Spain could not be subject to “blackmail and threats” from its neighbor across the Mediterranean.

World.title: UK launches mini solar scheme … into a thicket of red tape
World.content:
Regulation, regulation, regulation

The technology was badged as a simpler solution for renters or other people without space at home for traditional rooftop panels.

People who want to install the kit may need permission from landlords, freeholders or councils, therefore. And some are already not playing ball.

One housing association, Sovereign Network Group — which manages 86,000 homes across London and the south of England — said it has a blanket ban on letting residents install plug-in solar in the buildings it manages.

“While solar panels may be installed through our planned retrofit programme, we do not permit plug-in or ‘plug and play’ solar panels in SNG properties,” said Carol Bailey, SNG’s building and occupational safety director, citing potential “electrical safety risks.”

Claire Hibbit, corporate affairs director at another housing association in England, Notting Hill Genesis, which manages over 60,000 properties, said they wanted to help tenants use cleaner power — before listing all the hurdles tenants would need to clear before plugging in solar panels: ensuring they were bought from a reputable outlet, holding an electricity safety certificate, safe installation, no extra fire risk, the right weight for a balcony, and not breaking any rules governing conservation areas.

A third, L&Q, which manages over 105,000 properties, said it welcomed the potential of plug-in panels to help cut bills. But its Director of Health and Building Safety Steve Pettitt added: “As this technology is new, we're still considering the detail, including how it can be used safely in residents’ homes.”

World.title: Merz unites EU budget-cutters as Costa gropes for deal
World.content:
With the bloc racing to strike a deal on its budget before elections next year in France, Spain and Italy that risk turning the chance of agreement from difficult to nigh-on impossible, the next four months are critical for the EU’s stability, Costa’s legacy and whether leaders like Merz and Stocker can prove to their voters that Brussels isn’t wasting their money.



The leaders meeting in Berlin don’t just want the size of the budget to shrink by hundreds of billions of euros, they also want shift the way it is spent away from areas such as agriculture toward defense and security. And they want to impose conditions to stop governments getting cash if they breach democratic standards.

The discussion is unlikely to result in the publication of any precise numbers but instead produce a united front for the negotiations to come, three people familiar with the preparations said. Ireland, which is shepherding the budget process as part of its role at the helm of the six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, is to put forward fresh compromise numbers in October ahead of a summit of EU leaders later in the month.

“The general priorities of the [budget] proposal are worthy of support and in line with Finland’s objectives,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement. “However, the overall level of the proposed framework is too high.”

Some countries, such as Spain, believe the Commission shouldn’t reduce the size of the proposed budget and are resisting moves to direct expenditure away from agriculture.

Getting closer?

Costa, who has already visited Bratislava, Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius, believes governments aren’t as far apart as their public statements suggest, according to a senior EU official familiar with the negotiations, who like others mentioned in this article were granted anonymity because the talks are at such a sensitive stage.

While leaders are defending domestic red lines they do all seem to be committed to reaching a deal by the end of the year, the official said.

World.title: Beyond heatstroke: 33 conditions linked to extreme heat, from skin rashes to violence
World.content:
This summer, Europe has faced some of its most extreme temperatures, with thermometers reaching record high temperatures over several consecutive heatwaves.

 

The scorching weather has caused thousands of excess deaths, strained healthcare facilities and highlighted the need for better preparedness going forward.

Extreme temperatures can have dangerous health consequences, with heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration being among the most common.

However, researchers have identified more than 30 diagnoses associated with high temperatures, ones that show a significant increase during periods of intense heat.

The research, published in the journal Science Advances, found strong links to under-recognised problems such as multiple sclerosis flare-ups, skin eruptions and various physical injuries.

“It is a public health obligation to protect the individuals and communities most vulnerable to the harmful effects of climate change,” said the study’s author Hyojung Jang, from Northwestern University in the United States.

“If we’re only tracking the more commonly known heat-related illnesses, we’ll underestimate the true heat-related health burden, which could result in vulnerable people and communities being overlooked.”

This study examined 1,803 diagnoses recorded across almost one million emergency department and urgent care visits in Chicago between May and September between 2011 and 2023.

The researchers identified diagnoses such as skin rashes and swelling, acute kidney failure, multiple sclerosis, mental and behavioural disorders and insect bites and stings, which were associated with heat and are often overlooked in emergency settings.

The authors noted that urban environments face additional risks because of the so-called “ urban heat island effect,” which can raise local temperatures by several degrees and extend the length of such events.

The findings also suggest that extreme heat may be linked to a rise in accidental and violent trauma, including assaults and firearm-related incidents. The researchers identified 23 specific injury, poisoning or external-cause diagnoses that met their criteria for being heat-related.

“Previous research has shown that when people are exposed to extreme heat, they often act more aggressively, so that may be playing a factor here,” said co-author Daniel Horton, associate professor at Northwestern.

“When it’s hot out, your body is stressed, and your mind is stressed, so that may be distracting or aggravating, and it could lead to more accidents.”

Improving preparedness

According to the researchers, the findings could help improve preparedness for future heat-intense periods.

This includes updating clinical alerts for a broader range of conditions, specifically renal and fluid-balance complications, which often manifest several days after the actual heat exposure.

Considering these possible diagnoses, emergency departments and urgent care settings can better anticipate and prepare for surges in demand for dehydration- and renal-related care during and immediately after extreme heat events.

The authors noted the findings are currently limited to the Chicago study and should be replicated in other populations, climates and health care systems.

World.title: Is Stuttgart’s air-con free train station a genius design or the megaproject’s next blunder?
World.content:
Deep beneath Stuttgart, a vast new transport hub is emerging. Known as Stuttgart 21, the subterranean replacement for the city’s main train station is designed to stay cool without air conditioning.

 

Having sweltered through record-high temperatures this summer, residents of the German city were surprised by this design detail, which was highlighted in an explainer released by rail operator Deutsche Bahn (DB) in August.

“Next video: Why the Titanic didn't need lifeboats,” one commenter quips. “When the train station was planned, there were no air conditioners yet,” jokes another.

The megaproject was first conceived of in the late ‘80s and presented to the public in 1994. Construction began in 2010 and has been beset with costly delays.

Defending its air-con free design, Deutsche Bahn says that temperatures will remain stable – both during extreme heat and cold – in part thanks to the station being underground.

It also highlights that Stuttgart lies in a basin, with the station located at the lowest point. Tunnels will slope upwards from there, allowing air to cool as it’s pushed down into the station, its flow aided by passing trains and glass "light eyes" with automated ventilation flaps, DB says.

Glass 'light eyes' will provide natural light and ventilation in the Stuttgart's new main station. © Bahnprojekt Stuttgart-Ulm e.V.

Emissions-cutting design or the train station’s next blunder?

“The future Stuttgart central station will operate entirely without artificial climate control,” Deutsche Bahn’s head of communications, Jörg Hamann, tells Euronews Earth.

Air flowing into the station will be cooled on its journey through tunnels ranging from three to 9.5 kilometres, Hamann explains.

With heating and cooling making up a significant portion of energy consumption in train stations, the air-conless design could help slash the railway hub’s carbon footprint long-term.

According to the IEA, air conditioning is currently responsible for emitting around one billion tonnes of CO2 per year, out of a total of 37 billion tonnes emitted worldwide.

Hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) and hydrochlorofluorocarbon (HCFC) refrigerants used in air conditioning also trap thousands of times more heat in the atmosphere than CO2, driving global warming.

But critics have been quick to question the functionality of the Stuttgart 21’s design.

Commenters on DB’s video wonder whether the natural airflow will be able to offset the heat of human bodies and operating trains in the station, especially as the trains’ own air-conditioners emit waste heat. They question how much heat will enter through the glass skylights.

Some worry the project risks falling into the same trap as other projects across Europe. “The underground Barcelona Sants train station gets unbearably hot in late summer,” one commenter says, while another points to Lisbon Metro’s costly cooling retrofits amid escalating summer heatwaves.

Stuttgart 21 has been under construction for 17 years. © Thomas Niedermuller / Bahnprojekt Stuttgart-Ulm e.V.

Stuttgart 21: A project fraught with setbacks

It’s unsurprising the news has been met with skepticism.

From intense protests in 2010 over the felling of 300-year-old trees in Schlossgarten – Stuttgart Palace Gardens – to the discovery of threatened lizards along the route, which had to be relocated to the tune of over €15 million, the Stuttgart 21 project has had a bumpy ride.

Setbacks like these have propelled it to farcical status among locals, with many wondering whether it will ever be completed at all.

A recent internal audit exposed the project’s latest crisis: a delayed opening that will now begin in phases from 2027, a ballooning €14.5 billion price tag, and what the railway’s own boss called “shocking” failures in planning and oversight. DB has faced scrutiny from the mayor over lack of transparency in refusing to release the report, while campaign groups are threatening legal action.

Deutsche Bahn tells Euronews that the audit was intended solely for internal use and cannot be made public for legal reasons.

Stuttgart's main station is being relocated underground. © Arnim Kilgus / Bahnprojekt Stuttgart-Ulm e.V.

Will the new station make life above ground hotter?

Above ground, concerns have been raised over the Stuttgart–Ulm project’s impact on the city’s climate.

As DB itself points out, the city is located in a natural valley basin known as the Stuttgart Cauldron, surrounded by steep, vine-covered hills and forests. This traps heat and reduces wind speeds, making it one of the warmest regions in Germany.

Moving the main station underground will free up 100 hectares of inner-city space, much of which is earmarked to become a new district called Rosenstein.

DB says Rosenstein will feature 10 hectares of green spaces and public squares among 50 hectares of residential and commercial space. A further 20 hectares will be added to the Schlossgarten park, expanding it onto former railway lines.

Campaign group Aktionsbündnis gegen (Action alliance against) Stuttgart 21 says the current railway yard acts as a vital fresh air corridor that cools the city. It warns that building on this site is likely to restrict air flow in the city basin and add to the urban heat island effect.

The group has also raised concerns over soil sealing – concreting over land – which can prevent rain from soaking into the earth, destroying ecosystems, drying out greenery and compounding flood risks.

Relocating Stuttgart's main station underground will create 100 hectares of space above ground for two new districts. © Arnim Kilgus / Bahnprojekt Stuttgart-Ulm e.V.

Will Stuttgart’s railway project get cars off the road?

With 56 kilometres of new tunnels connecting to high-speed and regional lines, Stuttgart’s railway project promises to better integrate the southwest into the wider train system.

It will also slash travel times: the journey from Ulm–Stuttgart will become 28 minutes instead of 58, while Stuttgart Main Station–Stuttgart Airport will be slashed from 27 minutes to just six.

This could encourage more people to take the train over driving. However, critics say it could also entice more people to use the airport.

These shorter journey times are partly made possible by the transition from the old 16-platform terminal station to an eight-platform through station, where trains will no longer change direction and higher approach speeds will be possible. Critics, however, warn that reducing the number of platforms leaves very little safety margin or buffer for delays.

DB says that the station’s performance was proven in a 2011 stress test, and that it will be able to handle “significantly more” train traffic than the current terminal station, which has only five inbound and outbound tracks versus the new station’s eight. Efficiency will be further aided by the digitalisation of the railway network.

DB says the future station will enable many new direct regional connections, which will also relieve some of the pressure on the busy S-Bahn. It anticipates an increase in demand by around two million passengers as a result of the project.
