World.title: Thailand, Japan or Australia? The travel destinations dividing Gen Z and Millennials
World.content:
Ask a Gen Z or Millennial traveller where they’re heading this year, and you might get very different answers.

 

New research has shown that the two generations travel dissimilarly, and it’s down in part to budget or social influence.

Youth travel specialist Adventure360 analysed more than 4,700 bookings made over the past year to see where the two generations are actually travelling.

Thailand tops the Gen Z list, while Australia takes the Millennial crown, with Cambodia, Laos and New Zealand emerging as Gen Z favourites and Japan, Greece and Iceland proving more popular with slightly older travellers.

To rank the most popular options, travellers were split into Gen Z and Millennials, and each country was measured on the share of bookings. In the end, percentages showed how many of every 100 bookings in each age group included a visit to a particular country.

The differences between Gen Z and Millennials’ travel habits

For Gen Z, Thailand was far and away the most popular choice, featuring in 29.2% of bookings – that’s the single highest figure recorded for either generation.

Thailand was also in second place for Millennials, with a score of 17.4%, behind Australia, which had slightly more at 17.8%.

Cambodia and Laos as well as New Zealand all ranked in the Gen Z top 10, but none of them appeared in the Millennial list at all.

At the same time, Japan, Greece and Iceland all made the Millennial top 10 and not one of them came close to ranking for Gen Z.

Experts at Adventure360 put Gen Z’s favourite destinations partially down to what’s trending.

For instance, video clips recreating the mobile game Temple Run through the corridors of Angkor Wat in Cambodia have passed two million views on social media.

Long Beach in Koh Rong, also in Cambodia, has been going viral this year, after it was named among the 10 best beaches in the world while, in Laos, the Kuang Si waterfalls are drawing millions of views from travellers adding them to their bucket lists.

From affordability to visas: Other trends revealed in the study

Thailand is popular with both generations due to its affordability – and there’s a reason why it’s been a favourite destination with young travellers for years, not least because the island of Koh Tao is the most affordable place on the planet to qualify as a scuba diver.

Cambodia and Laos used to be added on to trips to mega-popular Thailand and Vietnam, but the study shows they’re both being booked deliberately, and individually now.

That new popularity is partly thanks to TikTok videos, a significant source of travel inspiration for Gen Z, as well as its serious affordability, with rock bottom prices for decent accommodation very common.

The study shows the difference between the two generations and their travel habits Felix Rostig/Unsplash

New Zealand’s popularity with Gen Z seems to be down to its working holiday visa, which allows many passport holders aged 18 to 35 to stay for up to 36 months. The island nation ranks ninth for Gen Z but doesn’t feature for Millennials, as many have aged out of being able to get the visa.

Gen Z are also keen to visit places which are quieter, with the study looking at Skyscanner data which shows that 76% are open to picking a lesser-known destination over a popular one.

According to the data, 51% were found to have actively planned a quieter trip because of crowding, with one in three saying crowds have spoiled a previous holiday.

Financial differences come into play, too, with Japan, Greece and Iceland belonging to Millennials, because of their higher price points.

Interestingly, 60% of UK-based Gen Zs said they expect to travel abroad more this year, but only 45% plan to spend any more on flights to do it, which takes some destinations out of the equation.

“Iceland and Japan are the two I get asked about most frequently by millennial customers,” Jane McLellan-Green, travel expert at Adventure360, said.

“A £5 (€5.85) coffee in Reykjavík is a hard sell for Gen Z when the same money covers a bed for the night in Vientiane (the capital of Laos), but millennials are much happier to pay the price.”

Where Gen Z and Millennials travel: The top 10 countries

Gen Z

Thailand Australia Indonesia Vietnam Cambodia Laos Peru Phillipines New Zealand Morocco

Millennials

World.title: Around 1,000 people missing in Nepal and Tibet after catastrophic floods caused by a glacial collapse
World.content:
At least 162 were killed in Nepal and three others in Tibet after massive flash floods in a border area of Nepal and China swept through communities on Wednesday, China’s state media reported, warning that up to 1000 people remain missing in Nepal and Tibet from the disaster.

 

Mudslides in Tibet left three people dead and 558 missing; some 260 of the 558 missing people in Tibet were foreigners, and two villagers were rescued, both China's state news agency Xinhua and broadcaster CCTV reported Thursday morning.

Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the colour of wet cement.

“When I reached Dhunge bazaar, in half an hour, the flood came and damaged all the market. People were preparing to go to the office then,” a Tibetan resident, Shoyam Rajbhandari, said. “How many people are missing or dead, we don’t know.”

Foreign nationals are among those missing

Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong told reporters Thursday at least 34 Australians on pilgrimages and hiking tours were missing.

“We understand these Australians were part of separate pilgrimage and tour groups,” Wong told reporters in Adelaide, Australia.

The Nepalese government had not yet requested help, but Australia was coordinating with Nepal, the United Nations, the Red Cross and other organisations on a humanitarian response, she said.

Rescuers use earthmovers to reach submerged houses after flash flooding along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shre AP Photo

55 Malaysians in Kathmandu are now unreachable due to serious infrastructural delays, according to Malaysia's Foreign Ministry, which increased the number of missing on Thursday. It stated that it is closely collaborating with authorities to determine the safety and locations of Malaysian casualties, but there is no formal confirmation of their presence.

Early Wednesday, the US Geological Survey reported a magnitude 4.4 earthquake about 66 kilometres north of Kathmandu, near the border.

The USGS later updated its analysis to say the seismic event it measured was a magnitude 5.2 glacial collapse that sent debris flowing downstream with catastrophic impact on communities.

It said its determination was based on data from nearby seismic stations, long-period seismic waves and satellite imagery, and that no earthquake had occurred.

Avalanche from glacier caused disaster, experts say

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday’s flash flood.

“Hydrological observations indicate the exceptional speed and magnitude of the flood wave,” they said in an emailed statement, noting that water levels at one point on the Trishuli river rose by as much as 9 metres over half an hour.

The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, had maximum flooding, they said.

“The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.

The catastrophe in Tibet and Nepal is not a one-off. Over the past year, the Lhende Khola river system has flooded twice, and in one of the most heavily inhabited areas of the globe, populations, infrastructure, and water supplies are at risk due to the increasingly unstable Himalayan glacier system.

The region’s steep valleys are economic lifelines and travel corridors but are precarious when disaster strikes.

The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures.

Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

World.title: Iran to allow no military ship in Hormuz under potential deal with Oman
World.content:
Iran and Oman have reached a potential agreement for managing ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz that would exclude military vessels from traversing the vital waterway.

 

Tehran won’t allow military vessels to transit through the Strait of Hormuz under the agreement that the Islamic Republic is negotiating with Oman, Minister Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, said on Tuesday.

It comes after top diplomats of the two countries met to discuss managing commercial shipping traffic in the vital waterway, which remained largely shut down nearly six months after the Iran war began.

Gharibabadi told state television late Tuesday that commercial shipping traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman’s waters.

He said the routes would be temporary and that Iran and Oman must discuss a permanent maritime traffic plan within 30 to 60 days.

The latest development comes amid US President Donald Trump's threat to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way", as his administration opposes parts of the evolving deal.

The Trump administration has told Oman it is opposed to parts of the yet-to-be-announced deal, including the joint Iranian and Omani management of the exit route out of the passage that’s critical to global supplies of oil and natural gas.

Washington believes Oman has not been tough enough in its negotiations with Iran and is unhappy with Oman’s agreement to collect voluntary fees from vessels, even if the charges are related to security and maritime environmental protection

Trump not in a hurry to resume talks with Iran

On Wednesday, Trump, in an interview with a Qatar-based broadcaster, Al Jazeera, said that he believes the United States is “winning very big” as the conflict with Iran nears the six-month mark.

“I have no time schedule; whatever it takes,” he told the Qatar-based broadcaster.

In another interview Wednesday, Trump said he thinks Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Motjaba Khamenei, is “very seriously wounded", but not dead.

Motjaba Khamenei became supreme leader after his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war. The younger Khamenei was badly wounded in the attacks and has remained out of public view.

The war has devastated the Iranian economy but also heavily stalled business across the Middle East, disrupting vital shipping lanes, halting regional trade, and driving up energy and transport costs.

Dubai airport traffic dropped sharply during Iran war

On Wednesday, Dubai International Airport, one of the world’s busiest travel hubs, said that it saw a sharp drop in passengers as the Iran war disrupted air travel across the Middle East.

The airport recorded 13 million passengers in the second quarter of 2026, bringing the total to about 31.5 million passengers for the first half of the year. That’s down 31.3% compared to last year at the halfway mark.

According to the airport, aircraft movements totalled 150,600 in the first half, down 32.1% year on year, with only 62,500 in the second quarter.

However, according to CEO Paul Griffiths, there has been a consistent monthly growth in passenger volume during the second quarter, and this momentum is anticipated to continue.

“The events of the disruption, which lasted two months, that had an impact on traffic ... but I'm very confident we'll be back to full operation in a very short space of time. " Griffits said.

Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in a letter to the United Nations on Tuesday, urged the world body to condemn the latest US move to cut off Tehran from the rest of the global economy.

The “economic onslaught" that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared this week amounts to the deliberate targeting of Iranian civilians with the “intentional deprivation of access to food, medicines, medical equipment, energy and other necessities", according to Araghchi.

World.title: Nvidia smashes Q2 forecasts with $96.2bn in revenue as AI hits 'inflection point'
World.content:
Nvidia posted quarterly revenue of $96.2 billion (€82.4bn) on Wednesday, comfortably beating the $92.2 billion (€79bn) Wall Street had expected, as chief executive Jensen Huang declared that artificial intelligence had reached a turning point and guided next quarter revenue to $108 billion (€92.5bn) — again, above forecasts.

 

"AI has reached its inflection point," Huang said in a statement. "It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue, and demand is accelerating."

Days on which Nvidia reports its quarterly results have an outsized importance for the world's most valuable company.

At a market capitalisation north of $5 trillion (€4.3tn), it is worth more than the GDP of Japan, the fourth largest economy.

Shares fell 1.8% in after-hours trading shortly after the release. The stock had already ended the regular session 1.6% lower.

Yet there is a strange rite that plays out each quarter: Nvidia beats expectations, and the stock falls anyway. It happened after the first-quarter beat this year, when shares slid close to 5% in the days that followed.

The pattern has left a dynamic where the company needs to significantly outperform an already-bullish consensus, or provide a stronger-than-expected outlook, to move the share price higher.

The concentration problem

The main concern around Nvidia is not whether it can grow, it is more of a question of who it is growing for.

The firm still draws the bulk of its revenue from Amazon, Google and Microsoft, each of which is now designing its own chips to reduce reliance on the company. The new disclosures show precisely how large that dependence remains.

Chief Executive Jensen Huang's commentary on demand into 2027 therefore carries more weight than any single figure. The question has grown sharper since July, when markets fell on doubts about whether vast AI investments will ever generate proportionate returns.

Nvidia's answer has been to help finance the buildout itself. This month alone it assembled a $500bn (€428bn) capital pool with six Wall Street asset managers for data centre projects, and separately committed up to $105bn (€90bn) to back an OpenAI data centre in Pike County, Ohio, with an initial capacity of 4.25 gigawatts and an option for a further 3.75.

The road ahead

Washington barred sales of the China-specific H20 chip in April 2025, reversed course, and Nvidia has since received approval to ship the more capable H200 chip to vetted Chinese customers.

Reports have surfaced of large allocations to ByteDance and Tencent, though Beijing has been encouraging domestic firms to limit their purchases and prioritise homegrown alternatives.

Nvidia's current growth is being driven by its Blackwell chips, the generation of processors powering most AI data centres today. Their successor, known as Vera Rubin, is expected to begin shipping in the second half of the year.

Nvidia has a tradition of naming its chip architectures after scientists and past generations include Ampere, named after physicist André-Marie Ampère; Hopper, named after computer scientist Grace Hopper; and the current Blackwell chip, named after mathematician David Blackwell.

Vera Rubin continues that pattern. She was an American astronomer whose observations of how galaxies rotate provided some of the strongest early evidence for the existence of dark matter, the invisible mass thought to make up much of the universe. She died in 2016 and is widely seen as someone who was overlooked for a Nobel Prize during her lifetime.

The company has pointed to an order backlog it says is worth around $1 trillion (€857bn) across 2026 and 2027, though that figure comes from company commentary rather than independently verified financial disclosure.

A week stacked with catalysts

Wednesday's data offered no relief on inflation.

The personal consumption expenditures index, the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge, rose 0.2% in July against expectations of 0.1%, leaving the annual rate at 3.7% rather than easing to the 3.6% forecast. Core prices held at 3.3% over the year, above the Fed's 2% target for a 65th consecutive month.

The Federal Open Market Committee held rates at 3.50% to 3.75% in July, with three regional Fed presidents dissenting in favour of a quarter-point increase.

Markets currently put the probability of a September hike at around 40%.

Attention now shifts to Jackson Hole, where Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his keynote on Friday morning, his first since taking office in May, 19 days before the next rate decision. The ECB's Isabel Schnabel joins a panel the same afternoon.

US stock markets drifted through a quiet session on Wednesday after data showed inflation last month was a touch higher than economists had expected.

The S&P 500 edged down less than 0.1% and remains near the all-time high it set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 0.2% and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.1%.

Treasury yields ticked higher after the inflation update, which has traders still largely betting the Federal Reserve will raise the federal funds rate before the end of this year. Oil prices fell after another volatile session.

World.title: La Tomatina 2026: thousands turn Spanish town red in annual tomato fight
World.content:
Thousands of revellers descended on the Spanish town of Buñol on Wednesday for La Tomatina, hurling up to 165 tonnes of overripe tomatoes at each other in just over an hour.

 

Trucks loaded with tomatoes ploughed slowly through the crowd as people in the cargo beds pelted those below, who threw them straight back. White shirts turned pink within minutes while residents doused participants with water from balconies. Buildings along the route were covered with tarpaulins beforehand.

More than 20,000 people were expected this year. Spanish news agency EFE reports that roughly 40% of participants over the past three years have come from outside Spain, with a marked rise in visitors from India since the 2011 Bollywood film "Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara" recreated the festival.

Held on the last Wednesday of August, La Tomatina dates back to a street brawl in 1945. There is one rule: squash the tomato before you throw it.

World.title: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama dies at 97
World.content:
From works of "self-obliteration" to polka dotted nudes, the pioneering artist developed a unique body of work likely to be relevant for years to come.

Yayoi Kusama gained fame in recent years for her Instagrammable "Infinity Rooms" — immersive installations using mirrors, lights and reflective surfaces to create the illusion of endless space — as well as her large-scale polka dot sculptures. While her works often appear playful, behind them lies the story of a woman who has faced major social and mental health challenges.

Around the age of 10, Yayoi Kusama began experiencing hallucinations, seeing dots and net patterns enveloping everything in her mind's eye. She attributed these early visions to the psychological strain of growing up with an unloving mother, who forbade her from painting and tried to impose traditional expectations on her behavior. Although she continued to experience hallucinations until late in life, Kusama learned to live with them and channel them into her art. "My artwork is an expression of my life, particularly of my mental disease," Kusama once told US arts publication Bomb Magazine.

Yayoi Kusama: Dots, mirrors, infinity To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

After attending the Kyoto School of Arts and Crafts, Kusama held her first exhibitions in her hometown of Matsumoto. She was unusually open about her mental health at a time when such topics were heavily stigmatized.

"It was extraordinary that she addressed it so openly," said Stephan Diederich, curator of the Kusama retrospective at Cologne's Museum Ludwig which took place in 2026.

"For her, art was a survival strategy and a form of therapy, which she always made clear without making it the main focus," Diederich told DW.

Stephan Diederich in front of Yayoi Kusama's "My eternal soul" at the Museum Ludwig Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

Kusama's escape to New York

For Kusama, who was born on March 22, 1929, life in Japan soon became too stifling.

"[My parents] were always trying to rope me into arranged marriages with men I'd never met who came from very particular families," Yayoi once told writer Andrew Solomon, referring to her early 20s as "my era of mental breakdown." She increasingly felt like "a prisoner surrounded by a curtain of depersonalization."

Finally, she broke free from the conventions and expectations of postwar Japan and moved to New York in 1958. "She was exceptionally self-confident and determined to go her own way and pursue a career," said Diederich. Kusama's mother provided her with financial support to get started — on the condition that she never return to Japan. Fellow artist Georgia O'Keeffe, to whom Kusama had previously sent a selection of her works, helped her gain a foothold in the United States.

Kusama often spent entire days working and produced a vast body of art. She became part of the New York avant-garde scene, where her meticulous "Infinity Net" paintings drew attention for their hypnotic, repetitive patterns.

Kusama's work drew attention for their hypnotic, repetitive patterns Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/newscom/picture alliance

Her works, including soft, often phallic fabric sculptures, paralleled some of the approaches of contemporaries like Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg.

"She was very confident in saying that she set the benchmarks that her male colleagues later drew on," explained Diederich. However, he added, it's impossible to determine definitively who was first. In any case, her male fellow artists were more commercially successful than the young Asian woman, contributing to her attempted suicide, which she fortunately survived. Kusama made a statement about the gender pay gap with her sculpture "Traveling Life" (1964), which features a ladder covered in phallic shapes with women's shoes on the steps.

Phalluses are another recurring motif Kusama used to process her "fear of sex as something dirty," as she wrote in her 2022 autobiography. Returning to the universe through self-obliteration in the 1960s, Kusama held "happenings" as protests against the Vietnam War. They were often provocative, sometimes involving nudity and sexual activity, although Kusama often noted that she didn't personally participate in the sexual aspects of these events.

"Why should people who share pleasure with each other go to war and kill others? Through free sex, the wall between me and others can be torn down," Kusama wrote in her autobiography.

She was known for painting nude female and male bodies with dots, with the aim of erasing the individuality of those painted. She calls this "self-obliteration," and it runs through her entire body of work. "By obliterating one's self, you return to the infinite universe," Kusama once said.

Kusama once told an interviewer she wanted 'to become more famous, even more famous' Image: Dagmara Jakubczak/DW

In 1966, Kusama staged her work "Narcissus Garden" at the Venice Biennale. She placed 1,500 mirrored spheres on the lawn outside the entrance of the Venice Biennale, which she hadn't been invited to, and attempted to sell them for $2 each. Biennale officials eventually intervened and stopped the sale, but the work still served as a pointed critique of the commercialization of the art world and the role of artists in it.

Fame later in life

In 1993, Kusama returned to the Venice Biennale as an officially invited artist, representing Japan.

She later told the Financial Times that she wanted "to become more famous, even more famous," a remark that reflects how important recognition had become in her career and one that some commentators critiqued as overly focused on fame.

Over the past decade she reached a level of fame any artist would be envious of. In 2018, The Broad museum in Los Angeles quickly sold 90,000 advance tickets for a Kusama exhibition. A yearlong show at London's Tate Modern in 2022 sold out in no time, as did the one-year extension. Her artworks went on to fetch millions at auction.

Yayoi Kusama returned to Japan in 1973 and chose to live in a psychiatric clinic in Tokyo, where she received treatment for her mental health. She remained highly productive, creating paintings, sculptures, installations and other works that are exhibited around the world until her last days.

"I will continue to create artwork as long as my passion keeps me doing so. I am deeply moved that so many people have been my fans," she said in a previous interview. "I suppose I would not be able to know how people would evaluate my art until after I die. I create art for the healing of all mankind."

Image: John Angelillo/IMAGO/UPI Photo

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: US Army to spend $2 billion nuclear microreactors for bases
World.content:
The US Army has announced a plan to install what it calls nuclear microreactors at five of its bases across the country. The move would ensure the facilities' energy independence from the rest of the electric grid.

The United States Army said Wednesday that it will award $2.2 billion (€1.7 billion) in contracts to five companies to build and operate small nuclear reactors on military bases. The program set a goal of deploying the first such reactor by the end of September 2028.

Called microreactors, developers say each of the nuclear plants would be easy to transport and provide up to 20 megawatts of power.

The reactors will adhere to all environmental and safety regulations that apply to commercial reactors, but an Army spokesperson said the reactors will be regulated by the Army rather than the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, which regulates commercial reactors.

"The whole idea here is that at the back end of this we want a commercial product," said Jeff Waksman, principal deputy assistant secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said the awards will speed up the military's ability "to deliver safe, reliable baseload power directly to our installations."

"We are building the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids," he added.

What companies are involved?

The Army selected the following companies to work at its bases:

Antares Nuclear at Fort Bragg, North Carolina

BWXT Advanced Technologies ​at Fort Campbell, Kentucky

General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems at Fort Hood, Texas

Radiant ​Industries, Fort Benning, Georgia

Westinghouse Government Services at Fort Drum, New York

Radiant's Chief Commercial Officer Mike Starrett told Reuters news agency that the project, called Janus, will help the company scale up its business to meet the needs of commercial customers, like data centers, in about 2030.

Rex Geveden, president and chief executive officer of BWXT, said, "As we commence work on the Janus program, we are delivering the nation's most credible and reliable path to deployable nuclear power."

Nuclear plants: Billion-dollar graves? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Hidden subsidy' for expensive reactors, critics say

Critics of microreactors say they will be expensive compared to conventional reactors. Safety advocates point out that nuclear technology carries significant risks that other low-carbon energy sources don't, such as the danger of accidents or targeted attacks.

The Army program uses the military's "deep pockets to provide a hidden subsidy" to nuclear companies that can't find private-sector customers for their hypothetical and uneconomical reactors, Alan J. Kuperman, associate professor at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and coordinator of the Nuclear Proliferation Prevention Project, told the AP news agency.

The Army's Waksman said nobody thinks that microreactors will be lower in cost than conventional plants.

"What we are trying to do here with Janus ... is to flesh out how can we get those prices down," he said.

The toll of nuclear power on generations to come To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What will happen with the radioactive waste?

Waksman said the microreactors would safely shut down in case of a failure and that the Army wouldn't add them to installations without being certain they are safe.

He added that the Army is working on a deal with the Energy Department to remove radioactive waste, and there won't be any long-term storage on these installations.

Last month, five states offered to accept nuclear waste in exchange for federal support in developing nuclear energy facilities.

Trump pushing nuclear power in US

Executive orders signed by US President Donald Trump in May 2025 aimed to accelerate the development of nuclear power. Trump has called for the US to quadruple its nuclear energy production — just two new large reactors have been built from scratch in the United States in nearly 50 years. Those two reactors were completed years late and at least $17 billion over budget, AP reported.

The nation's 94 nuclear reactors supply about 19% of U.S. electricity, compared to about 60% for fossil fuels and 21% for renewables, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

World.title: France: Car rams crowd at bus stop in Caen
World.content:
At least one person was killed and several injured when a car drove into a bus shelter in the northern French city of Caen.

A person drove a car into a crowd in the northwestern French city of Caen on Wednesday, killing at least one person and injuring about a dozen others, firefighters and police said, according to the AFP news agency and BFM TV.

A police source said the driver rammed the car into the crowd near the city's train station after a fight in the area, and one suspect was arrested, AFP reported.

BFM TV reported that two people had been killed in the incident.

The driver fled and was later arrested 20 kilometers (12 miles) away, a source told AFP.

The incident occurred around 10:00 p.m. local time (2000 UTC/GMT) near a bus stop close to the Caen train station. According to initial reports, a black vehicle drove into several people who were in the area.

Police cordoned off the area while emergency services attended to the victims.

Authorities are investigating the circumstances of the incident and trying to determine whether the attack was intentional.

World.title: Ukraine airstrike on bus in Russian-occupied Luhansk kills 9
World.content:
Russian authorities in the occupied territory say the drone attack caused injuries. Kyiv also destroyed another Wildberries warehouse.

A Ukrainian airstrike killed nine people in Ukraine's eastern, Russian-occupied Luhansk region on Wednesday, according to Leonid Pasechnik, leader of Russia's occupying forces there.

Pasechnik labeled the strike "a war crime," saying it had killed eight people on the spot and that another person, a 20-year-old woman, died of her injuries shortly thereafter.

The bus was said to have been carrying 15 people, with five more reported injured.

Ukraine keeps up strikes in Russia, destroys another major warehouse

With US-brokered peace talks failing to get off the ground and the Kremlin sticking to its maximalist demands before agreeing to end its four-and-a-half-year invasion, Kyiv and Moscow have continued to escalate their air campaigns.

Kyiv again targeted logistics infrastructure on Wednesday, using drones to destroy another Wildberries warehouse, this one in Russia's Tambov region, southeast of Moscow.

Tambov's governor said the 100,000 square-meter (1.1 million square-foot) facility — an area roughly the size of 14 soccer fields — had been "completely destroyed by fire."

Wildberries is Russia's biggest online retailer.

Ukrainian strikes on its facilities not only disrupt the Kremlin's military logistics — Kyiv says Wildberries aids the military war effort — they also strike at Russia's civilian economy and thus touch everyday Russians.

This week, Kyiv expanded its target list to include Russia's number two online retailer, Ozon.

In an analysis of satellite imagery, Reuters news agency estimated that at least 1.9 ​million square meters of warehouse space had been severely damaged in Ukrainian drone attacks on more than 20 Wildberries and Ozon facilities in recent weeks.

World.title: No, this wasn't a "completely normal summer", despite far-right climate denial
World.content:
Some political messaging denies the role of human-caused climate change in this summer's extreme heat. The science tells a different story.

As a summer of European extreme heat draws to a close, politicians are looking back at the toll. Germany recorded around 14,000 heat-related deaths, almost two-thirds in one scorching week of June alone. A Dutch bank estimated summer heat will cost the EU €180 billion ($209 billion) in lost GDP. And in June, European farmers lost approximately 9 million tons in grain crops.

Climate change, long a politically charged topic, has become a daily reality for people around the world. These effects and more are making it increasingly difficult to challenge what people are seeing with their own eyes.

Yet that hasn’t stopped the global populist right from trying. Richard Tice, deputy leader of the UK’s far-right Reform Party said "climate change has always happened, it always will," adding that it was arrogant to try to stop it. He encouraged the British public to enjoy the heat.

In the US, Harriet Hageman, a Republican politician and potentially Wyoming’s next senator, told far-right channel Real America’s Voice that Europe’s heatwave was business as usual. "It's called summer. Some years are hotter than others and some years are colder than others," she said. "But that's just the cyclical nature of weather."

And Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of Germany’s far-right AfD party told a journalist in recent days that it’s been a "completely normal summer." He dismissed climate change as "hype."



But claims like these don’t stand up to scientific scrutiny.

A pharmacy thermometer in Cologne hit a record-breaking 42.2°C as last month ranked among the two warmest ever recorded globally. Image: teutopress/picture alliance

As NASA states plainly: "Scientific evidence continues to show that human activities (primarily the human burning of fossil fuels) have warmed Earth’s surface and its ocean basins, which in turn have continued to impact Earth’s climate."

This was not 'a completely normal summer'

This summer has been historically hot. Independent climate monitoring bodies, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the US, the Copernicus Climate Change Service in the European Union and the Japan Meterological Agency , all called last month either the joint-warmest or joint-second warmest month on record.

The conditions have led energy plants to halt production, outdated concrete motorways blowing up, and older buildings overheating during the day and barely cooling down at night — threatening inhabitants with exposure to heat stress.

The extreme heat was felt almost everywhere on the globe. According to NOAA’s data, it was the warmest July ever for North America, Africa and Asia.

The continental United States just surpassed its warmest July records. They were previously set in 1936, during the infamous Dust Bowl that scorched the US Great Plains with extreme temperatures, and in 2012, when North America suffered an extreme heatwave.

And the daily average sea surface temperature hit its highest level since records began in 1979 — reaching 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) this month. That’s a result of both human-driven warming as well as El Nino, a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures.

How climate change supercharged this summer's fires

In Spain, the far-right Vox party said fires — which burned more than 254,000 hectares of land across the country this season — were not connected to climate change.

Yet experts agree rising global temperatures played a major role in the intense wildfire season that also scorched large parts of France and Canada. That’s because extreme heat creates ideal conditions for wildfires to start and spread.

Attribution science clearly connects hotter temperatures with a far greater likelihood of wildfires Image: Angelos Tzortzinis/AFP

A field of climate research called attribution science explores the extent to which climate change exacerbates extreme weather events like this summer’s wildfires. Using models, researchers compare the likelihood and intensity of an event in today's climate with a simulated world in which there is no human-caused warming.

Analyses done this summer show that hotter global temperatures created conditions that made the wildfires in Spain 20 times more likely to happen, and twice as probable in France.

This is due to a phenomenon known as weather whiplash, where ecosystems swing dramatically between wet and dry conditions.

When the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, rainfall is intensified, and plants grow. Then, in summer, that same warm atmosphere draws water from soil and plants, worsening drought and drying out vegetation, turning it into the perfect fuel for fires.

"We know — and this is mathematically proven — that the probability of having fire weather that can sustain and create this kind of event has been altered by climate change," Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, told DW about this summer’s fires in Spain and France.

Climate change’s ripple effects

Overall, this summer has left its mark in numerous ways that are impossible to ignore.

Bodies of water across Europe are drying out under the intense heat. Parts of the Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, making it impossible for ships to pass through in some spots.

Drought and heat have pushed the Rhine to historic lows, forcing cargo ships to carry lighter loads Image: Martin Meissner/AP Photo/picture alliance

This has a number of knock-on effects. Drinking water costs could rise dramatically as much of Germany’s clean water first passes through reed-filled riverbanks that are crucial for filtration.

Supply chains are also be disrupted, as vessels can’t carry as much cargo when water levels are lower, increasing prices across the economy in products like steel or petroleum.

In America, drought conditions are wreaking havoc on crops and livestock. In June, the US Department of Agriculture said the 10-month stretch from August 2025 to May 2026 was the nation’s driest period since 1976-77.

Now, 59% of the country’s sorghum is being grown in areas experiencing drought . More than half the nation's cattle production and almost two-thirds of spring wheat production is happening under water scarcity.

Such conditions can put direct strain on the country's food supply, increase prices and threaten rural livelihoods.

By any measurement — thermometers, drought maps, or death tolls — and in much of the world, this summer has been historically extreme.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: Tim Curry, of 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show,' dies at 80
World.content:
The gender-bending role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter put Curry on the map in 1975. He then went on to play a number of villainous roles like Gomez Addams, Pennywise and Bill Sikes, but also Mozart and William Shakespeare.

Actor Tim Curry died at the age of 80, Variety, TMZ and other celebrity news outlets reported on Wednesday.

A cause of death was not immediately given but Curry had been in poor health for some time following a severe stroke that left him confined to a wheelchair and wrote in his memoir "Vagabond" last year that he was still not able to walk.

Curry won Laurence Olivier and Tony Award nominations for his work on stage in the UK and the US, as well delivering Emmy-winning TV performances later in his career.

Curry was another member of the class of 1946 to feature in 'Home Alone 2,' as was the current US President Donald Trump Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Who was Tim Curry?

Curry was born in Cheshire into a Navy family in 1946 and spent his life bouncing around an array of different homes in the UK and even Hong Kong. He ultimately went to school in Bath, impressing as a soprano singer, and university in Birmingham.

He played in London musicals in the late 60s and early 70s seeking his big break, which came in a 1973 unusual musical ultimately destined to graduate to the silver screen.

One review at the time referred to Dr. Frank-N-Furter as an 'ambisextrous' character in the cult musical Image: Collection Christophel/picture alliance

Curry was given the role of the lingerie-clad sweet singing transvestite Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic film "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" in 1975. Despite the very German sounding name and initial rehearsals with a German and American accent, he ultimately played the mad scientist with an exaggerated upper class Belgravia accent, in what a Guardian newspaper 1973 review referred to as a "garishly Bowiesque performance as the ambisextrous doctor."

Curry played everyone's least favorite clown — at least in Derry, Maine — Pennywise in 1990 Image: United Archives/Impress/picture alliance

He went on to play an array of other roles that involved elaborate costumes, unusual mannerisms, and often a fairly pronounced dark but also comedic side in his career.

Curry was able to cross threatening Kermit the Frog with an antique pistol off his bucket list in 1996 Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

These included Gomez Addams in the "Addams Family Reunion" cinema reboot, Long John Silver in "Muppet Treasure Island," the suspicious Plaza Hotel concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Pennywise the Clown in a miniseries based on Stephen King's novel "It," and even as the voice of Chancellor Palpatine in "Star Wars: The Clone Wars."

In another Star Wars connection, Curry was even cast as the Joker for "Batman: The Animated Series," having been considered for the role in the 1989 film as well, until Mark Hamill supplanted him.

Curry took up the arm-kissing role of family patriarch Gomez in "Addams Family Reunion," the 1998 movie reboot of the hit TV series Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Curry also played some of history's most consequential figures like Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, William Shakespeare, and even King Arthur — albeit in the Monty Python musical stage show "Spamalot." He was also among the first actors to branch out into video game roles, perhaps most notably as the fictional Soviet military officer Anatoly Cherdenko in Command and Conquer: Red Alert 3.

As well as Mozart and Shakespeare, Curry played the 'Red Eminence' Cardinal Richelieu in "The Three Musketeers" released in 1993 Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

He released several solo studio albums and also contributed to various soundtrack records throughout his career, with his musical background apparent in many of his acting roles.

Edited by: Rana Taha
