World.title: Could Trump save Orbán’s international lobbying organisations from collapse?
World.content:
It had previously been suggested that former prime minister Viktor Orbán could, with Trump’s help, secure a deputy secretary-general’s post at the United Nations, granting him diplomatic immunity. Meanwhile, the MAGA movement associated with Trump could take over some of the international organisations established by Orbán’s governments and operate them as its own lobbying vehicles within the European Union – an economic and commercial rival.

A vast and costly international lobbying operation

Over 16 years, Viktor Orbán built not only a formidable, if politically unstable, power base in Hungary. In Brussels, too, he established an institutional network designed to support conservative and radical-right forces, influence policy debates and cultivate European alliances.

Following the electoral defeat, however, one of the system’s most important pillars – funding from the Hungarian state and its affiliated bodies – appears to be crumbling.

J. D. Vance in Budapest – the organiser is the MCC. Source: MCC

One of the network’s central players was the Brussels office of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC). Opened in 2022, the institution focused on issues favoured by the Orbán system and its wider alliance network, including migration, gender politics, climate change and the external funding of civil-society organisations in the European Union.

Its work was supported by an annual budget of more than €6 million – equivalent to between 1.8 billion and 2 billion forints – underpinned by assets worth roughly 500 billion forints provided by the Orbán government. This is what Péter Magyar’s government, backed by a two-thirds majority, effectively stripped from the MCC with a single stroke of the pen.

Alongside the MCC, the Danube Institute, The European Conservative magazine and the foundation behind CPAC Hungary were also part of the circle of organisations supported by the Orbán government with many billions of forints in public money.

The House of Hungary was another important element of the network. In 2021, the Hungarian state bought the Brussels building, dating from the 18th century, and opened it as an events venue ahead of Hungary’s EU presidency in 2024. The property is now standing empty, however, and no decision has been made on its future use.

Trump and Orbán in the White House last November. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Trump could rescue some institutions

After the change of government, the new administration ended or reviewed state support for several of these institutions. The MCC found itself in a particularly difficult position. Frank Furedi, the head of its Brussels organisation, has said that the centre could eventually be forced to close without a new source of funding, although it might continue operating on a smaller budget.

Expert assessments suggest, however, that maintaining a network on the scale and with the intensity seen during the Orbán era is no longer realistic.

This is where Donald Trump and the American MAGA movement could enter the picture. According to a Bloomberg analysis cited by Portfolio, programmes have already emerged in the United States to support European conservative civil-society organisations working on sovereignty, migration, censorship and “lawfare”.

If you missed – Fundamental changes in Hungary’s foreign policy reflected in new UN guidelines

The institutions linked to Orbán could therefore find new American backers – particularly as Trump’s allies are themselves seeking to strengthen ties with Europe’s radical right in order to expand their influence over EU affairs.

The question, then, is not necessarily whether Orbán’s Brussels network will disappear, but who will take over its funding, in what form it might survive and whose interests it would serve.

Influence is valuable amid mounting conflict

As is well known, neither Trump nor his movement regards the European Union or the NATO member states as allies in the same way as previous American administrations did. The threat of a tariff and trade war is gathering over both sides of the Atlantic; the dispute over Greenland remains unresolved; and Washington and Brussels do not necessarily share the same view on how to bring Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to an end.

There are also disagreements over American intervention in Iran and the regulation of US technology giants in Europe. For Trump, an effective lobbying organisation could therefore prove valuable on several fronts: in academia, among civil-society groups and in politics.

Hungarian FM Anita Orbán names new ambassadors: historians tapped for Paris and Warsaw

World.title: Renowned Hungarian author Péter Nádas dies
World.content:
World-renowned author Péter Nádas died on Wednesday morning in his home in Gombosszeg, in southwest Hungary, the author’s official Facebook page said.

Nádas was born in Budapest in 1942. He worked as a photographer and journalist at several outlets in the late 1950s and the ’60s. His first book, The Bible, was published in 1967. He published novels, dramas, essays continuously afterwards while continuing to work in journalism and the theatre. His seminal work, A book of memories, was published in 1986 in Hungarian and in 1997 in English. It was lauded as one of the outstanding achievements of post-war Hungarian writing, and one that had mapped out new ways of literary expression. His last book, Halott barataim (My dead friends), was published in 2025, MTI wrote.

Péter Nádas in 2025. Photo: Facebook/Nádas Péter

Throughout his career, Nádas was awarded the Kossuth and Jozsef Attila Prizes, the Szechenyi Prize, the Middle Cross of the Order of Merit of the Republic of Hungary, the Austrian State Prize for European Literature, and the Grand Cross of the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Nádas has lived and worked in the remote village of Gombosszeg in southwest Hungary since 1984. The family has asked the public to respect their privacy until further communication.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar commented on Nadas’s passing on Facebook, saying: “Kossuth prize holder, world-renowned author Péter Nádas passed away this morning. Farewell, Maestro!”

How a classic Hungarian comic heroine became a global animation sensation – Jucika racks up 60 million views!

Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony said on Facebook: “This country, this city has a lot to thank to Péter Nádas. We will now forever regret not to be able to repay that debt.” Nádas, an honorary citizen of Budapest, “has shown to the wide world where this city is in Europe,” he added.

“Péter Nádas represents simultaneously the highest levels of world literature and the most beautiful, delicate, heart-warming Hungarian literature,” Karácsony said.

World’s third public statue of Freddie Mercury unveiled on Lake Balaton – but it bears a striking resemblance to a Hungarian poet

World.title: Cause of poisoning at Debrecen battery plant revealed — but there is good news too
World.content:
We have previously read reports about battery plants and several companies in the battery industry allegedly seeking to evade Hungarian regulations, doing so with political backing and, when all else failed, simply paying derisory fines. The action taken over the latest incident at CATL’s Debrecen battery plant, however, could be good news for the workers there and their colleagues elsewhere in the sector. That is so even if, judging by the available evidence, the company appears to have made a serious mistake over personal protective equipment — and that mistake appears to have caused the problem.

Serious poisoning at Debrecen battery plant — but the factory reported it itself

Work has been suspended in three production areas at CATL’s Debrecen battery plant after elevated nickel exposure was identified in a total of nine employees. An official inspection found that the company had failed to provide the required personal protective equipment properly and in full. Proceedings have also been launched with a view to imposing a fine. Enikő Tompa, the Tisza Party’s MP for the area, has been particularly active in the case.

The incident came to light after CATL Hungary Kft reported seven cases to the occupational safety authority on August 10, followed by a further two on 13 August. The company then began the necessary investigation. According to information obtained by Debreciner, elevated nickel levels were detected in several cases during mandatory biological exposure monitoring involving more than 400 employees.

The good news, at any rate, is that the company did not attempt to cover up the incident but followed the appropriate procedure. This could prove important for the remaining 391 employees, particularly in light of previous cases in which companies opted to pay a fine while continuing to expose Hungarian and guest workers to danger.

Telex: Samsung’s Göd plant may have poisoned its workers for years because the Orbán government helped it

The Mikepércs Mothers for the Environment Association previously reported that, according to information in its possession, a cathode-powder spill may have occurred at the plant, sending heavy metals into the air. The civic group claimed that nickel and cobalt levels in some workers may have reached several times the permitted limit, and said it had also received reports of exposure to chromium and lithium.

Te Debrecen battery plant of the Chinese CATL. Photo: Facebook/Tompa Enikő

These claims, however, have not been confirmed by the official information currently available. The authorities have formally reported only elevated nickel exposure among nine employees.

Work halted in three areas as substantial fine looms

The occupational safety authority inspected the plant on 11 and 12 August. It found that the employer had failed to provide personal protective equipment adequately. As a result, from 10.30 AM on 12 August until the breaches were rectified, work was prohibited in the cathode- and anode-foil laser-cutting, anode- and cathode-foil winding, and cell-drying areas of the cell-production building.

According to a follow-up inspection carried out by the authority on 17 August, CATL had not resumed the suspended activities. Proceedings to impose a fine are nevertheless under way over the breaches.

Enikő Tompa, the local MP, contacted the Ministry of Rural and Settlement Development to request information about the incident. She said that, if the violations were confirmed, CATL could face a substantial fine. She cited the case of SK On in Iváncsa, which was fined 100 million forints for breaches of occupational safety regulations.

Meanwhile, according to government information, the investor was granted an occupancy permit for the first phase of the project on 25 August after remedying the outstanding deficiencies. Permission for the second phase had previously been refused because the completed building had not been shown correctly on the site plan.

Debrecen’s municipal authorities said they had learnt of the incident from the press and had no jurisdiction over the matter. CATL did not respond to Debreciner’s request for comment.

World.title: Romanian tour developer Christian Tour registers 15% higher net profit in H1 2026
World.content:
Christian Tour (BVB: TRIP), a major integrated tourism platform and the first Romanian tour operator listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, announced its results for the first half of 2026. According to the company press release, total revenues increased by 12% year-over-year to RON 184.7 million, while EBITDA advanced at a faster pace, by 24%, to RON 9.8 million, resulting in an EBITDA margin of 5.3%, compared with 4.8% for H1 2025. Net profit reached RON 6.3 million, up 15%.

“Despite inflationary pressure, geopolitical uncertainty and higher costs across the travel industry, we delivered record first-half booking sales, while EBITDA grew twice as fast as revenues,” said Cristian Pandel (in photo), Founder and CEO of Christian Tour.

Commercial performance remained strong despite a more challenging operating environment. Sales at booking date reached a record RON 460.1 million for the first half, increasing by 8% year-over-year, while average revenue per booking rose by 18% to EUR 505.

The increase in average transaction value more than offset lower passenger and booking volumes, supported by the company’s ability to adapt its commercial mix toward higher-value travel categories, including organized circuits, exotic and long-haul destinations and specialized travel experiences.

Packages remained Christian Tour’s largest business segment in H1 2026, generating booking-date sales of RON 331.5 million, up 9% year-over-year, and representing approximately 72% of total booking-date sales. Groups & Experiences recorded the strongest organic growth, with booking-date sales increasing by 18% year-over-year to RON 72.8 million, supported by demand for organized circuits, exotic and long-haul destinations and other higher-value experiences.

Flights, Bus & Accommodation remained broadly stable at RON 50.3 million, while Other segments decreased 44% to RON 5.5 million as the company continued to prioritize profitable growth in its core activities rather than pursuing volume in lower-margin categories.

Christian Tour generated RON 76.8 million in net cash from operating activities during H1 2026, reflecting the seasonal cash-flow dynamics of the business ahead of the peak summer travel period.

Separately, the company’s financial position strengthened significantly following the IPO. As of June 30, 2026, Christian Tour had RON 182.6 million in cash and cash equivalents and no outstanding bank borrowings, resulting in a net cash position of approximately RON 143.7 million, compared with net debt of approximately RON 38.7 million at the end of 2025.

At the same date, the company had RON 265.6 million in contract liabilities, largely representing customer advances for travel services yet to be delivered, providing visibility over activity and revenue recognition during the second half of the year.

Christian Tour also continued to advance the growth priorities presented during the IPO. In digitalization, the company continued to develop its digital ecosystem, with the flight module scheduled for launch in Q3 2026, while dynamic packaging capabilities, an AI-assisted Trip Builder and the Hello Romania domestic tourism platform are expected to enter testing during Q4 2026. In customer loyalty, Travel Prime reached approximately 2,000 active subscribers, with members generating approximately EUR 8.3 million in cumulative sales since joining the program.

Christian Tour’s performance in the first half of the year also reflects the continued resilience of Romanian demand for international travel despite pressure on household purchasing power. According to data published by the National Bank of Romania, Romanians spent EUR 4.88 billion on travel abroad during the first six months of 2026, approximately 18% more than in the same period of 2025.

For the full year 2026, Christian Tour targets RON 1.042 billion in sales at booking date, RON 843.0 million in IFRS revenue, RON 46.3 million in EBITDA and RON 33.2 million in net profit.

World.title: Romanian Parliament again passes controversial integrity law invalidating mandate of Timisoara mayor
World.content:
The Romanian Senate, acting as the decision-making chamber in the case, passed the controversial law governing the National Integrity Agency, or ANI, on Wednesday, August 26, after it was amended to take into account decisions of the Constitutional Court. The bill passed the upper house of Parliament with 106 votes “for” and 19 “against," according to Digi24.

Earlier this month, in a 5-3 vote, the Romanian Constitutional Court approved the so-called “Fritz Amendment,” introduced by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) into the law governing ANI. The same law is a PNRR milestone with EUR 770 million attached to it.

A new vote in Parliament was necessary after CCR judges ruled that parts of the initial bill were unconstitutional. The problematic provisions concerned the asset declarations of public officials, which would have made them partially public.

The most controversial amendment of the bill, however, was approved by CCR. It stipulates that elected officials in office lose their mandate within 30 days if they receive a final decision of incompatibility or conflict of interest, even if this decision predates the new law. This means that the law would apply retroactively.

The "Fritz amendment"

In June, Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Timișoara Court of Appeal ruling that found Timișoara mayor and leader of Save Romania Union (USR), Dominic Fritz, in an administrative conflict of interest. As such, under the amendment, Fritz is expected to lose his position within 30 days of the legislation entering into force. The USR leader announced that he will challenge the decision at the European Court of Human Rights, and argued that the measure applies to a past action, although the Romanian Constitution states that laws should apply only to the future.

During debates in the Senate before the final vote, PSD representatives stood by the amendment. “Fritz was convicted by the courts in Romania. Fritz must go home. You cannot sacrifice Romania’s interests just to sacrifice Fritz,” said Social Democratic Senate leader Daniel Zamfir after the final vote in the Senate.

“This is how the establishment of communism began in Romania: through laws that eliminated political opponents. You deserve the phrase – the red plague,” responded USR Senate leader Sorin Șipoș.

The Liberals (PNL), allies of USR, also voted in favor of adopting this bill, although they initially opposed the amendment targeting Dominic Fritz.

"The vote on the ANI law was a difficult one for PNL, because a provision that changes the rules in the middle of the game is deeply immoral and unfair, regardless of the legal tricks used to explain it,” said PNL leader and interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan in a post on Facebook. He argued that Romania direly needs the EUR 770 million in PNRR funds connected to passing the law.

“The lack of these European funds would have implications for the country’s budget, with investments being financed to a significant extent from this money. In addition, the risk of Romania being severely downgraded in terms of its sovereign rating would increase significantly, with serious consequences for the standard of living of all Romanians,” he concluded. Nevertheless, Bolojan said the law could be changed in the future.

Earlier this week, the political groups to which PNL and USR belong at the European level, namely the European People’s Party (EPP) and Renew Europe, asked European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen not to allocate the PNRR funds connected to the integrity law to Romania due to the retroactive application of the law.

Less transparency in officials’ assets

The incompatibility section is not the only change in the new law. Under the new version, even less information will be published about the assets of public officials than provided for in the initial bill. A “public financial interests sheet” will be generated, which will not provide details about assets owned by a public official, while their value will be included in ranges.

For example, in the case of cars, the year of manufacture or model will no longer be declared, while in the case of homes and land, addresses, areas or values will no longer be published.

World.title: Via Carpatia: 3,000 km unified road network project to cross seven CEE countries, including Romania
World.content:
Via Carpatia, a new international road corridor that will cross seven countries in Central and Eastern Europe, starting from the city of Klaipėda, Lithuania, and reaching Thessaloniki, Greece, is currently being built and connected, according to Greek publication Caradmotor. The same network will pass through Romania.

Major road infrastructure projects have been at the center of investments across Europe to strengthen transport, trade, and connections between countries in recent years. A prominent project, Via Carpatia is meant to be a unified network of highways and national roads with common technical characteristics and high standards.

At the same time, the project's objective is also to provide a significant economic boost to the regions through which it will pass, by developing freight transport and international road connections.

The project was first presented in 2006, when Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary signed a joint declaration to create a unified north-south road corridor.

The current form of the Via Carpatia was finalized in 2010, when Romania, Bulgaria and Greece joined the initiative, extending the route to Thessaloniki. In total, the highway will cross Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Greece.

Although the initial plan provided for Thessaloniki as the final destination, recent developments are extending this corridor even further. Turkey has been included as a partner in the project, through a declaration providing for its connection to Via Carpatia. More precisely, the highway will have a southern branch that will cross Bulgaria and reach the Bulgarian-Turkish border, in the Svilengrad–Edirne area, from where it will continue towards Istanbul.

The first works for the implementation of the project gradually began during 2010-2015, mainly in Poland and Hungary, where existing national roads were modernized and transformed into modern high-speed highways.

Back in 2025, then-acting president Ilie Bolojan said that Via Carpatia was "one of the most important projects" for Romania. He also detailed the exact route through Romania.

“On the territory of our country, there is an expressway route that enters Romania from Debrecen, through Oradea, goes south, along the Arad-Timișoara route, and then towards the Constanța area, towards Bulgaria, Calafat, and towards Serbia, towards Belgrade and then towards the Balkan Peninsula," Bolojan said, cited by Euronews Romania. He also underlined the importance of the Constanța port and its connections to Europe.

The total length of the highway network is estimated at approximately 3,000 kilometers, and the project is expected to be completed in 2030, according to the most optimistic estimates.

World.title: Fast food chain Popeyes expands in Romania with first restaurant in Timisoara
World.content:
US fast-food chain Popeyes announced the opening of its first restaurant in Timisoara, western Romania.

The chain, which launched in Romania four years ago, currently has 23 restaurants, of which 8 are in Bucharest, 2 in Iasi, 2 in Constanta, 2 in Cluj, and one in Pitești, Craiova, Buzău, Ploiești, Brașov, Sibiu, Oradea, Suceava and Târgu Mureș.

"The inauguration of the first Popeyes restaurant in Timisoara represents an essential step in our 2026 expansion plan in Romania.," said Jakub Aleksandrowicz, Popeyes Marketing Director for Central and Eastern Europe.

Founded in 1972, Popeyes is one of the world's most famous fast-food brands. The brand owns 4,800 restaurants worldwide.

Polish company Rex Concepts, the exclusive master franchisee for Burger King and Popeyes in Poland, Romania and the Czech Republic, debuted on the Warsaw Stock Exchange at a valuation of PLN 1.3 billion (approximately EUR 315.3 million), marking the sixth listing of a Polish company since the beginning of the year, according to Profit.ro.

The company said it would use the funds to expand the network to 850 restaurants in Poland, Romania and the Czech Republic over the next 6 years. Last year, Rex Concepts opened 59 restaurants, 20 of which were in Romania, reaching a total of 159 directly operated locations at the end of December.

World.title: Romania’s First Lady, UNICEF reaffirm commitment to children's rights and participation
World.content:
The First Lady of Romania, Mirabela Grădinaru, met on Tuesday, August 25, with a UNICEF delegation led by Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF Regional Director for Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, to discuss promoting children's rights and strengthening the participation of children and young people in decisions that affect their lives.

The discussions highlighted the progress made by Romania in promoting the views of children and young people in the public decision-making process, including through legislation adopted in 2024, which strengthens children's opportunities to contribute to the development of policies and legislation that concern them.

“I know how important it is for every child to have access to care, protection, education and opportunities to develop. We must never forget that they are our number one priority. The way we care for children today will shape tomorrow's society. I welcome the continuation of cooperation between Romania and UNICEF to support children and families, to ensure that the voices of young people are heard and to make sure that every child can reach their full potential, regardless of where they live or the circumstances in which they were born,” said Mirabela Grădinaru.

In turn, Edouard Beigbeder said that Romania has taken important steps to strengthen children's participation and integrate it into the decision-making process, and its experience can offer valuable lessons both to countries in Europe and to those outside the region.

The meeting addressed Romania's experience in implementing the integrated community services model, as well as the implementation of the European Child Guarantee. Opportunities to promote internationally the lessons learned and good practices developed in Romania were also discussed.

The discussions also focused on continuing cooperation in areas such as children's participation, education, combating climate change, online safety and preventing violence against children.

Earlier this summer, Romania’s First Lady presented the "Romania in Light" project during a panel within the NATO Summit in Ankara. The project focuses on protecting children in the context of technological development and educating them in an environment where the virtual world supports learning and development.

World.title: Social Monitor: Romania exceeds EU average for household internet access but ranks last in digital skills
World.content:
Romania has moved above the European Union average for household internet connectivity, with 95.47% of homes having access in 2025. However, the country ranks last in the EU for the share of people with at least basic digital skills, according to Eurostat data analyzed by the Social Monitor, a Friedrich Ebert Foundation project.

The share of Romanian households with internet access increased by almost 10 percentage points from 86.24% in 2020. Romania now ranks 12th among the EU’s 27 member states and exceeds the bloc’s average of 94.76%.

The Netherlands recorded the highest household connectivity rate at 99.28%, followed by Luxembourg at 99%, and Malta at 97.77%. Croatia ranked last with 87.91%, behind Greece at 88.73%, and Lithuania at 89.35%.

Internet use among Romania’s general population also rose significantly, reaching 93.15% in 2025 compared with 78.46% in 2020, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ireland had the EU’s highest internet usage rate at 99.78%, followed by Denmark and the Netherlands, both at 99.71%. The lowest rates were recorded in Croatia at 85.9%, Bulgaria at 86.85%, and Greece at 89.15%.

“The data also show that the share of Romanians who have never used the internet fell sharply to just 4.91%, compared with 14.05% in 2020. However, Romania continues to perform below the EU average on this indicator,” reads the Social Monitor report.

The highest proportions of people who had never gone online were recorded in Croatia at 10.33%, Portugal at 9.56%, and Greece at 9.14%, while Ireland, the Netherlands, and Sweden had the lowest rates.

According to the same source, despite the improvement in access and usage, only 31.84% of Romania’s population has basic or above-basic digital skills, placing the country last in the EU and well below the bloc’s average of 60.4%.

Bulgaria followed with 38.26%, while Slovenia and Latvia recorded 46.5% and 48.43%, respectively. The Netherlands led the ranking at 83.61%, followed by Ireland at 82.82%, and Denmark at 81.45%.

Digital skills are assessed based on activities performed online or with software by people aged 16 to 74. The evaluation covers information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety, and problem-solving.

World.title: L’Étape Romania by Tour de France brings traffic restrictions to Bucharest this weekend
World.content:
The fifth edition of L’Étape Romania by Tour de France will take place in Bucharest on Sunday, August 30, with almost 2,000 cyclists expected to participate. As such, traffic will be restricted on several major streets and boulevards in the city between 7 a.m. and 2 p.m.

The restrictions will affect Unirii Boulevard, Mircea Vodă Boulevard, Splaiul Unirii in the direction of Bucharest, Decebal Boulevard, Basarabia Boulevard, Calea Victoriei, Regina Elisabeta Boulevard, Schitu Măgureanu Boulevard, Știrbei Vodă and Ion Câmpineanu streets, Kiseleff Road, Buzești, Berzei, Vasile Pârvan and Bogdan Petriceicu Hașdeu streets, and Libertății Boulevard.

The organizers said they were working with the Traffic Police to establish alternative routes.

Constituției Square will serve as the starting and finishing point for all three races.

The 14 km City Adventure route, open to participants aged 7 and over, will begin at 7:30 a.m. The 42 km Ride will start at 8:30 a.m. and is open to cyclists aged at least 15, while the 85 km Race will begin at 10 a.m. and has the same minimum age requirement.

The race routes are scheduled to close fully at 1 p.m., followed by the awards ceremony at 1:30 p.m.

Almost 2,000 cyclists from 17 countries and more than 170 cities and towns have registered. International participants include cyclists from Bulgaria, Greece, the United Kingdom, Serbia, Moldova, Ukraine, Germany, Cyprus, France, Belgium, and Austria.

The 42 km route is expected to attract the largest field, with approximately 1,200 cyclists at the start. More than 250 children and teenagers under the age of 18 have also registered.

“To make sure race day is exactly what every participant has been looking forward to, my advice is simple: have your bike checked - brakes, tires and gears - and don’t leave this until the last minute. Also, avoid overtraining during this final week: your fitness has already been built, and now it’s all about rest, hydration and sleep. Don’t try anything new on race day, whether it’s equipment or nutrition, and come to the Race Village on Saturday to collect your race kit, so you can enjoy every kilometer on Sunday morning without a worry,” said Răzvan Jugănaru, MTB Academy, event organizer.

Registration is open until the end of August 26 or until all available places are filled. Participants must collect their race kits on August 29, between 10 a.m. and 7 p.m., from the Race Village in Constituției Square.

Further details are available here.

World.title: Drone fragment discovered on beach in Romanian seaside resort Olimp
World.content:
Video

A drone fragment was found on Wednesday, August 26, on a beach in the Romanian Black Sea resort of Olimp. The fragment was brought onto the beach by waves and was noticed by several people who notified the authorities.

Authorities restricted access to the area, and specialists went to the scene to analyze the object. Around 10:30 AM, they decided to detonate a part of the fragments that contained explosives. A separate drone fragment is still on the beach and does not contain explosives, according to Digi24.

Another drone fragment was discovered on Tuesday, August 24, near the Casino in Constanţa. The object was noticed near the seafront by people walking in the area. They notified the authorities, who recovered the object, which most likely did not have an explosive payload.

Drones on the Black Sea coast

The discoveries in Olimp and Constanța are part of a series of similar incidents reported in recent weeks on the Romanian coast. Fragments or devices that authorities determined came from drones have been found in several coastal areas, including Costinești and Saturn.

Earlier this month, the Romanian Army also recovered drone fragments from other Black Sea resort towns like Port Tomis, Eforie Sud, Eforie Nord, Costinești, and Năvodari. Around the same time, other drone parts were spotted near a Constanţa beach. In all cases, specialized crews intervened to remove the fragments.

According to the Ministry of Defense, Romania has seen 59 attacks near its borders with Ukraine since the start of the year, and 25 unauthorized entrys in its airspace. Four drones were also brought down by Romanian or allied fighter jets after infringing the national airspace.

Increased defense measures

Romania's Senate Defense Committee met yesterday to discuss an incident from the beginning of June, in the Port of Constanţa, when a Ukrainian drone self-detonated after it was lost from control. General Dragoş Iacob, deputy chief of the Defense Staff, said that following the incident, the security of maritime ports had been strengthened, and the warning system was working better than three months ago. Representatives of the Naval Forces, as well as of the Ministry of Defense, SRI and STS, were present at the meeting.

“There are several questions that institutions need to answer in the chain of response. Who detects the drone, who identifies what type it is, who coordinates, who tracks, and who destroys the drone,” said liberal Nicoleta Pauliuc, chairwoman of the Senate Defense Committee, cited by Radio Romania Actualitati.

World.title: Romania Passes Controversial Law on Officials’ Integrity to Access EU Funds
World.content:
A plenary session of the parliament in Bucharest, Romania, 05 May 2026. Photo: EPA/Robert Ghement.

Romania’s parliament on Wednesday overwhelmingly approved a new integrity law intended to strengthen sanctions for abuses by public officials, in order to allow the country access to a 770-million-euro EU-funded National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The legislation was also supported by the centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL), which is part of the interim government led by Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, alongside two smaller centrist parties.

“Although we initially opposed the law in its current form, we decided to vote in favour because the country’s interest in meeting the PNRR milestones takes precedence over any other debate,” Bolojan said. He added that the PNL would seek to amend the law in the near future.

The law revises Romania’s rules on public officials’ asset and interest declarations, and strengthens the penalties if discrepancies or conflict of interest are determined. It also replaces detailed public wealth declarations with financial-interest forms that disclose less information about officials’ assets and holdings.

But it has sparked controversy after the Social Democratic Party (PSD), with support from the far-right Alliance for Unity of Romanians (AUR), introduced a provision stipulating that officials who have been found responsible in conflict-of-interest cases and whose three-year sanction period barring them from public office temporarily has not yet expired, would have their mandates terminated within 30 days of the law entering into force.

The amendment has been criticised as being specifically aimed at Dominic Fritz, the mayor of the western city of Timisoara and president of the centrist Save Romania Union (USR), part of the interim government.

Fritz, a German national who was first elected mayor in 2020, was found to have been involved in an administrative conflict of interest related to an urban planning document he approved that year.

Critics, including USR and PNL members as well as civil society representatives, have argued that the amendment could violate the principle of non-retroactivity and amount to the use of the law against political opponents.

The criticism has also been echoed at European level. The centre-right European People’s Party and liberal Renew Europe in the European Parliament groups on Monday asked European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to withhold the 770 million euros from Romania, citing concerns over the rule of law.

The integrity law is part of a broader package of reforms Romania has committed to adopt by the end of August in order to unlock further EU funding under PNRR. European funds are vital to Romania’s strained budget, supporting healthcare, education and infrastructure projects. EU funding is equivalent to around a third of the country’s GDP.

The present political crisis stems from Romania’s prolonged political instability. Last June, a coalition comprising the PSD, PNL and two smaller centre-right parties took office, with a primary mandate to stabilise the economy.

However, a series of unpopular austerity measures introduced by Ilie Bolojan to curb the deficit placed increasing strain on the coalition. Tensions came to a head in May , when the PSD withdrew its support, deepening the political turmoil.

The PSD subsequently allied with the far-right AUR to oust the government. Since then, Bolojan has been in a caretaker position, after two nominations for premier made by President Nicusor Dan were rejected by the main political parties.

World.title: Kosovo’s Ruling Party Optimistic About Resolving Deadlock Over New President
World.content:
Photos of Kosovo’s presidents to date on the wall at the presidency office. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja.

Vetevendosje deputy leader Glauk Konjufca expressed optimism on Wednesday that an agreement can be reached with the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, to give the country a new president when the leaders of two parties, Albin Kurti and Lumir Abdixhiku respectively, hold their next talks on the troubled issue.

Kurti and Abdixhiku are expected to meet this week to discuss concrete names following two previous meetings in recent weeks in which they both said they have been focused more on “principles” of a deal which would avoid new potential snap elections, the fourth within less than two years

“I consider that there is a great probability of having a [new] president, an agreement on a president,” Konjufca said.

“Vetevendosje is ready, Prime Minister [Albin] Kurti is ready. We have [proposals for] names but, I am sorry, I will not share them with you because then the negotiation process would lose its meaning,” he added.

Konjufca’s comments came amid political deadlock, with the parliament derived from the June 7 polls yet to be inaugurated.

MPs have failed for three weeks to elect a new parliament leadership, creating a fresh institutional logjam as the provisional parliament speaker, Avni Dehari from Vetevendosje, refuses to resume the inaugural session which started on August 6. Vetevendosje is refusing to submit a name for the speaker, as it first demands an agreement with other parties on the election of a new president.

Parliament’s rules require him to invite the MPs to a session every 48 hours until they elect a speaker.

But the last time Dehari actually presided over a session was on August 8, and that session lasted only a few minutes after Vetevendosje leader and incumbent Prime Minister Kurti asked for “more time” for negotiations with other parties about a new president.

In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting them well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats and has insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti is likely to obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved. The parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new assembly, otherwise a new election will be triggered.

With two other opposition parties, Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and the Alliance, AAK, snubbing Kurti’s calls for further meetings while holding daily makeshift sessions in the parliamentary chamber, the LDK is the only party who could strike a deal over the presidency.

“As far as I am aware of, there is still no exact date for the new meeting [between Kurti and Abdixhiku],” Konjufca said. But he added: “They will meet to propose concrete names and I believe that new President of Kosovo will derive from those names.”

World.title: North Macedonia Sees Drop in New School Pupils amid Demographic Woes
World.content:
A child near North Macedonia’s capital, Skopje, going to school. Photo: Robert Atanasovski.

In the latest indication of the country’s demographic problems, Education Minister Vesna Janevska said on Tuesday that enrolment for the 2026-27 school year, while still not final, is already sharply below last year’s 17,921 first-graders.

“We expect this trend to continue next year, which is disappointing,” Janevska told media.

The decline is even more striking over a longer period. In the 2016-17 school year, 23,266 children entered first grade (f, data from the State Statistical Office shows. The number fell to 21,656 the following year and, despite occasional slight increases, continued a broadly downward trend.

By 2025-26, it had dropped to 17,921. The current preliminary figure of 14,500 means the country has lost about 8,800 first-graders, or nearly 38 per cent, in just a decade.

The shrinking cohorts are already forcing changes to the school network. Janevska said that around 200 fewer classes will operate in primary education this year, while secondary education will have around 100 fewer classes.

The government also expects 26 rural schools to close during the school year because they have either too few or no newly-enrolled first-graders.

Some have only five to eight pupils in total, Janevska explained, arguing that keeping very small schools open can leave children in combined classes with pupils from several grades, limiting both the quality of teaching and opportunities for socialisation.

She said that pupils would generally be transferred to larger schools, but that combined classes in smaller schools would still remain where necessary, particularly where they are at a significant distance from more populated areas.

Demographer Donco Gerasimovski, a former director of the State Statistical Office, told Meta.mk news website that low birth rates and the emigration of young families are driving the decline.

Gerasimovski noted that many children also disappear from school rolls during a school year as families leave the country.

“According to my calculations, we ‘lose’ between 1,500 and 2,000 pupils in just one school year because of emigration,” he told Meta.mk.

The shrinking number of first-graders is only the clearest visible signs of a demographic decline that has been building for years.

Over the past three-and-a-half decades, the small landlocked country has failed to produce tangible economic and democratic uptick that could have kept people from leaving, or join the EU, in large part due to the former Greek blockade over its name and the current Bulgarian impasse that centres around contested identity issues.

The results of the last national headcount carried out in 2021, showed the country’s population has shrunk by 9.2 per cent over two decades since the previous census, from roughly 2.1 million to just over 1.8 million.

World.title: Plea Deals Reveal Logistics of Smuggling Macedonian Marijuana into Serbia
World.content:
Shortly after midnight on January 15 this year, a truck crossed from North Macedonia into Serbia. Several hours later, having crossed the length of the country, it caught fire near Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad.

According to paperwork, the truck was carrying textiles for export to Britain. In reality, it was stuffed with tonnes of marijuana; the smugglers set it on fire to cover their tracks.

Two weeks later, police seized five tonnes of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, near the central Serbian town of Krusevac.

According to plea bargains reached last week between prosecutors in North Macedonia and two of the smugglers, the January shipment was just one of five carried out between mid-2025 and early 2026.

More people are under investigation. Sources close to the probe say prosecutors in North Macedonia are also looking into the finances of three companies tied to Skopje-based Alfapharm Group, which allegedly served as a front for the drugs production.

The case is the latest to raise questions about North Macedonia’s legal medicinal marijuana industry, legalised in 2016, and whether it is fuelling the smuggling. In recent years, 14 firms have lost their permits to grow medicinal marijuana for failing to comply with the law, the Health Ministry said.

World.title: Riots, Teargas and ‘Gruesome Photos’ Behind Serbian Photographer’s Success
World.content:
An Orthodox priest talks to a young man during street protests in Belgrade. A police cordon faces the crowd in Serbia’s capital, holding plastic shields. A wounded demonstrator lies prone as riot police run past him.

These images date back to March 2011, when protesters packed the streets after the arrest of Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic. They were the first photos that Andrej Cukic sent to EPA Images (European Pressphoto Agency). Now he is set to lead the organization, as editor-in-chief.

“I was in the right place at the right time,” he tells BIRN. “I had some gruesome photos. Somebody thought that they were very good, and they ran them, and the photos were kind of published everywhere.”

The photos led to Cukic gaining regular work from Belgrade for EPA Images, an international news photo agency based in Frankfurt. BIRN has a contract with EPA and regularly uses its images.

World.title: Greek Neo-Nazi Casts Himself as Political Martyr Ahead of Prison Release
World.content:
On the Greek capital’s bustling Omonia Square, a group of young men held Greek flags and chanted: “Ilias, stay strong on the road to freedom” and “Remember Ilias, we are with you”.

It was July 20 and Ilias Kasidiaris - on day release from prison - was inaugurating the offices of a new party he had announced the previous month.

Convicted in 2020 of directing a criminal organisation, Kasidiaris has no legal grounds to lead a political party, but media reports this month suggest a relative of his has submitted a request to do so before the Supreme Court.

Addressing his supporters, Kasidiaris called on them to gather outside Domokos prison come mid-September, when he is due to be released.

Together, he said, they would “send a message of resistance to all those who are selling out Greece”, and vowed to run in the next parliamentary election, expected in the spring of next year.

World.title: Bulgaria Violated Rights of Roma Families by Demolishing Settlement, Court Rules
World.content:
Bulgaria breached the human rights of dozens of Roma families in Sofia by demolishing their homes without giving them a chance to contest the decision, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on Tuesday.

The government must pay 10,000 euro in damages to each party to the case and reform its demolition procedures.

The demolition took place in Sofia’s Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in August 2023, despite residents insisting that the authorities had not consulted them over the plans. Some of the families said they had lived in their homes since the 1950s.

The authorities insisted that they had carried out a formal process for issuing demolition orders. This was denied by the residents, who said the authorities deliberately concealed their intentions, gave evasive answers to repeated requests for information and refused to engage directly with the community.

The court ruled that Bulgaria had violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects family life and homes. It found that residents had no effective procedure to challenge the plans for demolition based on their personal circumstances, including length of residence, vulnerability and the availability of alternative housing.

The court also ruled, however, that the residents held no property rights in the demolished houses that would be recognized under Bulgarian law.

The ruling is not yet final and Bulgaria has three months to request that the case be referred for further review. The residents may make a similar application.

The flattening of Roma settlements in Bulgaria has become a repeated problem and a source of tension between the ethnic minority and local authorities. Demolitions also took place in the Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in 2017.

The ECHR has now heard four cases involving Roma settlement demolitions since 2012. In 2025, BIRN covered two similar cases: in April 2025, despite an ECHR ruling warning the municipality not to “proceed with the demolition of the homes of the applicants until further notice”, authorities still flattened houses in the enclave which had been there for decades.

A similar operation followed in the town of Stara Zagora in August the same year.

World.title: Serbia Again Requests “Humanitarian” Release of Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic has once again called for the release of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic. On Tuesday, he asked the UN war crimes court in The Hague to consider a new request by the family of the former Bosnian Serb military leader.

Vujic made the plea in a letter to Graciela Gatti Santana, the president of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, IRMCT. It follows last week’s decision by the IRMCT to reject a request by Mladic’s defence for conditional early release and transfer to Serbia on health grounds.

Vujic noted a report by the medical officer at the detention unit in The Hague stating that Mladic had entered the final phase of his life, after a rapid decline in his health. The minister argued that, under these circumstances, Mladic should be allowed to spend his final days in Serbia. The government has offered to transfer him to Belgrade’s Military Medical Academy and accept restrictions and monitoring imposed by the court.

In last week’s decision rejecting an early release, the IRMCT ruled that Mladic was receiving comprehensive medical care and assistance, as well as an exceptional visitation regime allowing meaningful contact with his family. It said that his condition alone did not justify humanitarian early release, given the gravity of his genocide conviction and life sentence. The court stressed that it would continue to protect Mladic’s fundamental rights and dignity.

This is not the first time that Mladic’s defence has sought his release on humanitarian grounds. During his time in custody in the Netherlands, Mladic has had several serious medical problems and has suffered two strokes and a heart attack.

In June 2025, Mladic’s lawyers made an urgent request to the IRMCT for his release after he was transferred to palliative care, saying he had only has months to live. His defence again sought his immediate release in May this year after a serious medical episode, arguing that he was approaching the end of his life.

Mladic has been in custody in The Hague since his arrest in 2011. He is serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The court confirmed his conviction and sentence after an appeal in 2021.

World.title: Croatian Firefighters Receive New vehicles for Extinguishing Forest Fires
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – Croatian firefighters have received six new, highly specialised modern vehicles for extinguishing forest fires.

A ceremony for the handover of new vehicles for extinguishing forest fires was held yesterday at the State Firefighting School in Zagreb. Index reports that the attendees included Chief Fire Commander Slavko Tucaković, county fire commanders and presidents of the firefighting associations of the counties receiving the vehicles, Buzet Mayor Damir Kajin, and representatives of the firefighting units to which the vehicles were allocated.

The six new specialised firefighting vehicles for extinguishing forest fires were financed from funds for the general-purpose functions of forests (OKFŠ). Those funds are distributed through the competent ministry in cooperation with the Croatian Firefighting Association.

a total of 78 new vehicles have been ordered

Chief Fire Commander Slavko Tucaković said that continuous investment in firefighting equipment further strengthens the operational capabilities of Croatian firefighters.

“By distributing these brand new vehicles, we’re raising the operational readiness of units not only for extinguishing outdoor fires, but also for a range of other sorts of interventions. These vehicles will immediately be put into operational use. Previously allocated vehicles have already been used on major fires on Korčula and near Lokva Rogoznica,” said Chief Fire Commander Tucaković, emphasising that the vehicles were built according to the requirements of fire commanders in the field.

where in croatia will they be put into function?

These vehicles are modernly equipped firefighting vehicles designed entirely for extinguishing forest fires and interventions in very demanding terrain. They have 4×4 drives, large water tanks, a fire pump and additional equipment for work in the most difficult conditions. A total of 40 vehicles with 2,500-litre water tanks and 38 vehicles with 5,000-litre tanks have been ordered. Today, five larger-capacity vehicles and one smaller-capacity vehicle were handed over.

The new vehicles were received by the Public Fire Brigade of Petrinja, the Public Fire Brigade of Buzet, the Public Fire Brigade of Imotski, the Public Fire Brigade of Županja, the Senj Volunteer Fire Department and the Brestovac Volunteer Fire Department.

World.title: Croatian Fires Often Occur on Overgrown, Neglected Private Land
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – Croatian fires often occur on overgrown and neglected private land where it’s difficult or impossible for Croatian Forests (Hrvatske šume) to enter and deal with the situation.

Large fires have become a European reality and no longer pose a threat only to the extreme south of Europe. As never before, fires have also hit the United Kingdom, the continental part of France and Germany. Marija Brnic reports for Poslovni that there have been fires up in Scandinavia as well, and in conditions of increasingly frequent extreme heatwaves they represent a greater threat than before for a far larger number of countries. The authorities have duly recognised this, as a joint defence has already been established, so that unlike earlier times, member states help one another by sending firefighting teams and firefighting fleets.

According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), forest fires already reached a historic record last year – more than one million hectares of forest burned within the EU back in 2025. This year, according to data from the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, as of the first week of August, 506 thousand hectares of forest area had burned, which is a third more than in the same period of the most devastating 2025.

Since the recovery of a destroyed forest ecosystem is measured in decades compared with agricultural crops or buildings, the question arises of what to do with these areas, and how this changes the picture on the timber raw material market. As of the first week of August, 506 thousand hectares of forest area had burned – a third more than in the same period of the most devastating 2025.

it’s still too early to make educated estimates

These questions are also relevant at the Croatian level, although, fortunately and thanks to a well-organised fire defence, the areas burned so far are still below the record levels of 2017 and the devastating 2022. By mid-August, 9.6 thousand hectares had been affected by fire.

Croatian Forests were asked for their estimates of damage to forested areas under their management that were affected by fires, and what the ratio of affected areas is compared with the previous year. They revealed that it is too early for any estimates; more concrete information will only be possible after the end of the fire season. However, they significantly emphasised that in the largest fire this year, the one in the wider Omiš area, only about ten percent of the total burned area was under the management of Croatian Forests.

As for the rehabilitation of the fire-affected areas, they explain that the law provides that it must be carried out no later than two growing seasons after the fire occurred. They are responsible for rehabilitating areas owned by the state, and they carry it out mainly independently or by engaging external subcontractors. The first step, if it concerns so-called high forest, is the extraction of timber mass, followed by preparation for the replanting of trees, which is done purposefully, in accordance with the adaptation of the tree species to the particular terrain.

However, some forest areas also regenerate on their own, especially those under pine trees, because during a fire the cones practically explode and disperse seed up to about ten metres. This brings us to the increasingly frequent and louder public questioning of replacing the flammable Aleppo pine with another tree species. Europe, precisely because of fires and climate change, is intensively considering abandoning conifers and switching to mixed and more resistant deciduous forests.

changes are unfortunately not likely

As for changes along Croatia’s long, heavily irregular coastal area, this is not currently likely. Experts have long pointed out that on karst and rock, where there is no fertile soil, deciduous trees cannot survive, and that the Aleppo pine is precisely suitable because it has extremely modest requirements. Moreover, it is the best at creating conditions for the start of humus production. That is also the reason why on the areas affected by fires that are under Croatian Forests, a rapid change of tree species is not likely.

“Given the conditions we constantly encounter, the pioneer species, in this case the Aleppo pine, simply does not manage to perform its primary function because of fires – creating conditions for the successful growth of other species. Unfortunately, we find it increasingly difficult to wait the sufficient number of years that are approximately needed for that process of conversion into mixed forests, because fires due to the climate and human behaviour have become ever more frequent and destructive,” they emphasise from Croatian Forests, reminding that 90 percent of them are caused by human negligence and carelessness or malicious intent.

Among other things, they note that fires often start from neglected and overgrown agricultural areas in private ownership, for which they are not responsible and which they are not allowed to enter, and which are very often overgrown precisely with Aleppo pine that has not been maintained there and has no firebreaks.

World.title: How do Croatian Fuel Prices Compare to the Rest of the EU?
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – Croatian fuel prices have been up and down like a yo-yo, but just how do they compare to those across the rest of the EU?

Energy expert Jasminko Umićević assessed that Croatia is not facing a fuel shortage, but warns that high prices could persist. Drivers in Croatia are once again paying more for fuel as of Tuesday. However, Eurostat data show that the rise in fuel prices over the past year was still milder than the European Union average. Diesel in Croatia rose by 14 percent, and petrol by eight percent.

Poslovni reports that according to data issued for July 2026, the average diesel price in the European Union was 20 percent higher than a year earlier. The largest increases were recorded in Romania and the Netherlands, both at 31 percent, followed by Germany at 27 percent, France at 24 percent and Greece at 22 percent.

croatia remains below the eu average

With a 14 percent increase, Croatia remained six percent below the EU average. A slightly milder increase was recorded in Slovenia at 13 percent, while Hungary, with a rise of only one percent, is clearly at the bottom of the observed group of countries.The difference is even more pronounced for petrol specifically. Its price across the rest of the European Union rose by an average of 15 percent over the year, almost twice as much as in Croatia.

The largest increase was recorded in Lithuania at 25 percent, followed by Romania at 23 percent, Germany at 22 percent and the Netherlands at 21 percent. In France and Poland, petrol rose by 16 percent, and in Austria by 15 percent. Croatia and neighbouring Italy, both with an eight percent increase, are at the bottom of the presented ranking. In Slovenia, petrol rose by nine percent, and in Greece by 13 percent.

The annual growth data comes at a time when Croatian drivers are being hit by yet another new price increase. The government adopted decrees at a telephone session under which a litre of petrol costs 1.66 euros as of Tuesday, three cents more than before. Diesel rose by six cents to 1.86 euros per litre, and blue diesel by five cents to 1.32 euros. Liquefied petroleum gas also rose in price. LPG for tanks now costs 1.27 euros per kilogram, three cents more, while the price of gas in bottles rose by four cents to 1.85 euros per kilogram.

The government has retained reduced excise duties and limited traders’ margins. According to its calculation, without these measures petrol would cost 1.81 euros and diesel 2.07 euros per litre. The new prices are valid for seven days.

there will be no shortages, but prices will go up

Energy expert Jasminko Umićević assessed that Croatia is not facing a fuel shortage, but warns that high prices could persist. The problem is particularly pronounced on the diesel market, whose price has remained high even after the fall in the price of crude oil. Over the past twenty years or so, Europe has reduced its refining capacity by approximately 30 percent, even though it consumes more diesel than across the pond in America. After the interruption of imports from Russia, it has relied more on Arab countries, and disruptions related to the Strait of Hormuz have further reduced supply.

Croatia is in a more favourable position thanks to the Rijeka refinery. Although it isn’t yet operating at full capacity because testing is ongoing, domestic production reduces dependence on imports and the risk of shortages.

World.title: Croatian Economy Grows 1.8% in Second Quarter of 2026
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – The Croatian economy will likely see growth of 1.8% in the second quarter of 2026, pointing to an economic slowdown.

The movement of the CEIZ index suggests that the Croatian economy will grow by 1.8 percent in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same period last year, according to analysts at the Zagreb Economic Institute (EIZ). Poslovni reports that the CEIZ index fell by 1.24 index points back in June compared to the same month last year, while its value decreased by 0.15 index points compared to May.

In June this year, among the indicators tracking economic activity, tourism actually underperformed the most, with the number of tourist arrivals lower than in May. On the other hand, industrial production and retail trade turnover rose, and the state collected more VAT revenue. The number of tourist arrivals was also the only component of the CEIZ index that recorded a decline in June compared to the same month last year.

“The described movement of the index suggests that economic activity in the second quarter of 2026 is slightly slowing compared to the previous quarter. Despite this, we estimate that the Croatian economy will grow by 1.8 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, with a positive quarter-on-quarter rate of change,” the EIZ analysts state.

The Institute emphasised that the estimate based on the CEIZ index is not a precise forecast of GDP growth, but rather serves as a kind of ‘compass’ for monitoring current economic activity. The Croatian economy is therefore still growing, but at a somewhat slower pace than at the beginning of the year. CEIZ data so far doesn’t point to a turnaround, but rather to a gradual slowdown in economic activity.

World.title: Billionaires Gather on 200 Million Euro Yacht Near Mljet
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Multiple billionaires have come together on a 200 million euro yacht near the southern Croatian island of Mljet. Jeff Bezos, and Jan Koum are among them.

Poslovni reports that this impressive vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros. Mljet is set to be hosting a meeting of two of the world’s biggest technology billionaires, Jan Koum and Jeff Bezos, over the next few days. They met on Koum’s yacht worth nearly 200 million dollars.

Jan Koum, co-founder of WhatsApp whose wealth is estimated at 17 billion dollars, anchored his superyacht Moonrise near Mljet, and the same day Jeff Bezos, owner of Amazon, arrived in the company of American media mogul Barry Diller. Koum arrived on the Moonrise by helicopter on Monday, and Bezos visited him in the late afternoon hours. The three billionaires, Koum, Bezos and Diller, thus found themselves on the same vessel in the middle of the Adriatic Sea.

Koum is no stranger to the Croatian coast; he has holidayed in our beautiful country before. His superyacht Moonrise was photographed between the islands of Lopud and Šipan back in 2021 and 2024, and it was recorded that on one occasion he arrived for a summer holiday in Croatia with as many as three vessels: in addition to Moonrise he was accompanied by the 74-metre yacht Mogambo and the 55-metre Power Play, which served him as a helipad. The Amazon owner regularly summers on the Mediterranean on his superyacht Koru, where he cruised the Adriatic in the summers of 2023 and 2025, with recorded stays on Hvar, Mljet, Korčula, and a visit to the Šibenik archipelago.

The yacht Moonrise isn’t just an ordinary vessel. It’s a 100-metre superyacht from the Dutch shipyard Feadship, built in 2020. The sophisticated exterior design is by De Voogt, while the interior is the work of French designer Rémi Tessier. The vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros.

World.title: Pula Receives 12 Electric Buses Worth 6.8 Million Euros
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Pula has received 12 electric buses worth a total of 6.8 million euros with an aim of increasing passenger comfort and being more environmentally friendly.

Pulapromet has put another six new electric buses into service, thereby completing the project of acquiring a total of 12 electric vehicles for Pula’s public transport. Index reports that the project was fully financed with funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, and the total value of the purchased buses amounts to 6,763,900 euros. For the project, Pulapromet had been allocated 6,994,998 euros, but after the public procurement procedure the total value was somewhat lower.

Specifically speaking, Pulapromet acquired six MAN and six Iveco electric buses. Director Tomislav Josipović said that this is an important step in modernising the vehicle fleet and raising the quality of public transport.

“By putting these new six electric buses into service today, we are completing the project through which Pulapromet has received a total of 12 new electric vehicles,” said Josipović, adding that almost 6.8 million euros of investment has been directed into the development of public transport without any financial burden on Pulapromet. The new buses should reduce emissions of harmful gases and noise while increasing energy efficiency and passenger comfort.

an increase in public transport use in pula

Pula Mayor Peđa Grbin said that the project does not stop at the acquisition of buses. He announced the installation of solar panels on the canopy at the depot (Remiza), for which the City is waiting for the opening of appropriate co-financing tenders. “The goal is for these electric buses to run on electricity that will be produced here, in Pula, from the most ecological possible source, which is solar energy,” said Grbin. He added that since the beginning of the year the use of public city transport has increased by almost 10 percent. According to him, this has also been contributed to by the City of Pula’s decisions on free transport for pupils, students and pensioners.

Istria County Prefect Boris Miletić thanked the City of Pula, Pulapromet, the surrounding municipalities and the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure for implementing the project. He emphasised that electric buses, especially if powered by energy from solar sources, can contribute to reducing the impact of traffic on the environment. Miletić also said that Pulapromet first secured the infrastructure and charging stations, and then acquired the vehicles. He assessed that higher-quality public transport could further increase the number of passengers.

World.title: Istria Showcased in Front of Millions of German Viewers
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Gorgeous Istria has been showcased in front of millions of German viewers, shining the spotlight on Croatia’s largest peninsula.

Morski reports that one of the most successful German travel programmes, “Wunderschön”, devoted a full 90 minutes of airtime to Istria, presenting the diversity of the peninsula to a million-strong audience in the German-speaking world – from Kamenjak, Pula and the Brijuni Islands, via Učka, Buzet and Pazin, to Poreč and Rovinj.

The project was realised in cooperation between the Tourist Board of Istria County and its long-standing PR partner ART Redaktionsteam from Salzburg. Viewers are guided through Istria by well-known German television presenter Stephanie Müller-Spirra, under the direction of award-winning journalist and author Stephan Heise. Alongside numerous local protagonists, the programme also features Marko Purišić – Baby Lasagna, Rade Šerbedžija and extreme alpinist Ines Papert. Istria is presented to the audience through a blend of natural and cultural attractions, active holidays, local stories and top-class food and local wine.

The first broadcast of the report reaches around two million viewers, while through further screenings in Germany, Austria and Switzerland the total viewership is expected to exceed five million, making the project one of the most significant television promotions of Istria on its most important outbound market.

World.title: Belišće – The Croatian Town Around Which an Industrial Empire Grew
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Belišće isn’t a name you’ll likely have ever heard if you’re not from Croatia, but this Croatian town had an industrial empire grow out of it.

It’s also unusual because of the fact that it is one of the few Croatian towns whose beginning can be fixed almost like a date of birth. Putni kofer turns the hands of the clock back to the year 1884, and we find ourselves in a place with a pasture-and-arable clearing called Belistje. It sits just beside the banks of the Drava, and the reason a large sawmill that the Gutmann family builds there. Soon after, a railway, workers’ houses, a school, a post office, an electricity network and a water supply all arrive. In just a few decades, the industrial plant thus created an entire settlement around itself, and from it grew today’s town.

the family company that built an entire town

In 1884, two companies belonging to the Gutmann family from Velika Kanjiža bought from the Valpovo landowner the right to a ten-year use of a huge expanse of oak forests. They erected the sawmill on the Belistje clearing, after which the settlement later took its name. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon notes that the Gutmanns further expanded their business by purchasing forests from the Prandau family of Valpovo and that at the beginning of the 20th century they controlled massive swathes of of forest and land. From the very start Belišće was therefore tied to one of the most valuable resources of the area, Slavonian oak.

the biggest and most modern sawmill in europe

According to data from Belišće, the sawmill was one of the most modern of its time and probably the largest in Europe for cutting oak timber. Large-scale production also needed a good transport link, so already in 1884 the first kilometres of the forest-industrial railway were laid. Over time the network grew to 335 kilometres and developed into the Slavonia-Podravina Railway with public transport, a station, a locomotive shed and a workshop in Belišće. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon emphasises that this railway also carried passengers and thus compensated for the lack of state railways in this part of Slavonia.

Alongside the sawmill and the railway an industrial colony grew. Official sources state that the first residential houses were soon built and a fire brigade founded; in 1886 a school classroom and a post office were opened, and in 1890 a primary school was constructed. By 1892 the place already had an electricity network and a water supply with sewerage, which was still rare in the surrounding villages at that time. Development was also visible in the architecture. Next to the workers’ houses arose a house for the owners and offices, the officials’ social centre Casino, and in 1905 the Gutmann Palace, known in Belišće as Palej. Up to the First World War the workers’ settlement continued to expand, and some of its parts remained known by the names Five Stars, Green Houses, Mitrovica and Pekmez Street.

workers arrived from across the world

Industry drew workers from the Valpovo and Miholjac areas and from Lika, while specialists arrived from other parts of Austria-Hungary. Among them were many Germans, Hungarians and Czechs. With the newcomers cultural life also developed. The Rosenberg family arrived in 1888, and their son Sigmund spent part of his childhood precisely in Belišće. Later, in the United States under the name Sigmund Romberg, he became a well-known composer of operettas and musicals and dedicated the Belišće March to the place of his childhood.

By the time 1918 rolled around, the company moved its headquarters from Budapest to Belišće, and in 1927 the place became an independent municipality. After 1945 followed the period of the Kombinat, and a new major industrial phase began in 1960 with the opening of factories for semi-cellulose, paper and packaging. The old production lines and the narrow-gauge railways gradually closed down, but their traces still determine the appearance of the town today. The Gutmann Palace has been restored as an interpretation centre of industrial heritage; nearby is a gate from the first sawmill, installed in 1889; the complex of workers’ houses is protected as a monument ensemble; and a train with a locomotive from 1913 has also been preserved. Belišće has thus turned its industrial past, from which it literally arose, into the most recognisable part of its own heritage.

World.title: Media: CIA chief's Moscow visit to warn Russia against attacks on NATO allies, war in Iran
World.content:
U.S. media reported on Thursday that CIA Director John Ratcliffe's unannounced visit to Russia this week was focused on the Baltic states and the war in Iran.

U.S. publication Politico's sources said the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states." The Wall Street Journal published a similar story.

Spokespeople for the Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian embassies in Washington declined to comment, Politico added.

Additionally, Ratcliffe also used the trip "to press Russia to reduce military and economic support for Iran," Politico wrote.

A wave of speculation has followed the trip, as no information was given about the meeting's content and it was not announced before it took place.

The last time a CIA director visited Russia was late 2021, three months before Russia invaded Ukraine, to warn Moscow not to do so. This has led to speculation that a similar situation might be occurring.

Latvia: Not the same kind of military threat as 2021/2022

Ratcliffe's plane also landed in Latvia during the journey, which has been seen by some as a message.

On Wednesday, Latvia's Chief of Defense Kaspars Pudān said there is currently no basis for talking about a similar scenario.

"If we rely on the facts and the information available to us, this is not the same kind of military threat as in Ukraine's case at the end of 2021 or the beginning of 2022, when the previous visit took place," Pudāns told the Delfi news portal.

He did not comment on the reasons for the CIA chief's visit, saying he had no information and did not want to speculate. The chief of defense said the trip was coordinated with Latvia only to use the country's airspace.

Kaspars Pudāns. Source: ERR

Pudāns rejected claims that there were any signs indicating Russian plans to launch operations against NATO countries.

"If we had such signs, I would not be talking to you in the studio right now, but would be dealing with the mobilization of our forces," he said.

However, he agreed that Russia is carrying out hybrid attacks against Western countries to reduce allied support for Ukraine.

"For them, this may be the most effective way to eventually get out of this resource-intensive war. They are afraid that at some point they will no longer be able to lie to their public about victory or justify the decline in living standards," he said.

Lithuania: We knew about the meeting

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda at the JEF summit 2024 in Tallinn doorstep on December 17, 2024. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday he had been informed about Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow but declined to discuss the substance of the meeting, public broadcaster LRT reported.

"We knew about the meeting," the president said. "I would not want to discuss its content because, first of all, that is a matter for the parties to the meeting."

Nausėda added that Lithuania had been told that details about the meeting, including its purpose and content, would be shared promptly "probably next week."

The president said he believed the meeting was intended to help reduce geopolitical tensions in the region.
