World.title: PNP files complaint vs gun owner in Zamboanga school shooting
World.content:
'Based on the findings, investigators found no evidence that the incident was carried out as part of a conspiracy involving any group, organization, or other individuals,' the PNP says

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine National Police (PNP) has filed with prosecutors a complaint against the owner of the gun used by a junior high school student who carried out the August 18 school shooting in Zamboanga City.

In a statement on Wednesday, August 26, the PNP said it has completed its investigation into the shooting incident at Ateneo de Zamboanga University’s (ADZU) junior high school campus.

A 10th grader was killed before the perpetrator also shot himself. Another 15-year-old student was injured.

“With these findings, a complaint for Reckless Imprudence Resulting in Homicide and Physical Injury was filed before the proper prosecutorial authority against the registered owner of the firearms used in the incident and a school security personnel, based on the evidence established during the investigation,” the PNP said.

The PNP did not name the gun owner, but Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno previously confirmed that the minor used the handgun of his father, the district commander of the Enforcement and Security Services at the Port of Zamboanga. He has since been relieved from his duty.

According to the police investigation, the minor was driven inside the school campus via his father’s private vehicle, bypassing standard security checks. The student took his father’s gun bag, which was supposedly left inside the vehicle, and used a ramp for persons with disabilities to enter the junior high school building.

For the PNP, it showed that “gaps in firearm safekeeping and accountability allowed unauthorized access to the firearms used, while security deficiencies in the school, particularly in entry and exit screening, contributed to the circumstances of the incident.”

“Based on the findings, investigators found no evidence that the incident was carried out as part of a conspiracy involving any group, organization, or other individuals,” the PNP also said.

During a House budget briefing on Thursday, August 27, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla admitted that there was no conclusive link that the True Crime Community Group, an online subculture where violent content is shared and discussed online, influenced the actions of the minor.

The PNP also said it “found no established school-related or personal grievance that could sufficiently explain the shooting.” However, police investigation “identified prior preparation and exposure to violent online material as among the circumstances surrounding the incident.”

PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. reminded gun owners to exercise greater care in securing their weapons, and urged schools and security personnel to conduct regular review on their access and screening measures.

Nartatez also encouraged parents and the public to promptly raise concerns involving threats, violent behavior, or other warning signs.

The Zamboanga school shooting incident came over a month after the June 22 tragedy at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, where two students opened fire, killing three students and injuring 20 others.

The ADZU suspended regular classes until Friday, August 28, with the institution conducting in-person support activities, guided reflection, and pastoral care. – Rappler.com

World.title: Filipino family income grew 16.5% since 2023. So why doesn’t it feel like it?
World.content:
MARKET. Vegetables and various goods for sale at Commonwealth Market in Quezon City, March 13, 2025.

Filipino family incomes rose 16.5% from 2023 to 2025, but spending grew even faster at 24.7%, leaving households with less financial breathing room

MANILA, Philippines – On paper, Filipino families got a sizable income raise between 2023 and 2026, but there’s a reason why most still find their household budgets stretched thin.

The average Filipino family earned P411,350 in 2025, up 16.5% from P353,230 in 2023, according to the latest Family Income and Expenditure Survey (FIES). That’s about P34,300 a month, compared with P29,400 two years earlier.

But the headline figure doesn’t mean the typical worker got a 16.5% raise, nor that families suddenly have that much more money to spend .

The biggest reason: Expenses increased even faster than income.

Family income may have risen, but average annual family expenditure surged past that at 24.7%, hitting P321,850 in 2025 from P258,050 in 2023. That works out to about P26,800 a month.

In peso terms, average income increased by P58,120 over the two-year period, while expenditure rose by P63,800. The difference between average income and expenditure consequently narrowed to P89,500 in 2025 from P95,180 in 2023.

According to Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan, this suggests families had less financial breathing room.

“The fact that average income minus expenditure fell from 2023 to 2025 meant that Filipino families had less room for savings, emergencies, and debt payments,” Punongbayan told Rappler. “This may help explain why many families may not feel better off despite higher incomes.”

The squeeze also cut across income groups. No matter which income bracket you look at, expenditure grew faster than income between 2023 and 2025.

Among the poorest 10% of families, average income rose 19.1%, while expenditure increased 21.7%. For the fifth decile, income grew 16.8% against a 23.6% increase in spending. Among the richest 10%, income increased 15.6%, while expenditure jumped 27.2%.

Still, Punongbayan cautioned that faster spending doesn’t automatically mean Filipino families became worse off.

“Prices increased from 2023 to 2025, but inflation alone cannot explain the rise in expenses,” Punongbayan said. “Families may also have consumed more or shifted toward costlier items such as housing, utilities, transport, health, and dining out.”

Some families may also have accommodated higher spending by saving less, dipping into savings, or borrowing, he added.

“Thus, higher expenditure is not automatically evidence of worsening welfare. But its faster growth relative to income signals a squeeze on households.”

The FIES figures are also nominal averages, meaning they are not adjusted for inflation and don’t show what happened to every individual household. Punongbayan also noted that the latest poverty statistics, in fact, showed a decline in poverty.

Effects of Middle East crisis not yet reflected

The 2025 figures don’t yet capture how much harder household budgets have been squeezed this year.

Inflation accelerated sharply in 2026 as the conflict in the Middle East pushed up global oil and other commodity prices.

By July, Philippine inflation stood at 6.2%, bringing the average for the first seven months of 2026 to 5% — far above the government’s target range of 2% to 4%. Transport prices alone were 11.9% higher than a year earlier.

“In the wake of the 2026 US-Iran war, higher oil prices affected budgets directly through fuel and electricity and indirectly through fares, freight, and food prices,” Punongbayan said. “So the 2025 FIES data probably understate today’s squeeze, although its precise impact on the gap between incomes and spending can’t be measured until newer household data become available.”

Even before that latest shock, necessities already ate up most family budgets.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages accounted for 33.3% of average family expenditure in 2025, while housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels took another 21.6%. Together, those two categories accounted for nearly 55% of family spending.

Where does family income come from?

Across all Filipino families, wages and salaries were the biggest source of income in 2025, accounting for 54.6% of total family income collected across all families surveyed.

Entrepreneurial activities accounted for another 15.5% of total family income, while 8.7% came from imputed rent. Cash receipts from abroad, which include remittances, contributed 8.5%, while cash receipts from domestic sources made up 5.3%. Other sources, including pensions, gifts, rentals, dividends, and interest, accounted for the remaining 7.4%.

Imputed rent is different from the other sources because it is not cash a family actually receives. For owner-occupied homes, the PSA assigns an estimated rental value to the housing service the family gets from living in its own property.

Take note that the P411,350 figure itself is also a national average across families, not the income of a typical individual household. Actual family incomes can vary widely depending on location, number of earners, employment, businesses, remittances, and other sources of income. – Rappler.com

World.title: What it really takes to bring more Filipinos into the digital economy, according to GCash
World.content:
Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by GCash and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Financial inclusion has become one of Southeast Asia’s biggest digital ambitions. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the digital economy contributed P2.74 trillion to the country’s GDP in 2025, accounting for nearly 10% of the total.

With more of everyday life moving online, there is naturally more room for digital financial services to reach people who may have previously been left out of the formal financial system. But reaching more people, and eventually more markets, also brings up the less visible part that asks what it costs to keep these services accessible.

This was among the questions raised during the ASEAN Tech Summit’s “Futurecast Panel: Building Sustainable and Inclusive Financial Services Ecosystems in ASEAN”, where leaders from GCash, Maya Bank, Tala Philippines, and ATIN (Alliance of Tech Innovators for the Nation) talked about what it takes to make financial inclusion work for both the people using these services and the businesses building them.

For Barbie Rodriguez-Dapul, COO and general manager for consumer business at G-Xchange, digital payments play an important role in making that possible.

“It’s really the digital payments that enable us to make the investments needed to sustain the innovation and the infrastructure needed to be able to give quality services to our customers,” Rodriguez-Dapul said.

FINANCE FOR ALL. Barbie Rodriguez-Dapul discusses how reducing barriers to onboarding can help bring more Filipinos into the formal financial system.



From a user’s point of view, it could be seen as simply moving money from one account to another. But behind it is a business that has to keep investing in the systems that make those transactions possible — and, eventually, make them available to more people.

That becomes even more apparent when fintech companies start looking beyond the markets they already serve. Across Southeast Asia, people enter the digital economy from different starting points. Access to identification, familiarity with digital tools, and even the ease of opening an account can vary widely from one person to another.

A Filipino in a grassroots community may already have a smartphone and an internet connection to download a digital wallet, but still encounter difficulty proving their identity or completing the requirements needed to open an account.

For Rodriguez-Dapul, reaching these communities means looking at financial inclusion beyond affordability alone. “Our mission is to raise finance for all,” she said. “Inclusion is not only about affordability. It’s about designing services that are relevant to those that are traditionally excluded.”

This has led GCash to look at some of the barriers people encounter before they can even make their first transaction. Rodriguez-Dapul highlighted the company’s integration with the PSA, which makes identity verification easier through the national ID system, as well as KYC-on-the-Go, where GCash goes directly to grassroots communities to help people complete the onboarding process.

“We also want to make sure that onboarding is very easy. When they are not capable of doing it themselves because they are not digitally savvy, then we also have KYC-on-the-Go programs where we go to the grassroots to assist them in terms of their onboarding journey,” she said.

For GCash, financial inclusion is shaped by what access looks like on the ground. Those realities help inform decisions around onboarding, service design, and how the company reaches different communities.

As ASEAN moves toward a more integrated digital economy, financial inclusion becomes less of a standalone goal and more of a foundation for everything else the region hopes to achieve. The broader the participation, and the more technology is designed around the realities of the people it serves, the stronger the digital economy it can build. – Rappler.com

World.title: Supreme Court affirms ruling: No ‘second placer rule’ in local elections
World.content:
'For local elective positions covered by the Local Government Code, that vacancy is filled through the rule on succession, not by proclaiming the second placer as the winner,' the High Court reiterates

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) has affirmed its ruling that abandoned the “second placer rule” in local elections, in a decision made public on Thursday, August 27.

The “second placer rule” is the practice of declaring a candidate who received the second highest number of votes the winner after the original candidate who received the highest number of votes was later disqualified or found ineligible.

“The SC reiterated that no law authorizes the second placer rule. It emphasized that the Constitution recognizes as elected only the candidate who received the highest number of votes,” the High Court said.

In June last year, the SC issued its landmark ruling in the Mangudadatu v. Commission on Elections, scrapping the said rule. It explained that the rule on succession in the Local Government Code must apply in cases where a local elective official was disqualified.

According to the High Court, the second placer rule has no basis in law and that the second placer in the polls “is just that, a second placer who lost the elections.”

During its August 26 en banc session, the justices denied with finality the motion for reconsideration filed by Datu Pax Ali Mangudadatu, therefore affirming the 2025 decision that canceled his certificate of candidacy for Sultan Kudarat governor and abandoned the “second placer rule.”

The High Court reiterated that the vacancy should be filled by the vice governor.

“The SC explained that when the winning candidate is later found ineligible to hold office, a permanent vacancy arises. For local elective positions covered by the Local Government Code (LGC), that vacancy is filled through the rule on succession, not by proclaiming the second placer as the winner. Accordingly, the Vice Governor succeeds to the position of Governor for the remainder of the term,” said the SC.

The High Court said, however, that this ruling only applies to local positions covered by the LGC as the case did not include whether or not the decision applies to national positions.

“However, the SC stressed that succession for national elective positions like the President and Vice President is governed exclusively by Article VII, Sections 7 and 8 of the Constitution, which prescribe the order of succession when the President or Vice-President fails to qualify, dies, or is permanently disabled, removed from office, or resigns,” the SC explained.

Mangudadatu filed a certiorari petition — an action that seeks review of another body’s decision — with the High Court against the Commission on Elections and his opponent in the 2022 race, Sharifa Akeel Mangudadatu.

Datu Pax Ali was questioning the Comelec rulings that canceled his certificate of candidacy and assailed his 2022 victory. The former won the Sultan Kudarat gubernatorial race against Sharifa Akeel with over 100,000 difference in votes in 2022.

Datu Pax is the incumbent Sultan Kudarat governor after winning in the 2025 elections with over 300,000 votes. – Rappler.com

World.title: Resources Are Not Enough: How Energy Routes Are Becoming Geopolitical Battleground in Eurasia
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, the geopolitics of energy was largely understood through a familiar map of resource abundance: the Persian Gulf held vast oil and gas reserves, Russia was a major supplier to Europe, and countries such as Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan were important producers whose influence depended largely on how much they could extract and sell. But as wars, sanctions and geopolitical competition increasingly disrupt established trade routes, that logic is changing.

The strategic value of an energy resource is no longer determined only by what lies beneath the ground, but increasingly by whether it can reach international markets, through which route and with how many alternatives if that route is disrupted.

For oil and gas producers in Central Asia, the answer has become increasingly consequential. Kazakhstan remains heavily dependent on routes that cross Russian territory, Turkmenistan has enormous gas reserves but limited export options, and Uzbekistan is looking increasingly southward toward Afghanistan as it seeks additional connections to international markets. At the same time, China is building multiple routes into Eurasia as it seeks to reduce its exposure to maritime chokepoints and dependence on any single corridor.

When energy routes become strategic assets

Abzal Narymbetov, an oil and gas industry expert, framed the broader issue through the structure of global energy markets. While the United States and China dominate many categories of energy production, countries with large exportable surpluses are more narrowly concentrated, particularly in the Middle East, where reserves are vast relative to population and domestic consumption.

“The Middle East is the only region that can actually supply oil and gas to growing China and India’s needs,” Narymbetov said, noting that the central vulnerability lies in the routes through which those supplies move. For him, the Strait of Hormuz is the clearest example of how geography can turn an energy question into a strategic one.

“When you have a bottleneck like the Hormuz, then you will have the next road is only the inland,” he added.

The point is not that continental routes can replace maritime energy flows. They cannot, at least not on the same scale. Rather, the geopolitical value of inland routes rises when maritime routes become vulnerable, and that is precisely why China’s expanding network of pipelines and rail connections across the Eurasian landmass matters. Narymbetov said that China has little choice but to develop those alternatives because its energy needs cannot simply be reduced by changing transport patterns.

“China needs to develop inland routes, because there is no way that you will replace the oil and gas consumption that China now needs,” he said.

That logic places Central Asia in a strategically different position from the one it occupied when energy was discussed primarily in terms of exports and revenues. Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan are no longer simply producers supplying global demand; their infrastructure and geographic location are becoming part of a wider effort to make energy systems less vulnerable to geopolitical disruption.

Why Turkmenistan is suddenly at the center of the map

This is particularly evident in the case of Turkmenistan, which was repeatedly described during the discussion as an underappreciated energy power. The country possesses one of the world’s largest gas reserves, but its strategic significance comes from more than the size of its resource base. Turkmenistan sits between China, Iran, the Caspian Sea and the broader South Asian space, making it a potential junction for several competing east-west and north-south routes.

Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, referred to a discussion with a former U.S. administration official where he illustrated the point with a simple “tic-tac-toe” diagram, placing Turkmenistan in the middle of the map to show how several potential routes from China to the Caspian Sea converge around the country.

“So Turkmenistan is the key,” he said, recounting the logic behind the map.

The claim is deliberately stark, but it captures a broader shift in the way the country is viewed. But the question surrounding Turkmenistan is not simply how much gas it has, but how many viable ways it eventually has to move that gas. That question also explains why Uzbekistan’s interest in Afghanistan has become increasingly important. Moriyasu said one of the biggest takeaways from his meetings in the region was “how much the Uzbekistan leaders were talking about the importance about Afghanistan.” For Central Asian states, he said, Iran has historically offered one of the shortest routes to international waters, but political uncertainty and sanctions have made long-term infrastructure planning through Iran more difficult.

“I think there’s a collective souring of sentiment towards Iran because of the situation now,” Moriyasu said, noting that Central Asian governments may be increasingly unwilling to wait for a stable and business-friendly environment in Tehran before developing their external connectivity. His assessment of the emerging hierarchy of routes was blunt. “Right now I think Middle Corridor, then Afghanistan, and then the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), and then Iran is plan four.”

Read that as Moriyasu’s interpretation rather than a formal regional strategy, but it captures an important trend: Central Asian governments are seeking redundancy. Uzbekistan in particular has promoted the idea of Afghanistan as a potential connector between Central Asia and Pakistani ports, even while facing serious security, political and water-management concerns related to its southern neighbor.

The contradiction is striking. Afghanistan could provide Uzbekistan and other Central Asian states with a route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses some existing constraints, while developments such as the Qosh Tepa Canal simultaneously create new concerns for downstream countries dependent on the Amu Darya. Yet the prospect of Afghanistan becoming part of a broader regional transport architecture appears increasingly difficult for Central Asian governments to ignore.

From new corridors to new vulnerabilities

For China, these developments matter for a related reason: diversification. Moriyasu said Beijing does not want to become overly dependent on Kazakhstan because existing overland routes are concentrated there.

“China doesn’t want to be too dependent on Kazakhstan because, as I said, everything goes through Kazakhstan right now,” he said.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is therefore significant not simply as another transport project, but as part of a broader effort to create additional options. One possible route would connect onward towards Turkmenistan and Iran; another, under much more demanding political and security conditions, could eventually connect China through Central Asia and Afghanistan to Pakistan. The strategic logic is not necessarily to replace Kazakhstan, Iran or maritime trade, but to ensure that no single route becomes indispensable.

That same logic is increasingly visible in Kazakhstan’s own energy vulnerabilities. For Kazakhstan, the CPC is the clearest example of how a commercial asset can become a geopolitical fault line. The CPC is critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports, yet the infrastructure runs through Russian territory before reaching global markets, meaning disruptions caused by the war in Ukraine can affect Kazakhstan even though it is not a party to the conflict. Moriyasu said repeated Ukrainian attacks on CPC-related infrastructure reflect what he sees as a broader shift in Kyiv’s strategy.

“The whole purpose of the strikes on the CPC facilities is to internationalize the competition,” he said, noting that the objective is to make other stakeholders, including Kazakhstan, Japan and buyers of Kazakh oil, feel pressure to intervene and, from the Ukrainian perspective, increase pressure on Russia to move toward a ceasefire.

That interpretation is Moriyasu’s assessment rather than an established explanation of Ukrainian policy, and it is precisely because of that distinction that the CPC issue deserves attention. Whatever the stated rationale behind individual strikes, once infrastructure carrying Kazakh oil becomes entangled with another country’s military calculations, the consequences extend well beyond the battlefield.

Kazakhstan’s strategic problem is therefore not simply that its oil exports depend on a particular pipeline. It is that the pipeline connects multiple political and commercial interests, including Kazakhstan, Russia, international oil companies and foreign buyers, meaning that an attack on infrastructure can produce economic and diplomatic consequences across a much wider geography.

Moriyasu interpreted President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s engagement with Putin in Omsk through that lens, saying that Kazakhstan increasingly understands the changing character of the risk.

“The real threat he feels is the Ukrainian strategy,” he said.

That conclusion should again be treated as an expert assessment rather than a definitive explanation of Kazakhstan’s policy. Astana has its own reasons for maintaining high-level dialogue with Moscow, just as it has reasons to preserve relations with Ukraine, China, Europe and the U.S. But the CPC shows why the space to separate economics from geopolitics is becoming increasingly narrow. Kazakhstan’s oil exports remain economically essential, but the infrastructure connecting them to world markets can become exposed to a war in which the country has no direct military role. The larger lesson is that Eurasia’s energy map is being redrawn not necessarily because the location of resources has changed, but because the political meaning of the routes around them has.

For decades, energy security was largely discussed in terms of reserves, production and price. Increasingly, it is also about redundancy, chokepoints and political risk. In that sense, Central Asia’s strategic importance is growing for reasons that go beyond the size of its reserves. And resources are no longer enough. The decisive question is increasingly who can move them, through which route, under whose protection and with what alternatives when those routes are disrupted. Across Eurasia, pipelines and ports are no longer merely infrastructure. They are becoming bargaining chips, strategic assets and, in some cases, potential targets, making the geography of energy inseparable from the region’s geopolitics.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai: New Chapter for Parliamentary Institutions
World.content:
The election of August 23 should be understood as more than just the beginning of a new parliamentary term. It represents an important institutional founding moment. The transition from a bicameral Parliament to the new unicameral Kurultai under the Constitution that entered into force on July 1 creates not only a different institutional structure, but also an opportunity to shape new parliamentary conventions, practices and expectations for the decades ahead.

The preliminary results indicate a high level of electoral participation and the representation of five political parties in the new chamber. Yet from an institutional perspective, the most important question extends beyond the distribution of seats. The longer-term significance of this election will be determined by how effectively the first Kurultai develops its roles in legislation, representation, scrutiny, accountability and public deliberation.

Comparative experience demonstrates that unicameralism can offer important advantages. A single parliamentary chamber can simplify legislative procedures, reduce institutional duplication and contribute to more timely decision-making. These qualities may be particularly valuable for a country navigating rapid economic, technological and geopolitical change.

At the same time, unicameralism places a greater responsibility upon the Parliament itself. Where there is no second legislative chamber to undertake additional review, the quality of parliamentary committees, legislative scrutiny, consultation with experts and stakeholders, and opportunities for meaningful deliberation become particularly important. For this reason, the strength of the new Kurultai will ultimately depend not simply upon its constitutional powers, but upon the parliamentary culture and institutional practices that develop within it.

The first Kurultai carries a special responsibility. The procedures, conventions and norms established during its first five-year term may become precedents for future generations of parliamentarians. Strong committee systems, evidence-based legislative review, transparent parliamentary proceedings and meaningful debate across political viewpoints would therefore represent investments in the long-term institutional development of the Republic.

A second important dimension concerns the relationship between political stability and political pluralism. Stability has considerable value, particularly at a time of heightened international uncertainty. Kazakhstan occupies a strategically important position in Eurasia and must simultaneously manage economic modernization, regional connectivity, social development and increasingly complex relations among major international actors.

However, strong political institutions are most sustainable when stability is accompanied by channels through which different interests, regions, generations and social groups can participate constructively in public decision-making. Parliamentary diversity need not be understood as a source of political fragmentation. Properly institutionalized, it can strengthen the policy process by allowing competing perspectives to be debated within constitutional institutions rather than outside them.

The party-list electoral system may encourage the development of more programmatic political parties and nationally oriented policy platforms. At the same time, the evolution of the system could benefit from continued attention to internal party democracy, transparent political recruitment and meaningful engagement between parliamentarians and citizens beyond electoral periods.

This is particularly relevant in a geographically large and socially diverse country such as Kazakhstan. With the transition to a unicameral legislature elected through a nationwide party-list system, developing effective mechanisms through which the voices of different regions and communities reach the Kurultai will be important. Parliamentary hearings, regional consultations, public petitions, digital participation mechanisms and systematic engagement with civil society could all contribute to ensuring that greater institutional efficiency is accompanied by broad social representation.

Participation of women, young people and persons with disabilities as an important dimension of parliamentary development. Representation becomes most meaningful when inclusion extends beyond candidate lists to substantive participation in parliamentary leadership, committees, legislative initiatives and policy formation.

International election observers have recognized several positive aspects of the electoral process, including professional preparations and efforts to facilitate voter participation, while also identifying areas where further progress could strengthen political pluralism, media diversity, electoral transparency and public confidence. Constructive engagement with such observations can, in my view, complement Kazakhstan’s reform agenda and enhance the credibility of its institutions both domestically and internationally.

More broadly, the development of the Kurultai should be viewed as part of a longer process of institution-building rather than as a single constitutional event. Constitutions can establish institutional architecture, but political institutions acquire legitimacy through practice: through the quality of legislation they produce, their responsiveness to citizens, their ability to scrutinize public policy and expenditure, and their capacity to provide a credible forum for national debate.

Kazakhstan has entered a particularly consequential stage of its political development. The creation of the Kurultai provides an opportunity to strengthen the principle that durable governance rests not only on effective executive leadership, but also on capable, respected and trusted institutions.

The ultimate historical importance of the 2026 election may not be measured primarily by the result of the first electoral contest. It will be measured by whether the new institutional framework allows the Kurultai progressively to develop its own authority, professionalism, deliberative capacity and public legitimacy.

If this occurs, the establishment of the Kurultai may come to be regarded not simply as a restructuring of Parliament, but as an important stage in the maturation of Kazakhstan’s constitutional order.

Kazakhstan has often demonstrated an ability to pursue political and economic change while preserving state continuity in a complex geopolitical environment. The establishment of the new Kurultai now provides an opportunity to extend this tradition from stability-oriented governance toward deeper institutional development.

The first Kurultai can therefore play an especially important role: not merely as a legislature operating under a new Constitution, but as an institution capable of establishing the conventions and standards upon which Kazakhstan’s future parliamentary system will be built.

The author is Arifeen Yama, PhD from the Institute of Asian Studies at Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand.

World.title: Can Kazakhstan’s AI Strategy Deliver Both Growth and Smarter Governance?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is moving toward a broader AI-driven transformation of the economy and public services under a government action plan that sets measurable digitalization targets through 2029, with artificial intelligence increasingly integrated into education, healthcare, transport, finance and industrial management.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov approved the action plan on Aug. 26 as part of implementing the national Digital Qazaqstan Strategy through 2029, approved by presidential decree. It brings together measures to transform services for citizens, support businesses and the economy, and modernize the public administration system.

Rather than focusing solely on introducing individual digital services, the plan seeks to establish digital systems across entire sectors, with AI and real-time data becoming part of how government agencies and businesses make decisions.

AI moves from pilot projects to mass adoption

Education is among the areas where the strategy sets one of its most ambitious targets. Through the expansion of the AI-Sana program, at least 80% of school, college and university graduates are expected to acquire basic AI skills by 2029.

At the same time, the government will expand advanced AI training for students and professional development for teachers. By 2028, at least 80% of universities and colleges are expected to integrate AI technologies into educational processes and update curricula to meet economic needs.

The approach reflects a broader shift in AI’s role in Kazakhstan’s digital policy. Instead of treating artificial intelligence primarily as a technology-sector issue, the government plans to incorporate it into education, healthcare, infrastructure, industry and public administration.

From digital services to predictive government

Healthcare digitalization will focus on creating a unified data management system and expanding services that can be accessed without visiting medical institutions.

By 2029, the government plans to increase the number of citizens using medical self-service platforms, connect more healthcare organizations to a common digital environment with real-time data exchange and expand the use of AI in clinical decision-making.

A similar principle will apply to public services and social support. The government plans to expand proactive services, automated processes and auto-signing mechanisms, with a target of reducing the time required to provide government services and social support measures by at least 50% by 2029.

The objective is to reduce the number of steps citizens must take and gradually shift from a system in which people apply for services to one in which government systems can identify and provide eligible services proactively.

Digital infrastructure becomes part of industrial policy

The strategy also treats digitalization as a tool to improve the productivity and resilience of major economic sectors. In the fuel and energy sector, at least 70% of assets are expected to be connected to digital monitoring systems by 2029. This would allow operators to track asset condition in real time and identify potential reliability risks earlier. Digital traceability of energy resources will also be expanded.

Construction is another sector where the government plans to establish a digital environment covering the full project lifecycle, from design to operation. By 2029, all new technically complex facilities are expected to be managed within a unified digital system.

These measures could make digital data increasingly important not only for administrative purposes, but also for managing physical infrastructure and anticipating operational risks.

Kazakhstan targets digital logistics

Transport and logistics are another major focus of the plan, with digitalization extending across the movement of goods from border crossing points to major transport corridors and multimodal hubs.

One priority is reducing the time freight vehicles need to pass through selected border crossings. The government plans to expand digital tools that collect and process shipment information in advance, reducing the number of procedures that require manual intervention.

Under the Smart Cargo initiative, priority shipments will receive digital passports and end-to-end tracking, allowing cargo to be monitored throughout its journey.

Meanwhile, intelligent transport analytics will be introduced across key transport corridors, border crossings and multimodal hubs. Such systems could allow authorities to assess infrastructure capacity in real time, manage traffic flows and respond more quickly to bottlenecks.

This is particularly significant for Kazakhstan as it seeks to strengthen its position as a transit and logistics hub between major markets. The effectiveness of the digitalization effort will therefore depend not only on the technology itself, but also on how effectively different transport systems and border authorities can exchange data.

Digitalization targets businesses and financial institutions

For small and medium-sized enterprises, the plan emphasizes reducing administrative burdens and providing more targeted digital tools. Businesses will be able to assess their level of digital maturity and receive individual digitalization roadmaps. Digital compliance and risk-based supervision are also expected to reduce physical inspections of low-risk SMEs.

Tax administration is similarly set to move toward a more automated model, with more processes carried out without additional action by taxpayers. The government describes this approach as “invisible” tax administration, aimed at reducing the share of the unobserved economy.

The financial sector will also undergo digital transformation. By 2028, at least 80% of second-tier banks are expected to be connected to a secure digital information exchange system. The same target applies to financial organizations that provide products to individuals and are connected to the Unified Digital Platform.

AI investment expected to generate measurable returns

The strategy places particular emphasis on ensuring that digitalization produces an economic rather than purely technological effect. In Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund portfolio companies, digital and AI initiatives are expected to contribute 5% annually to EBITDA growth.

For Baiterek National Management Holding, AI monitoring is planned to cover 100% of investment projects by 2029. The government also aims to strengthen Kazakhstan’s domestic IT industry and increase its presence in international markets. Exports of IT services and digital solutions are targeted to grow by at least 50% by 2029.

Regional robotics competence centers and support for domestic technology integrators implementing commercial projects are among the measures intended to support the development of a technology-driven economy.

Data centers and cybersecurity become strategic priorities

The planned Data Center Valley is intended to attract global technology and cloud providers, expand computing capacity and create infrastructure for large-scale AI adoption.

The project is expected to increase Kazakhstan’s ability to process and store data domestically while providing infrastructure for new AI services and the development of the local digital industry.

At the same time, expanding the use of data and AI increases the importance of cybersecurity and personal data protection. The action plan therefore includes measures to strengthen government information systems, improve cybersecurity awareness and develop digital safety culture.

Government digital systems will also be connected to the Personal Data Access Control service, which is designed to give citizens greater visibility and control over how their personal information is used.

Taken together, the measures suggest that Kazakhstan’s digitalization agenda is moving beyond digitizing individual government services toward a model in which data, AI and interconnected digital infrastructure become part of the country’s economic and administrative architecture.

World.title: 262 Foreign IT Specialists Receive Digital Nomad Status in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – A total of 262 foreign IT specialists have received residency or visa statuses in Kazakhstan under the Digital Nomad Residency and Digital Nomad Visa programs, according to updated figures from Astana Hub.

As of August 2026, 250 foreign IT specialists have obtained permanent residence permits under the Digital Nomad Residency program, while another 12 have received Digital Nomad Visas after completing the required procedures.

The programs are designed to attract international technology professionals to Kazakhstan, strengthen links with the global technology community and facilitate the exchange of expertise with local IT companies and professionals.

Since the programs were launched, Astana Hub has received 1,517 applications from IT specialists representing 71 countries across the region, Europe, North America, Asia and the Middle East.

The number of applications does not correspond directly to the number of visas or residence permits issued, as applicants must complete several stages, including application review, obtaining an Astana Hub petition and subsequent procedures with government authorities. As of August, Astana Hub had issued 1,069 petitions following its review of applications – 1,030 under Digital Nomad Residency and 39 under Digital Nomad Visa.

Astana Hub stressed that a petition is neither a visa nor a residence permit and does not automatically guarantee that an applicant will receive the relevant status. The technology hub reviews applications and issues petitions when candidates meet the established requirements, while final decisions on visas and residence permits are made by authorized state bodies.

The 262 specialists who have received the relevant statuses account for nearly 17% of all applications submitted since the programmes were launched.

The programs target foreign IT professionals who meet established professional criteria and are considering Kazakhstan as a place to live and work. Eligible specialists include software developers, product managers, artificial intelligence professionals, data analysts, technology entrepreneurs and startup founders, as well as executives of international technology companies and other digital professionals, including those working remotely for foreign employers.

According to Astana Hub, the presence of international IT professionals could contribute to knowledge exchange with Kazakh teams, the development of technology entrepreneurship and the growth of the country’s professional IT community.

Foreign specialists living in Kazakhstan may also contribute to local economic activity through spending on goods and services. Over the longer term, some could launch projects in Kazakhstan, invest in local technology teams and create new jobs.

The programs therefore form part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to strengthen its technology ecosystem by combining international expertise with the development of domestic digital talent and businesses.

World.title: Central Asia Explores Islamic Finance as Path to Greater Financial Connectivity
World.content:
TASHKENT – Islamic finance is emerging as a potential new channel for connecting Central Asia with global capital, as Uzbekistan works to build regulatory and market infrastructure for Sharia-compliant investment. Speaking at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum in Tashkent on Aug. 26, Central Bank of Uzbekistan Governor Timur Ishmetov outlined Uzbekistan’s efforts to develop Islamic microfinance, banking and capital markets as part of a broader strategy to diversify the financial system and attract international investment.

The initiative comes as Central Asian countries seek to strengthen financial connectivity with markets beyond the region and develop new investment channels. Uzbekistan is positioning Islamic finance as one component of this emerging financial architecture, alongside fintech, digital payments, cross-border finance and capital-market development.

Speaking at the forum, Ishmetov said Uzbekistan is developing its approach to Islamic finance in stages, covering microfinance, banking and capital markets.

From Islamic microfinance to banking

According to Ishmetov, Uzbekistan has already established the first layer of its Islamic finance infrastructure through Islamic microfinance.

Twelve microfinance organizations currently provide Islamic financial services based on contracts including Murabaha, Ijara, Salam, Mudaraba and Musharakah.

The second stage began with the adoption of a law on Islamic banking on June 29, which established a legal framework for Islamic banking activities in Uzbekistan. The legislation allows both fully fledged Islamic banks and Islamic banking windows within conventional banks to operate under dedicated Islamic banking licenses.

“Furthermore, the two-tier Islamic finance governance framework has been traditioned in accordance with the best industrial practices, including the establishment of a central bank Islamic finance board and Islamic finance boards within conventional banks,” Ishmetov said.

“One of the key challenges in the development of Islamic finance is ensuring neutrality in taxation of conventional and Islamic financial transactions,” he added.

He noted that the new legislation introduced a dedicated taxation regime designed to provide neutrality in areas including value-added and income taxes, alongside relevant exemptions from state duties.

Next step: Islamic capital markets

The third stage of Uzbekistan’s strategy is developing an Islamic capital market. According to Ishmetov, a draft capital markets law includes a dedicated chapter on Sukuk, or Islamic bonds, and had recently been approved by the Legislative Chamber of Parliament at first reading.

Ishmetov said Uzbekistan has also developed a 2026–2030 roadmap for the national Islamic finance industry in cooperation with the Islamic Financial Services Board. The Cabinet of Ministers approved the roadmap, which includes 39 measures across five thematic areas.

“Accordingly, over the coming years, our efforts will focus on further strengthening the legal and regulatory framework, developing human capital and enhancing public awareness, deepening international cooperation, facilitating the start of Islamic banking operations, building supporting infrastructure for Islamic finance and other priorities,” he said.

FinTech as an enabler

Ishmetov also linked the development of Islamic finance to the country’s broader digital transformation.

“We see FinTech as an important enabler of Islamic finance as an overall ecosystem and one of the key drivers for innovation, investment and productive economic activity,” he said.

Digital financial services, he added, can improve efficiency and transparency while enabling financial products to be delivered at greater scale.

“In this new era of digital economy, we believe that provision of financial services, including Islamic financial services, through digital channels will play an increasingly important role in creating new opportunities for innovation, investment and economic development,” Ishmetov said.

This intersection between Islamic finance and financial technology was one of the broader themes of the Tashkent forum, which also examined digital payments, artificial intelligence, tokenization, digital assets and cross-border financial infrastructure.

For Central Asia, the development of Islamic finance could provide an additional connection to capital markets in the Gulf, Türkiye and South and Southeast Asia. Uzbekistan’s emerging regulatory framework could therefore serve not only domestic borrowers and investors, but also support wider regional financial integration.

World.title: Experts: Kazakhstan’s Oil Export Strategy Faces Growing Need for Diversification
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s decision to cut its 2026 oil production target from 98 million tonnes to 96 million tonnes after disruptions affecting the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) has highlighted the country’s continued dependence on a major export route and the need to strengthen alternatives, experts say.

Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said at an Aug. 25 government briefing that attacks on CPC facilities in January and again in July had resulted in nearly 3.5 million tonnes of lost oil production.

“We planned to produce 98 million tonnes, but the adjusted plan is now 96 million tonnes. The losses in production from the attacks on CPC will amount to 3.5 million tonnes,” Akkenzhenov said.

The minister said Kazakhstan and oil producers had also adjusted maintenance schedules to preserve as much production as possible in 2026. Tengizchevroil shareholders decided to postpone major maintenance until next year, while maintenance work at fields operated by North Caspian Operating Company was also moved to 2027. Maintenance at the Karachaganak field, meanwhile, is expected to begin in mid-September and is projected to reduce production by nearly 400,000-450,000 tonnes.

The developments highlight a broader challenge for Kazakhstan: as a major oil exporter, the country’s production capacity is only one part of the equation. Maintaining reliable access to international markets through secure and diversified export routes is equally important.

CPC remains critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports

Kazakhstan produces substantially more oil than it consumes domestically, making export infrastructure a critical component of the country’s economic security. The CPC remains the country’s principal export route for crude oil, connecting Kazakhstan’s major producing fields with the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.

Repeated disruptions have therefore created a challenge that goes beyond temporary reductions in pipeline throughput. They have raised questions about how quickly Kazakhstan can redirect crude if its main export route becomes unavailable or operates below capacity.

Economist and independent oil and gas reserves evaluator Abzal Narymbetov highlights that Kazakhstan’s position as a major net oil exporter makes diversification particularly important.

“Kazakhstan produces approximately five times more oil than it consumes domestically. This makes Kazakhstan a distinctly oil-exporting country,” Narymbetov wrote in his Energy Analytics Telegram channel.

He also said the strategic issue is not simply increasing production.

“The main question for Kazakhstan is not only how much oil to produce, but how to maintain export volumes, develop supply routes and increase added value within the country,” Narymbetov wrote.

According to him, in the longer term Kazakhstan should also focus on processing more crude domestically and developing petrochemicals and other higher-value products. This suggests that the current disruption could be viewed not only as an infrastructure problem, but also as a broader question of how Kazakhstan manages its dependence on oil exports.

Baku-Supsa emerges as an alternative

Akkenzhenov has identified the Baku-Supsa route as one potential alternative to CPC. Asked whether Kazakhstan had discussed transporting more crude through Azerbaijan, the minister said direct negotiations had not yet taken place, although preliminary groundwork existed.

“For this, first of all, we need to determine our position domestically in Kazakhstan. There is some groundwork from previous negotiations, but direct negotiations have not yet taken place,” Akkenzhenov said.

“Just imagine: we lost 3.5 million tonnes because of the attacks on CPC, although we could have redirected these volumes through the port of Aktau and the Baku-Supsa pipeline. Its capacity, by the way, is 5 million tonnes,” the minister added.

The minister’s comments point to a key limitation, however. An alternative route can provide strategic value even if it cannot replace CPC in terms of capacity. Baku-Supsa’s reported capacity of 5 million tonnes is substantially smaller than the volumes Kazakhstan exports through CPC. Its importance therefore lies less in replacing the main route and more in providing additional resilience when the main system is disrupted.

Diversification does not mean abandoning CPC

The current situation does not necessarily imply that Kazakhstan can or should move away from CPC. Instead, it highlights the economic value of having several export options. Political science expert Gaziz Abishev said that CPC remains an essential part of Kazakhstan’s economic security because the country invested in the project specifically to create an efficient route for its oil exports.

“CPC is an indispensable element of Kazakhstan’s economic security,” Abishev wrote on his Telegram channel, stressing that the pipeline was developed as an economic project rather than as a geopolitical instrument.

“Receiving oil revenues, Kazakhstan either accumulates them in the National Fund or spends them on social needs – in the interests of its people,” he wrote, adding that the country has maintained a neutral position while calling on all sides to pursue peace.

A test of Kazakhstan’s energy resilience

The latest production target adjustment shows how an external disruption to a major export corridor can translate into a measurable impact on Kazakhstan’s domestic production plans.

The loss of nearly 3.5 million tonnes and the reduction of the annual target to 96 million tonnes do not fundamentally change Kazakhstan’s position as a major oil producer. But they demonstrate the economic consequences of concentrated export infrastructure.

Akkenzhenov’s description of Baku-Supsa as “vital” suggests that the government is increasingly viewing alternative routes not simply as commercial opportunities, but as part of national energy resilience. At the same time, CPC will remain the backbone of Kazakhstan’s oil export system because of its scale and established infrastructure.

The challenge is that alternative routes have different capacities, infrastructure requirements and costs. Moving additional volumes through the Caspian requires sufficient port capacity, tanker availability and infrastructure on the other side of the sea. That means diversification is not simply a matter of signing agreements. It requires sustained investment in the entire logistics chain.

World.title: AqylSu: Turning Kazakhstan’s Shanghai AI Vision Into Working Water Platform
World.content:
Kazakhstan boasts to have an AI diplomacy and a digital-government track record. What it is missing is a platform that turns both into water reaching the people who need it.

During President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Shanghai this July, he addressed the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, describing AI as an industry now building out a “comprehensive infrastructure” that will shape the future of the global economy, trade and international connectivity. He cited the United Nations statistics showing that global investment in AI infrastructure is growing by an average of 47% a year, with the global AI market on track to approach $5 trillion by 2033. His main argument was about fairness: AI should become a driver of more equitable and inclusive development, and every country needs a chance to build its own human capital, digital infrastructure and institutions around it, not just the few states currently leading the field.

Kazakhstan did not just make the argument in Shanghai — it proposed and acted on it, co-founding the new World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other states within months of the idea being proposed, with Tokayev offering the capital of Kazakhstan as host of its first meeting. The obvious next step is what Kazakhstan actually builds with that vision once the delegation flies home. A very powerful candidate sitting in the country’s own fields is water.

A crisis moving faster than the diplomacy meant to fix it

Kazakhstan is among the world’s 30 most water-stressed countries and has lost over 21% of its per capita water availability since the start of the 2000s. More than 45% of its water actually originates outside its borders. The Caspian Sea is now at its lowest level in over 400 years and shrinks at a fast accelerating rate. None of this is moving on a diplomatic timetable. Yet the country’s main global response is a proposed International Water Organization (IWO) championed by Tokayev under UN auspices since 2025, but discussions are still focused on how the organization should eventually take shape. A parallel regional process, Tajikistan’s Dushanbe Water Framework, remains an important initiative, yet it is not expected to be adopted until the 2028 UN Water Conference.

Both processes matter, and neither is wrong to exist — a UN-backed framework can build an institution that carries international legitimacy, but that takes time and lasting credibility. The problem is that water insecurity is moving much faster than the diplomacy designed to address it. With every year that passes, the gap between the crisis and the response grows a little wider. Kazakhstan has already showcased that it can act quickly when it sees a strategic opportunity. Its recent leadership on AI cooperation in Shanghai showed its capabilities of bringing countries together and building new institutions. Water diplomacy now requires the same sense of urgency.

The idea: an AI platform that matches specific needs to specific help

The proposal currently taking shape is called AqylSu — meaning “smart water” in Kazakh. The idea was inspired by Kazakhstan’s own eGov.kz system, the main aim of which is to bring the same efficiency to international water cooperation. Instead of relying on long, case-by-case negotiations, AqylSu would provide a single digital platform where countries could submit their requests, find suitable partners, and track progress. While Kazakhstan has gained international recognition worldwide for its digital governance, no similar system currently exists for cooperation on water between countries.

The idea is simple. A country that faces a specific water-related problem, such as a shortage of water filtration equipment, would submit a structured request through the platform. An AI-powered matching system would verify the country’s request using independent data, including images and water-stressed indicators, before comparing it with registered countries and technical organizations that have already declared available equipment or funding. This would allow countries with specific needs to be matched with those who are available to provide practical support for those in need.

Where financing is required, countries with the resources could contribute voluntarily. Further complex requests could be reviewed by a committee working with UN-Water and the International Water Organization, while every request and outcome would be recorded on a public dashboard to further ensure transparency and accountability.

Fast precedents: Saudi Arabia’s Global Water Organization and Tajikistan’s Dushanbe Process

Kazakhstan does not need to guess whether a fast, nationally driven water initiative would work — Saudi Arabia has already begun running the experiment. In September 2023, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman announced the creation of the Global Water Organization (GWO). By May 2025, eight founding states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Spain, Greece, Senegal, Pakistan and Mauritania — had signed its charter in Riyadh, with Saudi Arabia funding the organization’s operations for five years and hosting its headquarters. At Saudi Water Week in Jeddah in mid-2026, the GWO had approved its bylaws, governance model, and a four-year strategy, and is preparing for its first General Assembly. Tajikistan’s own Dushanbe Water Process has moved on a similar diplomatic timeline: in May 2026, at its fourth conference, Emomali Rahmon proposed a brand-new Dushanbe Water Framework, expected to be carried forward by the UN Water Conference in 2028, which Tajikistan will host. Both paths show that nationally driven water diplomacy can move fast — but both remain platforms for coordination and policy dialogue, not systems that match one country’s specific need to another’s specific offer. That is precisely the operational layer AqylSu is designed to add.

Two working models for how the mechanism would actually run

AqylSu draws its inspiration from a system the United Nations uses. The UN Volunteers program, which supports agencies such as UNICEF, maintains a global roster of registered professionals and matches them with specific requests from country offices based on their skills. AqylSu follows a similar approach. Instead of matching people to jobs, it would match verified water-related requests with countries or technical experts that have already declared available expertise, equipment, and funding. This would make finding support faster and more targeted, instead of relying on traditional diplomatic outreach.

The financial model also has a practical precedent. Since 1967, the UN Women’s Guild in Vienna has raised funds through its annual International Festivals Bazaar to support small humanitarian projects. A review committee rates applications each year and recommends selected projects for funding, to ensure resources are shared fairly and transparently. AqylSu could adopt a similar approach for water requests that are too small or complex to attract a single sponsoring organization or country, by using a pooled fund overseen by a committee to provide support where it is most needed.

What it would look like in practice

Imagine a country whose water system can no longer hold or provide safe drinking water due to its lack of filtration equipment. Instead of beginning lengthy negotiations, the country submits a request through AqylSu, clearly outlining what is needed and when. The platform verifies the request using independent water data stored in its database, before matching it with a country that has available filtration capacity.

If the country cannot cover the full cost, AqylSu will first look for a state that is willing to help finance the request. If there is no direct sponsor available, the request can be reviewed through a pooled funding mechanism based on the UN Women’s Guild’s model. At every stage, from receipt to approval, this information would be posted on a public dashboard so that international water aid would be both swift and transparent.

Bringing the Shanghai vision home

Tokayev’s message in Shanghai was that AI should not remain the property of a handful of advanced economies — that every country deserves the infrastructure and institutions to use it well. Kazakhstan is now in the unusual position of having said that on the world stage and having, close at hand, the exact problem where it could prove it: a water crisis it cannot out-wait, a digital-government platform that already works domestically, and two very different but equally instructive templates — one Gulf, one Viennese — for how the money and the matching could actually flow. AqylSu is not a rival to the UN’s own water diplomacy; it is the operational arm that diplomacy has never had. Kazakhstan already knows it can build fast, charter-based institutions when it chooses to. The question now is whether it does the same for the resource its own president has called an emerging crisis — before the next round of consultations concludes.

The authors are Jansultan Syrymbet and Jamila Syrymbet, students of the CIS Astana and Corvinus University respectively.
