World.title: 'Backyard' e-bike battery repairs starting deadly fires, inquest told
World.content:
Lithium-ion battery fires are being caused by DIY e-bike alterations inspired by YouTube, an inquest has heard.

NSW Deputy State Coroner Kasey Pearce was overseeing the inquest in Sydney that was focused on the specific circumstances of four fires, two of which were fatal.

Videos from testing labs have been admitted into evidence, showing how hot and volatile the fires can get.

At least two of the fires, including a deadly blaze in Lake Macquarie, involved "backyard" repair jobs of e-bike batteries.

Judge Pearce's focus is on so-called micro-mobility vehicles, including e-bikes, e-scooters and hoverboards.

The inquest began in December and resumed this week.

Today, counsel assisting the coroner, Ann Bonnor, asked about repairs done by unlicensed people.

Andrew Low from Fire and Rescue NSW's Fire Investigation and Research Unit told the inquest that too often fires had been linked to homemade repairs or battery re-builds with parts bought online.

Fire and Rescue NSW has a special team to investigate and research battery fires. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

"There are backyard operations, they have soldering irons and they purchase things off eBay to do repairs," he said.

"Generally YouTube will show people how to do this [repairs] as well.

"Their exact motivations, I don't know, maybe whether to get more power, I am not really sure."

He said he had been to eight lithium-ion battery fires and most were linked to unauthorised repairs or people adding batteries to existing packs.

"I have been to a few where it has been evident that they have made some non-manufacture changes to batteries," he said.

His evidence echoed testimony given by Fire and Rescue Assistant Commissioner Brendan Cox in the initial hearing.

He said backyard repairers, purporting to be experts, had been linked to blazes in New South Wales and Victoria.

He said it was "unregulated and dangerous work, often sought after by people wanting to save money".

Fleeing fire

The first fire happened in short-stay accommodation at Cabarita Beach in Northern NSW in September 2023, a day after a man picked up his repaired e-bike battery.

He suffered severe burns to 40 per cent of his body, but survived.

In the second blaze being examined, a food delivery driver was injured in December 2023 when his second-hand e-bike battery exploded in his bedroom in the inner-Sydney suburb of Annandale.

Mazharul Haque Shohan, who suffered burns to 20 per cent of his body, gave evidence to the inquest today.

Three delivery drivers survived an e-bike battery fire in an Annandale unit in 2023. (Supplied: NSW Coroners Court)

Mr Shohan said he thought he was dreaming that night, before fleeing while on fire.

"I woke to a huge sound, I thought I was dreaming," he said.

"It was a matter of five seconds of my life, there was a really big bang and things were shaking."

He said there were flames and extra heat and he knew he had been burned.

"There were instant flames with the bang. The bang came out with a lot of sparks. Black smoke and smells," he said.

"It felt like it was blasting a couple of times."

Two other men fled the unit.

Mr Shohan told the inquest the month before he had his e-bike battery stolen, so he bought a replacement.

Explosions and death

The last two fires were fatal.

Patricia Kerr is one of two women who died in a house fire at Teralba, near Newcastle in 2024. (Supplied: Facebook)

In February 2024, two women died in a two-storey townhouse at Teralba, south of Newcastle.

The inquest heard a "backyard" repairer inserted mismatched pins and pierced an e-bike battery's casing before it exploded.

Patricia Kerr and Therese Harris were killed.

Therese Harris also died in the Teralba blaze. (Supplied: Facebook)

The inquest has heard temperatures could reach 900 degrees Celsius within minutes when lithium-ion batteries exploded.

The inquest heard battery cells could also be ejected from a battery pack up to 40 metres.

The two women died in a townhouse fire in 2024. (ABC Newcastle: Romy Stephens)

The fourth and final fire involved a battery charging 30 centimetres from the foot of a delivery driver's bed in Sydney last year.

The inquest heard he suffered incineration injuries, dying at the scene.

A bedroom that suffered significant fire damage after an e-bike battery overheated, resulting in the death of a man. (Supplied: Fire and Rescue NSW)

Fire Rescue NSW data tendered in court has said lithium-ion batteries caused about six fires in NSW per week.

The inquest is due to run until the end of next week.

World.title: Young Perth hackers key players in global cybercrime syndicate, says FBI
World.content:
Two young Western Australians have been charged for their alleged role in a "sophisticated cybercrime syndicate" that allegedly created malicious software to rob hundreds of organisations around the world.

Louis Michael Gaebler, 23, and Ruben Ian Thomson, 21, were arrested in Perth following a joint investigation with federal and state police working alongside the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

They faced court today charged with a combined 14 offences after police raided properties in Cottesloe, Hamilton Hill and Mandurah where electronic devices and other items were seized.

The men were arrested in Perth over their alleged involvment in the group. (Supplied)

Police allege the men were part of a highly organised syndicate involved in large-scale cybercrimes, including data intrusion, identity crime and cryptocurrency-based money laundering.

Investigations began in April after the Australian Federal Police and the FBI received tip offs about a syndicate that allegedly inserted malicious code into open source software available online which was then unwittingly used by other developers.

A sophisticated cybercrime syndicate allegedly created malicious open-source software to rob thousands of global businesses. (Pixabay: terydanphiri)

The term 'open source' refers to content that developers can modify and share because its design is publicly accessible.

Hackers allegedly paid crypto

Police will allege the infected software made its way into computer systems at across government, academic and private sector institutions, potentially compromising more than 1,000 organisations globally.

OpenAI model hacks startup OpenAI has announced one of its AI models went rogue and broke containment during testing.

The software allegedly enabled the syndicate to infiltrate those organisations to steal or harvest sensitive data, including more than 500,000 user credentials and authentication materials.

The financial impacts include remediation costs estimated to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

Police allege the WA men were key participants in the activities of the cybercrime syndicate and received payments in cryptocurrency for their roles, the value of which is still under investigation.

Louis Gaebler's lawyer made no application for bail and his client was remanded in custody for his next appearance on September 18..

Ruben Thomson's lawyer flagged a bail application although it was uncertain when this might occur.

Police say there may be more arrests as investigations continue.

World.title: E-scooter crash leaves teenage boy in critical condition
World.content:
Police are investigating an e-scooter crash that has left a teenage boy in a critical condition.

Emergency services were called to Macrossan Street in Childers, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, just after 6pm yesterday after reports of a single-vehicle e-scooter crash.

The rider, a 13-year-old boy, suffered serious head injuries and was airlifted to Queensland Children's Hospital in a critical condition.

Bundaberg Highway Patrol officer in charge Gordon Hard said the events leading up to the crash were not clear.

"To the best of my knowledge he was wearing a helmet," he said.

"Paramedics performed CPR before that child was flown to Brisbane."

Sergeant Hard said officers were examining the e-scooter to determine its capabilities, and whether speed was a contributing factor in the crash.

"If anyone has got dash cam footage or any other sort of footage that may have been around that area at 6pm yesterday afternoon, we're urging them to go to the police," Sergeant Hard said.

Police are appealing for witnesses to an e-scooter crash in Childers to come forward. (Supplied)

It is the second serious e-scooter incident in the region, after a 39-year-old Hervey Bay man died in a crash involving his e-scooter and an electric skateboard in July.

It was the first e-scooter fatality in Queensland this year.

"Anything that's travelling at 70, 80, 90, up to 100 kilometres an hour, either an e-scooter or an e-bike is dangerous and nothing good can happen for them," Sergeant Hard said.

"We're urging parents out there, if your child has one of these illegal scooters or high-powered bikes, you need to seriously consider taking it off them

"The government has changed the laws for a reason and police are trying their best to get these e-scooters and e-bikes off the road."

World.title: Parents worry kids will inherit climate impact of coal mine extension
World.content:
As the independent referee weighs up one of NSW's largest mine extensions, parents are grappling with what the decision will mean for their children.

The Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Continuation Project would result in mining continuing at the site near Singleton, in the Upper Hunter, until the end of 2045.

That would represent a 19-year extension of the Yancoal-Glencore joint venture's existing approvals, which expire in December.

HVO projections show the extension would allow an extra 429 million tonnes of coal to be mined, generating 809 million tonnes of CO2 emissions.

Activist group Parents for Climate today rallied against the project outside NSW Parliament House, with CEO Nic Seton saying he was "terrified" by the prospect.

Parents for Climate says the extension will negatively impact the next generation. (ABC News)

"My kids are in primary school now, and they haven't gone a year without being impacted [by climate change] in some way, whether that's being evacuated from a campsite or being sent to hospital for breathing too much bushfire smoke during the black summer," he said.

" I think a lot of other parents around the country are really worried about what the future of our society, our economy and our environment is going to look like for our kids. "

Mr Seton said he took no comfort from the HVO projection that about 98 per cent of emissions from the project would be Scope 3, or indirect, emissions produced when the coal was burnt by overseas buyers to produce electricity.

Nic Seton wants the extension to be rejected. (ABC News)

"It doesn't matter whether it gets burnt and transported locally or globally," he said.

"That pollution is still going to come back on people living all across the country in the form of extreme weather events, rising costs, disruptions of supply chains and food security.

"No-one's safe from it."

Job losses loom

But for Chris Bateman, a shift supervisor at HVO, a rejection by the IPC will come with a different type of social cost.

HVO employs more than 1,500 people and engages nearly 800 suppliers.

Chris Bateman says an extension of HVO would help secure his kids' futures. (Supplied: Chris Bateman)

"The Hunter Valley needs HVO," Mr Bateman said.

"It's massive in our community, most of my friends, if not all, are impacted either directly or indirectly by mining.

" Society itself is built around it. "

The former painter started at HVO about 15 years ago, working his way through the ranks.

He said the closure of the mine would impact thousands of children like his.

"I've been able to financially support us … we own our house, providing the kids with whatever they need to get through school," he said.

Hunter Valley Operations is one of the largest mines in NSW. (ABC News)

"HVO, and mining in general, provides a multitude of opportunities for our kids in apprenticeship programs [and] cadetships. It's also the fact that it's close to home, I'm able to come home every day and see my kids … [and] coach the football team."

Mr Bateman said both the climate and employment impacts of the extension were "valid things to consider" but HVO's current proposal continued to align with government requirements.

"The mine only equates to less than 1 per cent of NSW's annual emissions," he said.

"NSW mining is one of the most heavily regulated industries in the country as far as environmental constraints go, and we don't take that lightly.

" It's the community that we live in that we're doing it for, so we have as much, if not more, vested interest than anyone to make sure that we're doing it right. "

The IPC held two days of public hearings on the Hunter Valley Operations Continuation Project. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

But Mr Seton said approving coal mine extensions placed an unfair burden on the next generation.

"By the time they grow up and get to vote, a lot of these decisions will have been made and it will be too late," he said.

" We need to be the adults in the room so the kids can count on us to make sure their future is as bright as possible. "

The IPC is expected to announce its decision on the future of HVO early next month.

World.title: Pilot's family mourn 'great loss' as police continue search for plane wreckage
World.content:
A pilot believed to have died when their aircraft crashed into remote waters off the Northern Territory coast earlier this week has been identified as Tasmanian man Bob Bramley.

Police launched an investigation on Tuesday afternoon after a small charter plane operated by Air Frontier reportedly crashed in Angurugu waters, off the coast of Groote Eylandt in the Gulf of Carpentaria.

Police said around 11:40am on Tuesday, a witness onboard a boat in the area reported the "aircraft had crashed into the water near Isle Woodah".

NT Police Assistant Commissioner Peter Malley said authorities believed the pilot died in the crash but they had yet to locate a body.

Small aircraft crash reported in NT Police investigating a plane crash in the Gulf of Carpentaria have confirmed "no aircraft wreckage or persons have been located" yet, despite hours-long search efforts.

Charter company Air Frontier later released a statement confirming its Beechcraft Baron aircraft "was involved in an accident near Numbulwar" around midday.

According to Air Frontier, the aircraft was undertaking a "non-commercial repositioning flight" from Gove to Numbulwar with the pilot believed to be the sole occupant on board.

Mr Bramley circumnavigated Australia in a small plane as a 16-year-old in 2019 to raise awareness about youth suicide.

He also founded the youth mental health and suicide prevention initiative Surviving Turbulence.

In a statement, his family said they could not "comprehend this great loss in our lives".

As a teenager, Tasmanian pilot Bob Bramley circumnavigated Australia by himself. (ABC News: Manika Dadson)

"There are no words, deeds or silver linings that make this any easier, but our beloved Bob is gone," the statement said.

"Bob was a courageous individual, who inspired those around him with his infectious enthusiasm.

"He was a dreamer, who never let fear, problems or pessimists stop him from reaching his goals."

Debris located on Wednesday

The search mission coordinator, Acting Sergeant Nathan Conelius, said crews had managed to locate "aircraft debris" in the search area on Wednesday.

"That's helped refine our search planning so we're more hopeful today of finding something else," he said.

Acting sergeant Cornelius said the remote search location, which is roughly 50 kilometres north-west of Alyangula, has made the operation particularly challenging.

"There's no accurate weather data out there which is adding a lot of complexity to the search," he said.

"We're finding that sea and the weather conditions in the search area are much worse than what we're seeing online so we're relying on the limited communication we have."

Loading...

He said the location has also prevented additional crew members from being able to access the site.

"Because it's so remote we're not able to get any more people in there," he said.

" We just don't have the assets available. "

Police resources have been assisted by Anindilyakwa sea rangers and helicopter support from Nautilus Aviation with search and rescue crews also on the ground in Alyangula.

Acting Sergeant Cornelius said police divers would conduct searches of the sea floor throughout Thursday.

Anindilyakwa sea rangers are assisting with the search effort. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

'Incredibly difficult' time for pilot's family

Acting Sergeant Cornelius said police have been in contact with Mr Bramley's family.

In a statement earlier this week, Air Frontier said they were "deeply saddened" by news of the incident.

"Our thoughts are with our pilot and their family at this incredibly difficult time," the statement said.

"The family has been contacted, and we are supporting them as this situation unfolds.

"As is standard process, the cause of the accident will be a matter for the investigating authorities, and it would be inappropriate to speculate at this time."

Air Frontier said all of its Beechcraft Baron aircraft had been grounded "as a precautionary measure", pending advice from relevant authorities.

World.title: Anger and confusion over Labor's planned refugee cuts
World.content:
The Albanese government's plan to slash more than 6,000 places from its annual refugee intake have sparked anger and confusion within Labor, and prompted accusations it would amount to an "extraordinary betrayal" of the party's rank and file members.

A spokesperson for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has confirmed Labor plans to reduce the humanitarian intake next financial year by a third, from 20,000 to 13,750, as reported in the Australian Financial Review (AFR).

Mr Burke's office said Labor's decision to lift the intake in 2023 was always temporary and was only funded for four years.

But four Labor MPs, speaking on the condition of anonymity, have disputed this characterisation, telling the ABC they believed the higher intake was "enduring" and "not time-limited".

The proposed change has not been canvassed in any caucus forums, according to another MP, who said they expected the existing refugee intake to be maintained in line with Labor's National Platform when the funding comes up for renewal next year.

Last month at the ALP National Conference there was unanimous agreement on a resolution committing Labor to maintaining the intake at 20,000 per year "in the short-term" while continuing "to aspire to achieving" 27,000 places.

The issue has been described as "sacred" to party members, who have reluctantly accepted hardline border protection policies in exchange for the promise of Labor lifting Australia's refugee intake.

Speaking at the Daily Telegraph's Bush Summit in Dubbo today, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese suggested the government was still finalising its policy.

"Don't believe everything you read in the Fin," Mr Albanese said, referring to the AFR report.

Anthony Albanese cast doubt on the cuts despite confirmation from Tony Burke's office. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

When asked if Labor's crackdown on migration was in response to a populist push from parties such as One Nation, Mr Albanese said the government was responding "to the national need".

"There is a current spike in the support for One Nation, quite clearly," he said.

"But we’ve responded [to the migration issue] — we started lowering the numbers well before that occurred."

Employer wait for overseas nurses, teachers blows out Business leaders hope the current visa settings will be in place for 'a very short time'.

Australia has historically resettled a baseline of 13,750 refugees each year.

In 2022, the Morrison government temporarily boosted the intake to 17,875, for Afghan nationals, before then-immigration minister Andrew Giles announced a further increase to 20,000 per year in 2023.

At the time Mr Albanese said "the government will be tough on borders without being weak on humanity".

"When the Albanese government increased the refugee and humanitarian program to 20,000 places in 2023, there was no hint that this was a short-term increase," Refugee Council of Australia chief executive Paul Power said.

"If the cut goes ahead, the Albanese government would be implementing the policy Peter Dutton took to the 2025 election, turning its back on a commitment that has been Labor policy for 14 years."

Jana Favero says the reported cuts are an outrage and a betrayal. (ABC News: Erin Handley)

Asylum Seeker Resource Centre deputy chief executive Jana Favero said it was an "extraordinary betrayal" of Labor members who secured a commitment to maintaining Australia's refugee intake at its current level a month ago.

"I'm sure Labor MPs and members will be asking how a decision made openly and democratically at their own National Conference can be discarded so quickly by Anthony Albanese and Tony Burke," she said.

"This shows that they are panicking and it shows that One Nation is leading their migration policy."

Lifting Australia's refugee intake has been embedded in the Labor party's platform for a decade.

The promise to resettle more refugees was critical in convincing Labor's left faction to endorse a number of hardline border protection policies, including boat turn-backs, at the 2015 ALP National Conference.

While a reduction in the refugee intake is not being considered as part of the government's looming migration overhaul, Labor is under pressure to reduce overseas arrivals and achieve its target of cutting net overseas migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028.

PM quells UK's backpacker visa concerns The prime minister has vowed not to make British backpackers work in regional areas as part of a looming migration overhaul, defusing a potential diplomatic stoush with the United Kingdom.

Mr Burke has already paused or slowed down the processing of Working Holiday Maker visas and bumped workers applying for skilled visas from overseas to the back of the queue.

As revealed by the ABC, the minister was also considering removing the favourable treatment of British backpackers, which would be in breach of the UK free trade agreement, before the prime minister intervened.

Mr Power said cutting 6,250 refugee places would have little impact on migration numbers, noting that the program overhaul has has contributed just 6.6 per cent to NOM over the past decade.

World.title: Ex-NSW building commissioner tells ICAC of alleged $5m shakedown
World.content:
Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler has told a corruption inquiry that an allegation of an "extortion attempt" targeting construction company Toplace was used against him in efforts to get a prohibition order on its development lifted.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is investigating whether people linked to the NSW Liberal Party solicited funds from prohibited donors and other sources to advance the interests of the right-wing NSW Reformers faction.

It is also examining whether donations linked to fugitive property developer Jean Nassif were exchanged for political favours, including removing Mr Chandler as building commissioner.

The ICAC inquiry focuses on the relationship between fugitive property developer, Jean Nassif, Liberal Party operatives and potential breaches of NSW electoral laws. (ABC News)

Mr Chandler said the alleged shakedown was raised during a 2021 meeting between himself and Toplace representatives, including Sharangan Maheswaran, when they were discussing what needed to happen before a prohibition order of the developer's Skyview project in Castle Hill could be lifted.

The commission heard that Mr Maheswaran, a person of interest in the inquiry, allegedly claimed the company had received an email seeking $5 million to be paid into a trust account.

Under questioning from counsel assisting Juliet Curtin, Mr Chandler said he was implicated in the allegation because there was a suggestion that if the money was paid, he would lift the order.

Ms Curtin: "Was the inference to be drawn there that you would benefit from this money being paid somehow?" Mr Chandler: "Well, of course it was … but it didn't even sort of raise my blood pressure very much because I just said to them, 'Why don't we go straight to the police station now and report it?' and they said, 'No, no, no we're not confident about it yet'. "I said, 'OK, well if you are, let's do it straight away but until much more substance to this is attached, you're dreaming'."

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Mr Chandler was not provided with a copy of the alleged email but referred the matter to his department for investigation.

He said that when investigators sought further information from Mr Maheswaran, Toplace subsequently appeared to retreat from the unsubstantiated claim and did not assist with the investigation.

Mr Chandler is not accused of wrongdoing.

'I'll harm you'

Mr Chandler said he had few direct dealings with Mr Nassif himself but often dealt with Toplace.

He said Mr Nassif called him after his office issued a notice of intent to issue a prohibition order in relation to the Skyview site.

He recalled Mr Nassif saying: "Don't you harm my project and if you harm my project, I'll harm you."

Earlier in the inquiry, an intercepted call appeared to capture Mr Nassif discussing efforts to remove Mr Chandler from his position.

"I'm gonna step on his neck and strip him from his job," Mr Nassif said.

Eleni Petinos gave evidence at the inquiry last week. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

Mr Nassif also appeared to predict that then-fair trading minister Eleni Petinos would become one of his political allies.

The inquiry has heard evidence that a video of Mr Chandler was circulated and allegedly used as part of efforts to undermine him.

Mr Chandler was cleared of misconduct, but he said he believed Ms Petinos had lost confidence in him.

He resigned in 2022 following an investigation commissioned by Ms Petinos's office, but that was later reversed and he remained in the role until 2024.

Ms Petinos, who is not a person of interest or accused of wrongdoing, has told the inquiry she believed she was subsequently "used" in efforts to remove Mr Chandler and she was "disgusted" by the alleged conduct.

"Even the little I knew coming into here today is enough to leave me disgusted and to feel like personal relationships were lent on in a highly improper way," Ms Petinos told the hearing last week.

World.title: Plans to cool AI data centre using trucked-in water and rainwater
World.content:
A proposed AI data centre in north-west Tasmania plans to cool its facilities using rainwater and water that it trucks in.

Firmus Technologies wants to build a 52-megawatt AI data centre in Wesley Vale, at the old paper mill site in Mill Park.

The centre would produce AI tokens, needed for tools such as generative AI chatbot ChatGPT.

Latrobe Council has now released the project's development application, which is open for public submissions until September 9.

The council received the application months ago, but told the ABC it was waiting on Firmus to submit extra information before releasing it to the public and later voting on the proposal.

Earlier this week, George Town Council approved one of Firmus's other proposed data centres — a 288-megawatt facility in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone, in northern Tasmania.

Firmus is also building a 104-megawatt facility in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards.

Application details water use, noise emissions, jobs

Firmus came under scrutiny last month when it accidentally published information on its website about its water supply plans for the proposed Wesley Vale facility.

The company wrote that because there was no TasWater connection to the site, it planned to use rainwater and water from state-owned company Tasmanian Irrigation.

Tasmanian Irrigation supplies water to agricultural users and said at the time it could not legally provide water to data centres.

The development application shows Firmus now plans to use rainwater and water delivered by truck.

"We expect the trucking option to be needed only in extreme dry periods," the application states.

The AI data centre is proposed for the old paper mill site. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The biggest water requirement is for cooling, which Firmus states will only be required on days when the temperature exceeds 26 degrees Celsius.

On noise emissions, an assessment published in the application found they would "not cause a significant loss of amenity or environmental nuisance", but recommended the assessment be updated when details were finalised.

"As the predicted combined noise level of the data centre is very close to the background + 5 dB(A) target level, it is recommended that additional noise mitigation measures are applied to the emergency generators to achieve a sound power level of 85 dB(A)," it states.

"This would allow for issues such as periods of unusually high noise propagation or equipment noise emissions that are higher than predicted by the manufacturer's catalogue data or that change over time."

The development application shows there will be 40 backup diesel generators at the site.

Council will vote whether to approve or reject the proposal after members of the public have their say. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Firmus said the Wesley Vale facility would support 70 jobs in construction and 20 ongoing roles.

The company does not yet have a power deal for the site, but has previously indicated its preference to use Tasmania's hydro energy.

"Firmus is committed to supporting new renewable energy projects in Tasmania, with the goal of fully matching the electricity demand of our sites over time," the development application states.

"We are only contracting energy that is available today, and are working with Tas Hydro to underwrite new energy as part of future contracting."

Planning scheme 'not fit for purpose' to evaluate data centres, mayor says

Latrobe Mayor Peter Freshney said the council's role was to assess the project against the planning scheme.

"It really does highlight the almost tension between the two roles of elected members — that is community representation and the role as a member of a planning authority," he told 936 ABC Hobart.

"The planning authority, and members therein, can only consider those components of a planning scheme that are applicable under the legislation.

"The community would expect us to consider much more than that."

Peter Freshney does not believe the planning scheme is the best way to assess AI data centres. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Some community members and councillors, including George Town Mayor Greg Kieser, believe Firmus's facilities should be assessed by the state government, rather than local councils under the planning scheme.

Cr Freshney said he did not believe the planning scheme, legislated in 1993, was fit for purpose to evaluate a project of this scale.

"It was legislated at a time when data centres as such would not have even been considered feasible or on the horizon," he said.

"I don't believe that any framework can be fit for purpose for every situation.

"I think there's an opportunity for both federal and state governments to reflect that concern, that reality."

World.title: From 9 to 5 to Steel Magnolias: Dolly Parton’s cinematic legacy
World.content:
CultureTV & radioVale From 9 to 5 to Steel Magnolias: Dolly Parton’s cinematic legacy Michael Idato Updated August 27, 2026 — 3:36pm ,first published 2:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In one of Dolly Parton’s most memorable scenes in the film 9 to 5, secretary Doralee Rhodes flips the script on her handsy boss Mr Hart (Dabney Coleman) and puts him in his place. “Look, I’ve got a gun out there in my purse and up to now I’ve been forgiving and forgetting because of the way I was brought up,” she says. “But if you ever say another word about me or make another indecent proposal, I’m gonna get that gun of mine and I’m gonna change you from a rooster to a hen with one shot.” Dolly Parton (centre) with Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, in 9 to 5. 20th Century Fox That line, like many, has echoed in cinema history. Like 9 to 5 itself, it is a call to arms in the war against workplace sexual harassment. And for fans of Dolly Parton, it is one of her many, many memorable scenes in film and television. This week, under the headlines, you will have read essay after essay on the legacy of Dolly Parton. One of the world’s most beloved cultural icons, she was a legendary country singer, who cut an extraordinary path from the fringes to the mainstream, allowing many, including Taylor Swift and Orville Peck, to follow her path.



Perhaps just as well known – depending on your age – is Parton’s other life, as a movie star and a television personality. There was The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (1982) and Steel Magnolias (1989). And on television, in Hannah Montana (2006-2011), she was Aunt Dolly to Miley Cyrus’ Miley Stewart, a middle school student who leads a secret life as a pop star known as Hannah Montana. That guest role was also a nod to the fact that Parton was, in real life, Cyrus’ godmother. 9 to 5 (1980) In the Dolly Parton cinematic canon, one role stands above all others: that of secretary Doralee Rhodes in 9 to 5, who, with colleagues Violet Newstead (Lily Tomlin) and Judy Bernly (Jane Fonda), takes on their oppressive, harassing boss and transforms their workplace. Loading Dolly’s character Doralee was a caricature on paper – a busty secretary ostensibly hired by a sleazy boss because of her looks – but she was given great humanity and dimension by Parton’s nuanced performance.



“I’m as nice as I know how to be to every single person in that office,” she says in one scene. “Everyone treats me like a bastard at a family reunion.” Later, when Mr Hart’s corruption is exposed, she has this to say: “We keep underrating you, fella. We always knew you were an obnoxious, philandering, sexist backstabber ... but we didn’t realise you were a crook to boot.” What makes Doralee so perfect a reflection of Parton is that while the role itself was a step outside her real world, many of the smaller touches drew inspiration from Parton’s life. A feminist icon: besieged secretary Doralee Rhodes in 9 to 5. 20th Century Fox That iconic scene – the “rooster to a hen with one shot” scene – actually comes from Parton’s own encounter with a stranger in New York as a young woman. Parton told the story to Fonda, the film’s producer, and writer/director Colin Higgins, and it ended up in the scene. “We walked around ... and we ended up on 42nd street,” Parton told interviewer Conan O’Brien in 2005. “We didn’t know where we were. I was a country girl from the mountains, and I had a gun in my purse. This guy wouldn’t leave me alone because he was sure I was playing hard to get. So I just pulled my gun out, and I said, if you touch me one more time I’m gonna shoot you, so he backed off.”



Parton’s film work would see her go on to star in The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, as brothel owner Miss Mona Stangley opposite Burt Reynolds, Rhinestone (1984), a musical comedy in which she was paired with Sylvester Stallone, and then Steel Magnolias, in an incredible ensemble with Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Olympia Dukakis, Julia Roberts and Daryl Hannah. On television, as well as Hannah Montana, she had her own variety show Dolly (1976, 1987-1988), she produced and narrated the biopic Dolly Parton’s Coat of Many Colours (2015) and its sequel, Dolly Parton’s Christmas of Many Colours: Circle of Love (2016). In the latter, she played a small role, the town’s “painted lady”, on whom, in real life, she had modelled her style. There are many, many more. Dolly Parton as the angel Agnes in Grace and Frankie. Sebastian Smith/Netflix Grace and Frankie (2022) Then, in 2022, in the sitcom Grace and Frankie, Parton guest starred as Agnes, a working-class angel who is manning the reception desk at heaven’s gates when characters played by the show’s two stars Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin – Parton’s 9 to 5 co-stars – are electrocuted in a freak accident and wake up in the afterlife.



“I’m not the Almighty, just a working-class angel,” Parton says in the scene, with the kind of humble divinity that could have come from the woman herself. “I haven’t had a promotion in 250 years, but the benefits are heaven,” she adds. (Boom, boom.) Of course, their arrival in heaven is a paperwork glitch and Agnes returns Grace and Frankie to earth. But the audience reaction to the reunion of the three women, 42 years after 9 to 5, was testament to their friendship, the power of their performances and the enduring appeal of the film. Steel Magnolias (1989) While 9 to 5 may be recorded as Parton’s most commercially successful and even memorable cinematic outing, it is also hard to under-measure Steel Magnolias, in which Parton played wise-cracking beauty shop owner Truvy Jones. Of all her screen roles, this is the one which is perhaps closest to the real Dolly. “I don’t trust anyone who does their own hair, I don’t think it’s natural,” Truvy says in a scene. In another: “Honey, time marches on, and eventually, you realise it is marchin’ across your face.” And in another: “Oh, honey, God don’t care which church you go to, long as you show up.”

World.title: Fifty per cent of women experience this health condition. Why has nobody warned them?
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessWomen's health Fifty per cent of women experience this health condition. Why has nobody warned them? Sarah Berry August 27, 2026 — 3:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The memory is etched in Monique Vogt’s mind. It was 2022, and she was being wheeled down the corridor of the hospital, looking up at the fluorescent lights above. A nurse walked next to the bed and shook her, “Monique, stay with me, stay with me”. As everyone around her panicked, and the new mother haemorrhaged blood, she felt a wave of acceptance. Minutes earlier, her first child had been born, ripped into the world by forceps. “I remember this thought going, ‘OK, well, we didn’t know the sex of the baby and I got to find out I had a son and I got to give him his name. Mitch [her husband] is going to be a great dad without me, it’s going to be OK if I die’.” When Monique Vogt was diagnosed with pelvic organ prolapse, she had never heard of the condition. Steven Siewert Vogt, 33 at the time, was wheeled into the theatre where an anaesthetist squeezed her hand tightly. He said, “Monique, I’m going to save you.” And then she was unconscious.



When she woke up in intensive care two days later, her obstetrician explained she suffered a third-degree tear, where the vagina is torn down to the muscles of the anal sphincter, as her son, Levi, was being pulled out with the forceps. Editor's pick Fertility ‘Social egg freezing’ is on the rise, but at what cost? She would later find out that her pelvic floor had been partially ripped from the bone, and she had a pelvic organ prolapse, which is when the bladder, uterus or bowel loses some of its support and moves downwards through the vagina. The school teacher, now 37, recalls thinking, “I have no f---ing idea what this means. I’ve never even heard of this.” About 50 per cent of women experience a pelvic organ prolapse (POP) at some point in their lives, with about 20 per cent experiencing symptoms.



“This is a public health issue,” says Professor Anna Rosamilia, head of the pelvic floor unit at Monash Health. “Something like 22,000 Australian women per year have some form of prolapse surgery.” Independent Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie is one of those women. Last week, in an impassioned speech to parliament, Lambie told the Senate she suffered a prolapse six months ago, linked to an injury she sustained in 1997 while carrying a 40 kilogram backpack during army infantry training. “My vagina was collapsing, and three months later, it was taking my bladder with it.” Loading



Rather than wait years to find someone willing to operate for the “low rates” provided by Department of Veterans’ Affairs claims, and having heard nothing back from the department after putting in her claim, Lambie paid $7000 out of her own pocket to pay for surgery to treat the injury. She begged the government to abandon planned caps on allied health services for veterans: “What would they do if their penis was hanging by a thread? … Would they say ‘OK no worries, I don’t really need my penis?’ I don’t think so.” Birth Trauma Australia chief executive Amy Dawes says she sees women who are suicidal as a result of POP. “They are forever changed, they are shamed ... It’s still too often I hear women say, ‘Nobody told me that this could happen to my body’.” What causes POP? While vaginal childbirth is the main cause of POP, it can also be caused by repetitive heavy lifting, as Lambie experienced, being an elite athlete, having a chronic cough, asthma, obesity or chronic constipation.



“Women from all walks of life experience the condition,” says Dawes. Some people experience prolapse immediately after giving birth, but more often it develops over time. In one large US study, doctors performing routine pap smears could see that the vaginal wall had weakened and moved in about half of the women, yet few had symptoms. “It is very common that women going through menopause will start to experience incontinence and wonder what on earth’s going on,” says Margaret Wilson, a nurse continence specialist at Continence Health Australia, a not-for-profit operating a free helpline. “But incontinence associated with birth injuries sometimes doesn’t show up until the hormones start changing. There is less collagen and elastin, so that’s when prolapse or incontinence symptoms start to show.” Vaginal childbirth is the main cause of pelvic organ prolapse, but not the only one. Getty Images



Impacts that go beyond the injury According to a new report by Birth Trauma Australia, the impact of birth injuries, including POP, is costing the economy $17.5 billion annually, which includes health system, workforce, wellbeing and health costs. There are also consequences on a woman’s self-confidence, body image, and sexuality, says Rosamilia: “It has a profound effect.” For two years after her diagnosis, Vogt grieved the person she once was. “Everything that I knew about myself was changed,” reflects Vogt, now a mother of two.



That included her ability to move – “I haven’t run since the birth of my son” – and work. A teacher, she had to get her classes moved, to be close to a toilet. One in three Australian women experiences incontinence, and in about 60 per cent of those instances it is because of prolapse. “It’s a huge issue across the country, and we’re not talking about it,” says Continence Health Australia chief executive Jim Cooper. Treating and preventing prolapse “If women adequately do their pelvic floors [exercises] in pregnancy, you get a 30 per cent reduction in risk of like a longer-term urinary incontinence,” says Angela James, national chair of the Australian Physiotherapy Australia’s Women’s and Men’s Pelvic Health Group. But, James adds: “It’s not just a random bunch of Kegels.” It’s about learning which muscles to engage and how to engage them safely. That applies to all women, pregnant or not.





The research of Monash University’s associate professor Shayanti Mukherjee is focused on transforming how pelvic-floor injury and prolapse are prevented and treated. That includes hydrogels to prevent or heal prolapse, biodegradable and tissue-engineered implants in place of mesh, stem-cell therapy and earlier detection models. Vogt, who feels like she is finally emerging from the trauma, wishes there were more options, more support and more conversation. “A lot of my friends, when they had kids, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, prolapse’, were like, ‘What’s that?’. It’s important that I feel the message is out there, that prolapse can happen to anyone.” Well, half the population. When Rosamilia is asked if she believes prolapse would have been solved by now if it affected the other half of the population, she laughs.



“I think there’d be a lot more money thrown at it, that’s for sure.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: The NRL needs 60 players for two more teams. So where have all the rookies gone?
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 The NRL needs 60 players for two more teams. So where have all the rookies gone? Christian Nicolussi August 27, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rugby league will need to produce at least another 60 NRL-standard players to fill the rosters of the Perth Bears and PNG Chiefs in the next two seasons. But a brief look at the rookie of the year contenders would be enough to have fans wondering if there is enough young talent coming through to sustain a healthy, expanded NRL. Rookie of the year contenders (left to right) Cooper Bai, Cooper Clarke, Ethan Sanders and Oliver Pascoe. Artwork: Matt Willis That is not to question the quality at the top of this year’s rookie class, but the depth is a real concern. Who is in the mix to be crowned the best first-year player at the Dally M awards next month?



Cooper Clarke has been excellent for the Melbourne Storm in 2026, particularly given the 20-year-old had never played in the back row, nor against men, until this year. He has made the leap from SG Ball (under-19s) and Jersey Flegg (under-21s) in 2025 straight to the NRL, and played 22 games along the way. Ethan Sanders also deserves to take a bow after stepping into big shoes in the all-important halfback position at the Canberra Raiders, often behind a pack that had middle forwards out injured or forced to play wider. Cooper Clarke has had an outstanding rookie season for the Storm. Getty Images But who else is in the hunt? Maybe Gold Coast pair Cooper Bai and Oliver Pascoe? Possibly Newcastle’s Francis Manuleleua or Wests Tigers outside back Heamasi Makasini? There was a lot of hype when Manly’s Joey Walsh came into the top grade, but he has struggled for consistency, largely due to injuries.



They’re all fine players, but when you consider future Immortal Nathan Cleary played 15 matches in 2016 and was beaten to the rookie title, that shows how difficult the award has been to win historically. For the record, Gold Coast’s Ashley Taylor took home the award in 2016, while Latrell Mitchell and Suliasi Vunuvalu were the other finalists. Last year’s rookie winner was Sydney Roosters star Rob Toia, who beat Parramatta’s Isaiah Iongi and New Zealand Warriors cult hero Leka Halasima. The NRL changed the criteria so Toia’s teammate Mark Nawaqanitawase could not win because he had already represented Australia at a Rugby World Cup and the Paris Olympics. Ethan Sanders (right) is another in the mix for the rookie of the year award. Getty Images In 2024, Jack Bostock beat Cronulla’s KL Iro and Raiders playmaker Ethan Strange. Lachie Galvin was ineligible due to suspension. Bostock and Strange were part of the victorious NSW Origin squad this year, while Galvin spent time in Blues camp. Sunia Turuva took home the gong in 2023, beating future Wests Tigers teammate Jahream Bula and Melbourne flyer Will Warbrick.



Several NRL club officials, talking on the condition of anonymity to speak freely, said the lack of depth in this year’s rookie race was certainly a worry given the looming arrivals of the Bears and Chiefs, then potentially a 20th team from New Zealand or Queensland in 2029, and possibly more after that. Joey Walsh has been solid without being sensational for Manly. NRL Photos One coach suggested increasing the number of players who were allowed to train with NRL squads on a full-time basis so they know what to expect when they are called into the top grade. Another official suggested scrapping the Jersey Flegg competition, which would allow kids graduating from the under-19s SG Ball competition to go straight into playing against men. A third official even questioned if the standard of the NSW Cup had dipped and was still an adequate way to prepare the next generation.



Several club bosses have recently spoken about directing a large portion of the money from the game’s new $5.4 billion broadcast deal to development to address concerns about the depth of talent. Clarke said many of his mates had been lost to the game when it resumed after the COVID-enforced cancellation of the 2020 junior representative season and the abandonment of the 2021 campaign, even though the enforced lay-off helped him rediscover his love for league. The 20-year-old grew up in Campbelltown, played Harold Matthews with the Western Suburbs Magpies and was then poached by the Storm, where he will remain until the end of 2029. The one-time middle forward, who ballooned to 150kg during the pandemic, has certainly been one of the feel-good stories for Melbourne, who will miss the finals for the first time since 2010, when they were stripped of their competition points because of salary cap breaches.



“Coming into this season, all I wanted to do was play NSW Cup, not Jersey Flegg,” Clarke said. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Joker and the thief: Did the Roosters just rob themselves of a grand final run? Andrew Johns League columnist “‘Belza’ [coach Craig Bellamy] asked me before Christmas if I’d give the back row a shot. I’d never played there before – I’d never actually played against men – but told him I’d do whatever he needed me to do. “I was lucky to have [injured teammate Eli Katoa] there to teach me how to play back row. He made me look at the game differently, and to have that mindset of I’m going to go at you all game, and I won’t let you stop me when it came to your opposite. “To win rookie of the year would be a massive honour and a great achievement, even a confidence boost, but like everyone says, I really am all about the team.” Rookies cannot have played more than five NRL games in a previous season to be eligible. Sanders played two games for the Raiders in 2024 and again in 2025.

World.title: At Dollywood, I discovered the real reason she is America’s sweetheart
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVale At Dollywood, I discovered the real reason she is America’s sweetheart Michael Koziol August 27, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dollywood, Tennessee: When Sabrina Taylor’s property burnt down in the devastating 2016 wildfires that ripped through Tennessee’s Smoky Mountains, Dolly Parton came to the rescue. Not only did the country music icon contribute to a program that dispensed $US5000 ($6900) a month to fire victims who lost their homes, but Parton also helped find Taylor somewhere to live in the interim. Dolly Parton superfans Cody Dobbs, Jonathan Brashier, Aaron Hamby and Sabrina Taylor at Dollywood after the country music legend’s death. Michael Koziol “I got to stay in her best friend Judy Ogle’s home here,” Taylor says in her southern drawl. “She relocated myself and two other people that I know, let me stay there until I found other lodgings. That was a very private memory … People wouldn’t really know that she would do stuff like that.” Taylor spent Wednesday (US time) at Dollywood, the Dolly Parton theme park near her childhood home in east Tennessee. She was with three other Dolly superfans: Cody Dobbs, Jonathan Brashier and Aaron Hamby, all of whom found community here.



Singer Sunny Holiday poses for a photo near a mural of Dolly Parton in Nashville. AP Photo/George Walker IV What they all agreed was that Parton, who died this week at the age of 80, was much more than a musician. In her death, their overriding memory was about her generosity – of spirit and of dollar. A woman who could have been a billionaire but ultimately gave away an estimated $US600 million to all manner of charitable causes. The group has friends from all over the world through the Dollywood fan club, including Australia. Brashier, who is from South Carolina, says they have never missed a year. He has met her many times. Dolly Parton at Dollywood in 1993. Getty Images “Yesterday, when I was at home, sitting in my den grieving after this news broke, I found the very first picture I had with her,” Brashier says. “It was at the bottom of the steps of her apartment at the time. I was just this little skinhead, snaggle-tooth kid. I think I was 11.



“I’ll tell you this – the very next year, she remembered me. A very beautiful fan friendship just blossomed from then over the years. There is nothing like having a moment with her.” Related Article Vale Dolly Parton recorded more than 1000 songs – we’ve picked her top 10 It’s at that point that Brashier’s voice starts to break as he fights back tears. It is slightly jarring to see an adult man vulnerable in this way, and yet it is difficult not to share his emotion. “There is something magical about her that you have to experience, that you can’t really explain,” he says. “She makes you feel like you’re the only person in the room when she’s talking to you. “That is something that I never outgrew in my life, even when I was with her just a couple of years ago. I still get nervous; I still get the butterflies. But she didn’t know she made you nervous. It’s just something that happened. And it’s something that I will hang on to for the rest of my life.”



The four friends were among many Americans who felt compelled to travel to Dollywood on Wednesday to pay their respects to the undisputed queen of country music. Overall, it was a modest day for foot traffic. Tennessee schools have returned from summer break, and Dollywood is decidedly a family affair. But they are gearing up for a massive weekend ahead. Flowers and tributes left for Dolly Parton on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in Los Angeles. AP Photo/Jae Hong The sheer size of Dollywood is a testament to her cultural power. First opened in 1986, it occupies 462 hectares of land within the Smoky Mountains range, with only 73 hectares of that developed so far. “We have lots of room to grow,” says Dollywood president Eugene Naughton. “This is the second love of her life. She loved the mountains. She loved this place.”



‘We are all heartbroken’ Parton’s passing weighed heavily on the staff, though they were determined to stay open, as was apparently her wish. Naughton called her their “dreamer-in-chief”. Another staffer told me: “We are all heartbroken.” Dollywood contains a replica of her childhood home, which is located just a few kilometres away in Locust Ridge, just outside Sevierville. A modest, one-bedroom log cabin, it is the cornerstone of her well-known rags-to-riches story. Floral tributes pile up at the base of the statue of Dolly Parton in Sevierville, Tennessee. AP Photo/Camden Hall In many ways, that makes her a quintessential American icon: someone who harnessed talent and persistence to make it big and strike it rich. And yet, that is not Dolly Parton’s legacy at all. Almost everyone I spoke to over the past 24 hours in Tennessee mentioned her selflessness, grace and charity as her defining features.



Central Sevierville, in the foothills of the Smoky Mountains, is home to a Dolly Parton statue. It stands proudly just outside the local courthouse, in the middle of a town that is utterly devoted to its most famous daughter. Related Article Vale ‘She’s a mythological figure’: America mourns the one person everybody loved Just before dusk on Wednesday, about 80 people at any one time stood around the statue, laying flowers, taking photographs, paying their respects. It was not a solemn occasion; she had led a good, long life, and that was understood. Some people brought along old Dolly records. One child, Charlie, laid down a handmade painting of a cowgirl’s boot with flowers springing from it. Like many children here, she grew up reading books from Parton’s Imagination Library. Her favourite song is Coat of Many Colours. “I know every word,” she says. “We’re huge fans of Dolly,” says Charlie’s mum, Tori King. “She’s just always been so generous and so kind. The first time I heard her songs was on my grandmother’s cassette [player] – she’s just always been a big part of our lives.”

Philanthropy Michael Koziol is the North America correspondent for The Age and Sydney Morning Herald. He is a former Sydney editor, Sun-Herald deputy editor and a federal political reporter in Canberra. or email. Connect via X

World.title: How a woman gave birth to ‘sufficiently atypical’ unrelated twins
World.content:
NationalQueenslandFertility How a woman gave birth to ‘sufficiently atypical’ unrelated twins Dominique Tassell August 27, 2026 — 3:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two families have had to ask the court to separate biologically unrelated twins born on the Gold Coast, in what a judge referred to as “sufficiently atypical” circumstances. A woman, known as DZ in court documents, agreed to be a surrogate for a couple, known as BNJ and DRJ, in September 2024. A woman has given birth to unrelated twins in Queensland. iStock This agreement stipulated that any child born through the arrangement was to be treated as the child of BNJ and DRJ and not of the surrogate and her spouse, known as FZ. BNJ, then 25, is a childcare educator and DRJ, then 28, is a cabinetmaker. The surrogate and her partner, both then 27, have five other children including a child born in 2024.



A single embryo transfer occurred on April 11, 2025, and the surrogate produced a positive pregnancy test on April 15, 2025. Related Article Pregnancy ‘One in 15 million’: Mum gives birth to identical quadruplets in likely Australian first But an ultrasound two weeks later found the surrogate was carrying two children. Further tests discovered one child, a boy, was the result of the embryo transfer and the second child, a girl, was the biological child of the surrogate and her spouse. The children grew as gestational twins and she gave birth to both by caesarean section in November 2025. Under the Surrogacy Act, and as a result of the agreement entered into by both couples, the baby girl was considered BNJ and DRJ’s child and they were named her parents on her birth certificate.



The couples were always in agreement the boy was BNJ and DRJ’s child, and the girl was the surrogate and her partner’s child. The baby girl left hospital with the latter couple, and her name was chosen by them. However, the surrogate and her partner had to seek a parentage order for custody of their daughter, which BNJ and DRJ did not oppose. An independent counsellor found separating the children was not likely to cause psychological harm. “On the balance of probabilities and assuming both infants are raised in stable and nurturing family systems, the available research does not support the conclusion separation of the twins from birth is, in itself, likely to cause psychological harm attributable to separation alone,” she said. “The evidence more strongly supports the view developmental outcomes will be shaped by the quality of caregiving, family functioning, openness about origins, and the thoughtful management of relationships over time.”



The families connected through mutual friends and social media, and told the court they intend to raise the children knowing each other. Judge Jodie Wooldridge found making the order was in the best interest of the baby girl. While the act precludes separating birth siblings, Wooldridge concluded that under the unique circumstances they were not considered birth siblings and could be separated. World.title: From Dr Frank-N-Furter to Long John Silver, these are Tim Curry’s nine most memorable roles
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale From Dr Frank-N-Furter to Long John Silver, these are Tim Curry’s nine most memorable roles Nell Geraets August 27, 2026 — 3:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Tim Curry first pulled on his fishnets and uttered the word “antici … pation” through bold cherry-red lips, cult cinema was forever transformed. The British actor, who died at the age of 80 on Wednesday, brought a whole new meaning to camp and eccentricity as Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show film. But the lingerie-clad Transylvanian doctor was only one of many faces Curry wore. Throughout his decades-long career, the actor took on scheming 1930s villains, nosy hotel concierges and murderous clowns. He dabbled in voice work, and even won awards for his time on stage. Here are nine of Curry’s most memorable roles. With his resonant voice and devilish smile, Tim Curry was an unstoppable force on both stage and screen. AP Photo/Peter Kramer The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) Curry didn’t just stroll onto the film scene; he burst onto it in sky-high platform heels and a sparkly black corset. His debut film performance as the “sweet transvestite” Dr Frank-N-Furter is arguably his least forgettable role, still enticing massive audiences at dress-up midnight screenings around the world.



Tim Curry famously commanded attention as the mad scientist Dr Frank N. Furter in cult classic oddball musical The Rocky Horror Picture Show. 20th Century Based on The Rocky Horror Show stage musical, the film adaptation follows lost, virginal couple Brad and Janet as they become tangled in a kinky, feverish “mind flip” run by inhabitants of the planet Transsexual. As Frank-N-Furter, Curry plays host – one who constantly wants to get into the couple’s pants – and mad scientist, who attempts to bring the “perfect plaything” to life. “I can’t imagine a better role to enable me to embrace my contradictions and see them through,” Curry wrote of the role in his 2025 memoir Vagabond. “I learned not to limit myself – artistically, professionally, sexually or mentally.” Annie (1982) Curry cemented his turn as the villain in Annie, the film adaptation of the classic stage musical. Playing “Rooster” Hannigan, a slimy con who pairs up with his girlfriend to pose as an orphan’s parents to filch a massive cash reward, the actor takes on a slick New York brogue, and an even slicker hair-do.



Once again, he pulls out the tunes, singing Easy Street alongside Carol Burnett and Bernadette Peters. Here he proved his dance moves were just as strong as his vocal cords, tapping his way upstairs and swinging Peters around as if she weighed nothing. It’s a role that arguably positioned him well for future comedic-skewing (and more age-appropriate) villains. Clue (1985) Never trust the butler. Curry proved a worthy suspect as the butler Wadsworth in Clue, a film version of the murder mystery board game. Six strangers are invited to a New England mansion, only to end up embroiled in a whodunit spectacle after their host Mr Boddy inexplicably shows up dead. As the butler, Curry aced a particularly physical comedic performance, with many of his exaggerated facial expressions stealing the show. It confirmed his face was truly like putty that he could contort to his heart’s desire.



Tim Curry taught us to never trust the butler in the 1986 film Clue. Legend (1985) Despite being directed by Ridley Scott and starring Tom Cruise, Curry is by far the best thing about this fantasy-adventure film. He plays the Lord of Darkness, a demon of the night who wishes to kidnap a princess and extinguish the world’s light. It’s up to Jack (played by Cruise) to stop him. Despite having to sit in the make-up and prosthetics chair for over five hours each day – his entire body and face were red and exaggerated – Curry still clearly relished the role, delivering a cool, calm evil and a laugh as devilish as Satan himself.



It (1990) Andy Muschietti’s film adaptations of Stephen King’s seminal horror novel It may have stolen attention recently, especially with the release of the prequel television series earlier last year, but it was Curry who truly defined Pennywise the Clown. In his memoir, Curry said his turn as the evil alien clown who terrorises the children of Derry certainly wasn’t his favourite role. In fact, the actor never liked clowns. However, he noted that he still held great respect for King as an author and felt the two-part miniseries was a “strong” adaptation. Were the visual effects groundbreaking? Not by a long shot. But Curry’s Pennywise was so twisted, combining sick humour with genuine malevolence in every scene. Introduce razor-sharp teeth and a piercing, vacant stare, and you have yourself one of the scariest screen villains of the 20th century. It’s thanks to Tim Curry’s Pennywise that most adults today are afraid of clowns.



Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992) These days, most people remember Home Alone 2 as the film in which US President Donald Trump randomly cameos, but Curry should really be the standout. As the nosy, snobbish hotel concierge, he attempts to catch Kevin McCallister (Macaulay Culkin) in his lies and boot him from the Plaza Hotel. His efforts are in vain, of course, for he’s up against the master of pranks and booby traps. Few can pull off an obnoxious false sense of authority quite like Curry. And his wicked Grinch-esque smile? Exquisite. FernGully: The Last Rainforest (1992)



As much as we may know Curry for his facial expressions, we also know him for his voice. That deep baritone won him many voice-over roles throughout his career, especially across family films, television shows and video games. Related Article Vale Actor Tim Curry, known for stage and screen villains, dies aged 80 It all began with FernGully, an animation that cast Curry as Hexxus, the spirit of destruction who wishes to destroy the last remaining rainforest. His tone, pitch and cadence combined to deliver an impeccably eerie, yet at times humorous, performance. It’s one that millennials around the world still cherish to this day. Muppet Treasure Island (1995) Earlier this year, Curry told The New York Times that Muppet Treasure Island was his favourite film. That is quite the statement for someone with as diverse a career as Curry’s, but it speaks to how much fun he had on-set with the felt puppets and pirate shenanigans.



In the movie, Curry plays Long John Silver, a sneaky pirate who leads a mutiny to try to steal the treasure on-board. In an interview with the Guardian, the actor said he improvised a line that was ultimately cut for being too racy for family audiences. The line referred to a plot point in which Long John Silver and Miss Piggy were said to have had a past affair. The line? “Once you’ve had pork, you never go back.” Monty Python’s Spamalot (2004) Curry was perhaps most critically renowned for his time on stage. The British actor won a Tony for his role as King Arthur in the musical Monty Python’s Spamalot. He played this character for three years straight across various cities in the US, and also in London. Tim Curry, centre, appeared in the Broadway production of Spamalot. AP Photo/Tina Fineberg Before Spamalot, Curry won two other Tonys – one for his turn as Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart in Amadeus (1981), and another for his performance as washed-up alcoholic Alan Swann in the 1993 musical My Favourite Year. His resonant voice paired with his larger-than-life mannerisms and fierce energy made for an unstoppable theatrical force.
