World.title: Live: Hamilton couple identified as two of the five New Zealanders missing following Nepal flash flood
World.content:
At least five New Zealanders have been reported missing following a flash flood and landslide hit the Nepal-China border that killed at least 162 people.

162 dead, hundreds missing including tourists

The NZ High Commission is seeking information about Kiwis affected

New Zealanders in Nepal should follow the advice of local authorities.

Let friends and family know they are safe when able to do so.

New Zealanders requiring urgent consular assistance can call the 2/4 emergency line on +64 99 20 20 20

Former Honorary Consul of Nepal to Auckland Dinesh Khadka told RNZ Nepal Police had given him the names of five New Zealanders unaccounted for.

Follow updates in our live blog below:

Are you or is someone you know affected? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon described the images coming out of Nepal and China as "heartbreaking" and said New Zealand is in touch with Nepal authorities about New Zealanders who may be affected.

"My deep condolences to those affected and to impacted communities," he wrote in a post on X.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters echoed his sentiments, saying New Zealand is "deeply concerned".

Rescuers carry in their arms a flood survivor, following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Nepal. PRAKASH MATHEMA

Aid workers said entire settlements had been "wiped out". Surveillance footage verified by AFP shows dozens of people running for their lives as a stories-tall surge of debris slammed into the Chinese side of a border area, tossing lorries and buses aside.

A resident walks along a street covered in mud following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Devighat. PRAKASH MATHEMA

Chinese state media reported "major casualties" from a mudslide at a Tibet border hub, reporting three dead and another 265 people missing.

Nepali police said that they had recovered 157 bodies after "devastating floods", with officers "working to move families in flood-risk areas... to safer locations."

In a post on social media, humanitarian organisation the Himalayan Trust said they were "deeply saddened" by news of the flood.

"The flood originated by the Tibetan border impacting the Bhote Koshi valley. This is in the Langtang region halfway between Mt Everest and Mt Annapurna.

"The scale of the loss is heartbreaking," they wrote.

World.title: Two dead in serious incident in South Auckland
World.content:
Police are responding to an unfolding serious incident in South Auckland, which left at least two people dead.

"At about 1.45pm, emergency services responded to reports of a woman unresponsive at an address on Gambare Place," police wrote on Facebook.

"Sadly, she was pronounced dead at the scene.

"During a search of the property police have located a man who was also pronounced deceased."

Police hold up a sheet near the intersection of Gambare Place. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Cordons are in place on Mahia Road in Wattle Downs with residents not able to enter.

Members of the public are advised to avoid the area.

Police at the scene of an incident on Gambare Place, Manurewa. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The incident prompted two schools, Te Haikura a Kiwa and Leabank Primary School, to go into lockdown. Both have since come out of lockdown.

Te Haikura a Kiwa confirmed its response to the incident on Thursday afternoon.

"Please do not come to the school or phone the school as you will not be attended to and this may cause disruption to the management of this incident and could potentially place yourselves and/or our staff and student's safety at risk," the school wrote on social media and its website at the time.

Police at the scene of an incident on Gambare Place, Manurewa. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Leabank Primary School, which is located across the road, also went into lockdown in response to the incident.

"We have come out of lockdown and all students, staff, and persons on-site are safely accounted for. Everyone did extremely well and responded to instructions," Leabank Principal Caroline McLeod posted on social media after the lockdown had ended.

World.title: People miss out on benefit payments after second MSD error
World.content:
A rushed law change last year saw a number of people's benefit payments wrongly suspended because ministry officials could not keep up with the paperwork.

It's the second major error identified due to the law passed under urgency last year.

The new law requires some beneficiaries to re-confirm their circumstances at least once every 52 weeks, to check whether they are still eligible.

That saw thousands of pensioners missing out on their Winter Energy Payment this year, which the Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Social Development Minister Louise Upston apologised for last week.

The Winter Energy Payment should have been excluded from the legislation.

The Ministry of Social Development has now confirmed to RNZ another separate problem: due to the high volume of people confirming their circumstances, some of them missed out on their benefit payments.

"Some responses were not fully processed before their expiry date, and some payments were suspended despite people providing the information we requested," said service delivery group general manager Shannon Soughtton.

"We apologise to those affected and recognise the impact this may have had."

MSD could not confirm how many people were affected or how long payments were suspended for, because that information was held in individual client files.

All payments had resumed and been backdated, Soughtton said.

"Processing volumes are now back at expected operating levels, and we are keeping pace with incoming demand."

World.title: Xero shareholders reject executive pay report
World.content:
Xero's shareholders have delivered a stinging rebuke to its board, with more than 70 percent voting against the remuneration report at its annual shareholder meeting.

The remuneration report is the section of a company's annual report explaining how its directors and senior executives were paid, and why, including salaries, bonuses and share-based incentives.

It follows controversy over a revised remuneration structure for chief executive Sukhinder Singh Cassidy, lifting her target total remuneration from US$15.2 million to US$18.5 million.

Xero's share price has roughly halved over the past year, despite a strong operational performance, while Singh Cassidy recently sold the remainder of her direct shareholding, worth about US$1.9 million, which the company said was to meet personal tax obligations.

Xero said she continued to hold about 586,000 restricted stock units already granted under time-based and performance-based schemes.

The resolution itself is only advisory and non-binding and will not stop Singh Cassidy's revised pay structure coming into effect.

Xero said the major proxy advisers had recommended shareholders vote against the remuneration report.

It said concerns included incentive payments not being reduced to reflect the shareholder experience, too much of the chief executive's equity being tied to continued length of service, rather than performance, and Singh Cassidy's recent share sale.

Xero People and Remuneration Committee chair Susan Peterson said poor share price performance had "materially influenced" the vote outcome, and the board respected and understood "the strength of this feedback".

Xero said the voting outcome and comments from proxy advisers and investors would be considered when setting future remuneration strategy.

Peterson told shareholders the board understood frustration over the company's share price performance, but said Xero needed to pay competitively to attract and retain global technology executives.

She said the board would introduce a minimum shareholding requirement for the chief executive, requiring a stake worth five times annual base salary within three years.

World.title: New Zealanders missing after flash flood in Nepal identified
World.content:
The identities of the New Zealanders missing in Nepal following a flash flood are coming to light, with families awaiting information on their whereabouts.

At least five New Zealanders have been reported missing following the flash flood and landslide that hit the Nepal-China border and killed at least 160 people.

One of the New Zealand citizens missing is Suhasini Reddy, who has been living in Australia for the last four years.

Reddy's brother, Rajeev Reddy, told RNZ his sister, a mother-of-two, was believed to be in the Dhunche area heading towards the Nepal-China border on Wednesday morning local time.

Reddy was hiking with a group of friends from Australia with the Kailash Journeys Guides, her brother said. The floods occurred on day four of the 15-day trip.

Reddy said his sister was supposed to be meeting Chinese immigration about 11am local time. They had not heard anything from her since the flash flood.

"We really don't know. We've contacted the hotel, the person of contact says she's not there, and at the moment he can't provide any information regarding the checkouts and check-ins."

At least 160 people are dead following the flash flood and landslide. Supplied

He last spoke to his sister the night before the floods, while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was all good, excited," he said.

"She had this trip planned for a while."

Before heading on the trip Suhasini Reddy visited her parents in India where she left her youngest son. Her other son is with family in Australia.

Rajeev Reddy said the family were desperate for information.

"We actually don't know what's happening ... we're just saying that she'll be okay," he said.

The family appealed for anyone with information about her whereabouts to contact them.

Hamilton couple was celebrating 50th birthday in Nepal

Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel, who own the Best Value Urlich Ave Dairy in Hamilton, are among the New Zealanders missing. Supplied

The son of a Hamilton couple missing following the Nepal flash flood is holding onto hope his parents left the area in the hours before the landslide struck.

Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel, who own the Best Value Urlich Ave Dairy in Hamilton, were also among the missing New Zealanders.

Their eldest son, Drishya Patel, told RNZ the couple were visiting Nepal to celebrate his mother's upcoming 50th birthday. The couple had been gone for about a week, he said.

"They're just on a trip to go visit some of the mountains in Nepal. It's like a pilgrimage of sorts."

Drishya Patel spoke to his father the day before the flash flood. He said the couple's trip was going "really good".

"They were having a good time."

He last got a message from his mother on WhatsApp about 5.30am local time from Timure.

"Leaving for Kerung," the message said.

The earthquake that triggered the floods occurred at 8.37am local time.

Drishya Patel said he was "shocked" when he first heard the news of the landslide. The family has heard nothing from the couple since.

He hoped that the couple left when they sent the message, about three hours beforehand.

"As long as like they actually did leave when my mum sent me that message, I'm hopeful. These guys tend to run things on time, these tour guides," he said.

"But again, haven't heard anything confirming."

He had spoken with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT), but he said "they don't know anything either".

Drishya Patel, who is a medical student, had an exam on Thursday. He said he was still coming to terms with everything.

"I don't think I've processed it… realisations slowly setting in as every hour passes, and I don't hear anything, and no one knows anything."

Another missing Kiwi was on pilgrimage

Another New Zealander, Dejan Kuzmic was travelling on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, when the disaster struck.

Nepal's Tourist Police confirmed Kuzmic's name to RNZ on Thursday morning.

He was part of the Isha Foundation's Sacred Walks pilgrimage group, which was travelling towards Mount Kailash, revered by Hindus as the abode of Lord Shiva.

RNZ has also spoken to a family friend, who confirmed the family had been unable to contact Kuzmic since the floods.

"He was part of the Isha Foundation's walk group S3 and was at the border crossing, which was hit quite heavily within a reasonable time, which makes us believe he may have been involved," said Seyed Sepehr Hosseini, whose mother attends a meditation group with Kuzmic.

Hosseini contacted the Isha Foundation, which told him Kuzmic's emergency contacts had been notified.

He also contacted New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which said it had opened a consular case for Kuzmic.

Mount Kailash is revered by Hindus as the abode of Lord Shiva, while nearby Lake Mansarovar is also considered sacred.

India's official Kailash Mansarovar Yatra portal describes the pilgrimage as having deep religious and cultural significance.

World.title: Heavy snow closes highways, triggers severe avalanche warnings in South Island
World.content:
Heavy snow closed roads and triggered severe avalanche warnings in parts of the South Island on Thursday.

More than 20 centimetres of snow fell in some places closing state highways.

State Highway 73 was closed but reopened on Thursday afternoon, however State Highway 94 to Milford Sound remains closed due to snow and avalanche risk.

Large avalanches were expected to run to the valley floor in parts of the South Island as heavy snow prompted multiple alerts for very dangerous conditions.

Heavy snow at Arthur's Pass. Sean Moran

People were urged to stay out of the backcountry until the stormy weather had passed and snowpack conditions settled.

The Avalanche Advisory Council had its second highest danger warning in place for Arthur's Pass, Aoraki Mount Cook, Ohau, Queenstown, Wanaka, Fiordland and Aspiring.

A considerable avalanche risk was also in place for Craigieburn Range, Mount Hutt, Two Thumbs and Nelson Lakes.

The council's advisory said Aoraki Mount Cook had already received plenty of snow and rain with more snow predicted later on Thursday.

More than 3.5 metres could have fallen on the Tasman Saddle over recent days, the advisory said.

The advisory said the risk at Arthur's Pass meant large avalanches were expected to reach the valley floor and people should keep out of runzones which included tramping terrain.

State Highway 73 which was closed earlier in the day but has now reopened. NZTA / Waka Kotahi

In Queenstown, the advisory said local ski fields had reported multiple natural and ski triggered loose wet avalanches.

Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said the return to blue skies could be deceptive and there would be a lot of instability in the snowpack.

"Currently across the whole southern alpine region, it's what we describe as quite treacherous conditions and people that are thinking about exploring the backcountry, be that hunters, trampers, skiers, snowboarders ... we highly don't recommend any travel in that backcountry at the moment," he said.

It was not just high alpine areas that were at risk.

The size and scale of the potential avalanches could run all the way down to the valley floor in some areas, crossing paths and tracks that were not in alpine terrain, he said.

A worker at Aoraki Mount Cook's Hermitage Hotel said he had heard avalanches rumbling on the mountains as snow battered the area.

Hotel activities manager Tim Thorstensen said Mount Cook Village had had a huge dumping of snow.

More than 20cm of snow fell in parts of State Highway 73. NZTA / Waka Kotahi

Snow forecast to make way for heavy rain on Friday

MetService said more than 300mm of rain had been recorded around Franz Josef by 2pm on Thursday with more expected to fall.

Orange heavy rain warnings remain in place for Westland and the headwaters of lakes and rivers in Otago and Canterbury south of Arthur's Pass.

A slip on the road between Blackball and Atarau. Grey District Council

A heavy rain warning was due to start from midnight for the ranges in the Grey and Buller districts.

Canterbury's regional council said out-of-river flooding was unlikely despite heavy rain and snow falling on headwaters of major alpine rivers.

Moderately high flows have been reported for the Rangitata, Rakaia, Waimakariri, Hurunui, and Waiau-uha rivers.

Environment Canterbury said the rivers were expected to rise further on Thursday night and Friday morning and remain high through Friday with snowfall forecast to become rain on Thursday afternoon.

The council says the Ashley, Selwyn, Ashburton, Orari and Opihi rivers are all flowing slightly higher.

MetService meteorologist Devlin Lynden said the storm was expected to weaken as it moved across the country and the worst of the snow had passed, but areas of heavy rain would persist into Friday.

World.title: Person injured after car crashes into Palmerston North house
World.content:
A person has been taken to hospital after a car crashed into a home in Palmerston North on Thursday.

Emergency services were called to the house on Amberley Avenue - in the suburb of Highbury - at about 11.50am.

A police officer at the scene of the crash. Supplied

A police spokesperson said the vehicle has travelled through a perimeter wall and into the building.

The owner of the home said the vehicle ended up in the house's garage and they were grateful no one was home at the time.

They said the crash had come as "a very big shock" and they were facing a big cleanup.

Supplied

The owner said security cameras showed a man running away from the scene and police had told them he had been taken into custody following the crash.

"All we know from the police is that a car came around the corner smashed straight through the fence and into our garage and a man was taken into custody," they said.

Supplied

Locals took to social media to show a black SUV almost completely inside the brick building - with bricks strewn about the property and onto the roof of the home.

A police spokesperson said officers saw the car driving "erratically" on Amberley Avenue just before midday.

"Police initiated a pursuit briefly before abandoning due to the manner of driving.

"Police then received report of a car hitting a brick fence which had gone into a house on Strachan Way. The driver fled the scene and were located by police as they ran away from officers. They were injured, and police took them to hospital," the spokesperson said.

They said later enquiries showed the car had been stolen the previous day.

The car had since been removed from the house and police were continuing to investigate the matter.

Police said one person had received minor injuries and no arrests had been made at this stage.

The incident comes just days after a police officer was left in critical condition after being hit by a fleeing driver in Palmerston North.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said a driver had been signalled to stop about 2am on Amberley Avenue but allegedly fled.

"Minutes later, the vehicle, which was not being pursued, hit a police officer laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road. The officer suffered critical injuries and was airlifted to Wellington Hospital, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries."

World.title: NZ Post returns to profit as mail volumes fall
World.content:
NZ Post has returned to profit, but mail volumes are down.

The state-owned enterprise has recorded a $17 million net profit for the year.

The result followed a $2m loss last year and came after a major multi-year transformation project, which included changes to its mail network as well as mail and parcel processing systems.

Total revenue was up $44m to $1.267 billion.

However, total parcels delivered were down by about 3 million to 85 million, while letters delivered fell to 134 million from 158 million the year before.

NZ Post chair Dame Paula Rebstock said it was a very pleasing result and an important milestone in the business transformation.

"Through the disciplined execution of our strategy, NZ Post continues to strengthen its commercial position while delivering value for our customers," Dame Paula said.

She said the board was encouraged by the progress achieved during the year and remained focused on supporting sustainable performance, disciplined investment and long-term value creation.

The state-owned company declared a dividend of $12.5m.

Simeon Brown RNZ / Baz Macdonald

State Owned Enterprises Minister Simeon Brown said NZ Post's return to profitability after several years of losses was encouraging, but a sustained commitment to continued improvement was required.

"This improved financial performance is welcome and reflects NZ Post's focus on cost management and better operational efficiency," Brown said.

However, Brown said the results also highlighted the need for parcel revenue to improve in a competitive market.

"Group revenue growth for the year was 3.6 percent and while the return on equity of 2.9 percent is an improvement over last year, it remains below the company's cost of capital.

"Looking ahead, it's important that NZ Post continues to optimise its operations to enhance overall profitability and performance, while delivering an efficient and sustainable service.

World.title: AFL hits Geelong with monster fine over concussion waiver scandal
World.content:
Geelong has been fined $140,000 for failing to officially let the AFL know about the concussion waiver in Jake Kolodjashnij's contract.

The penalty is $100,000 plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong in October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

The amount will be paid into the AFL and AFLPA Players' Injury and Support Fund.

The AFL brought in James Peters KC to investigate Geelong after the league issued a "please explain" when the revelation about Kolodjashnij's contract broke this month.

Mr Peters found Geelong's failure to lodge the variation was an oversight.

Kolodjashnij, the 2022 Cats premiership defender who has not played since the story broke, returned to training this week ahead of the finals.

Long careers increase risk of brain damage As debate rages over Geelong defender Jake Kolodjashnij's controversial concussion waiver, what is the answer for players being exposed to potential brain damage in contact sports?

Mr Peters investigated the inclusion of a waiver in Kolodjashnij's 2024 contract, which followed several concussions.

"The review found Geelong had given careful and detailed consideration to the risk of Mr Kolodjashnij continuing to play following an uncertain outcome from the AFL Concussion Panel, and consulted extensively with the AFL, club doctors, lawyers, insurers, and Mr Kolodjashnij and his family," the AFL said in a statement.

"It further found there was no inappropriate or improper conduct warranting additional action under AFL rules by either Geelong or AFL representatives and made no adverse findings in relation to the club's decision to enter into an agreement with the player to mitigate its legal exposure.

"It also found that Mr Kolodjashnij was not coerced into signing the letter."

The review found Geelong did not intend to conceal the existence of the agreement or deceive the AFL or AFLPA.

Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking previously defended the deal, saying there was "not a lot" the club would change in how it had dealt with the issue.

The Cats had reached a deal with Kolodjashnij in 2024, requiring him to take all legal responsibility for future brain trauma, so he could keep playing at the club.

On the weekend, current Geelong president Grant McCabe referred to it as a "voluntary assumption of risk" and said there was extensive consultation when the agreement was reached, including with AFL officials.

The revelation had put pressure on Hocking and current AFL chairman Craig Drummond, who was Geelong president when the waiver was signed.

"Consistent with previously disclosed arrangements, AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond, who was president of Geelong at the time the letter was executed, was not involved in the commission's consideration of the matter," the statement said.

The AFLPA responded to the decision, re-emphasising its opposition to the waiver in the first place.

"Jake's wellbeing remains a priority for the AFLPA and we continue to fully support him. Jake should never have been put in this position," AFLPA chief James Gallagher said in a statement.

"Head trauma is the biggest issue facing the game and the health and safety of our members must be the priority at all times.

"We believed the letter was inconsistent with [CBA and player contract] documents and was therefore in breach of AFL rules, which the AFLPA communicated to the AFL and Geelong."

AFL, AFLPA to strengthen concussion network

In the wake of the decision, the AFL announced that it would join with the AFLPA to review the safety nets in place for players, clubs and the wider football industry.

The review would consult with clubs, players and medical staff, and the agenda would include:

Looking at the challenges of commercial insurance protection for players and officials

Increasing the scope of the Injury & Support Fund to cover both current and former players

Establishing clearer protocols for AFL Concussion Panel outcomes

The risks and responsibilities of all involved in football and how those risks can be acknowledged

Increasing education across the football industry on head trauma research, trends and risks

Reviewing data collection practices relating to concussion

In a statement, AFL CEO Andrew Dillon said the Kolodjashnij case had highlighted the challenges for all in navigating legal and risk management issues over head trauma and concussion.

"There is inherent risk for all contact sports globally, and Australian Football is no different, but we want our sport to be a leader in brain health and concussion and head trauma prevention and management," he said.

"That's why we have a comprehensive framework, based on world class medical advice, which has dramatically improved concussion and head trauma prevention, management, and education from the elite level to community football."

AFLPA chief Gallagher said: "Through collective bargaining, the players have advocated for the development and continual growth of the safety net as well as other protections relating to head trauma, and this will be the next evolution of that."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Aussie James Duckworth through to Winston-Salem quarterfinals
World.content:
It was a case of third time lucky for James Duckworth as the Australian romped into the quarterfinals of the Winston-Salem Open with a stirring victory over Lorenzo Sonego.

The Italian has proved to be a bit of a nemesis on Tour for the Sydneysider, who had gone down twice in their previous meetings.

Sonego first triumphed over Duckworth in 2021 at Wimbledon when he won 6-3, 6-3, 6-4 in the third round.

Then came the defeat also on grass at Eastbourne International in the round of 32 in 2022 when Duckworth lost 4-6, 7-6 (5), 7-6 (1).

So the 7-5, 6-3 victory on Thursday (AEST) in the ATP-250 event would have been coupled with sweet revenge and a tinge of relief ahead of next week's US Open at Flushing Meadows.

With his world ranking of 79, Duckworth has qualified directly into the main draw for the last grand slam of the year.

The 34-year-old needed one hour and 44 minutes to dispatch Sonego, breaking serve twice in the match and fending off all three break point opportunities.

Duckworth will now meet 15th seed Fabian Marozsan of Hungary, who beat American wildcard Martin Damm 2-6, 6-3, 6-3, for a place in the semifinals.

Earlier, Rinky Hijikata's bid to make the last eight came to a crashing halt when the Australian was defeated by Benjamin Bonzi.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

It was a bullseye performance from the Frenchman, who didn't miss much in a 6-1, 6-1 demolition that lasted just 57 minutes.

Bonzi won 96 per cent of points on first serve and converted five of seven break point opportunities.

In other results, top British player and number four seed Arthur Fery made light work of qualifier Mees Rottgering to progress with a 6-3, 6-3 win.

But the tournament is over for number seven seed Stefanos Tsitsipas, who was beaten 6-3, 7-6 (1) by American Aleksander Kovacevic.

AAP

World.title: Tszyu and Mahoney camps exchange verbal barbs after controversial draw
World.content:
Matt Rose has defended the integrity of his company after No Limit Boxing pin-up Nikita Tszyu's controversial draw with Ben Mahoney, who claimed any rematch would not be happening on their card.

Wednesday's IBF super welterweight world-title eliminator was a terrific back-and-forth between two unbeaten Australians that left more questions than answers.

The bout finished in a split draw after three wildly different scorecards.

Nikita Tszyu's stunning admission, says Ben Mahoney 'edged' thrilling Gold Coast draw Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

Experienced judge Phillip Holliday, who beat Jeff Fenech in a distinguished career of his own, awarded the fight to Tszyu 117-111, effectively giving the bookies' favourite nine of the 12 rounds.

But fellow official Sabrina Kerr scored it for Mahoney, 115-113, and the third judge, Carl Zappia, scored the fight a 114-114 draw.

Jeers followed from the pro-Mahoney crowd, who backed their local hope as he defied heavy fire through the middle rounds to finish stronger and leave Tszyu's face battered.

In dramatic post-fight scenes, Tszyu conceded Mahoney had been the better boxer while No Limit boss George Rose took offence to comments from Mahoney's corner, declaring, "I wanna slap the s*** out of someone" before challenging anyone booing "to meet him out front and we'll sort it out".

Tszyu walked back his assessment in the press conference, explaining he was simply disappointed he had not been more clinical.

George Rose (pictured) was left fuming after the split-decision draw between Tszyu and Mahoney. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Tensions flared further when Mahoney's promoter Mick Francis later said he would seek an official review of Holliday's scoring.

Mahoney, who fought to a controversial draw on his last fight on a No Limit card, poured his heart out.

"We're going to have to look at our [rematch] options; I'm open to it but it sure as hell isn't going to be on another No Limit card," Mahoney, who had otherwise shown great respect to Tszyu and his team, said.

"I don't want to throw any officials or judges under the bus. But athletes put their lives on the line for this. I just had a baby and have been in the gym for eight weeks of 14 weeks of her life.

" You come in here, your opponent believes you won and you get a draw. It's a hard pill to swallow. "

Francis, a rival to No Limit who also boasts Jai Opetaia and Justis Huni in his stable, said they "hadn't heard the end of it".

"Phil Holliday, I don't know what he was watching … those scores were way wide and I'm going to make an official inquiry about it because that's not right," he said.

Rose did not front the press conference, leaving co-founder brother Matt and manager Glen Jennings to flank Tszyu.

He confirmed there had been a "couple of comments made in the ring" that triggered George and welcomed a review of the scoring in the belief it would favour his man.

"I'd be happy for them to challenge because I don't think the scorecard of 115-113 was right at all," Rose said.

Ben Mahoney (left) and Nikita Tszyu (right) were gracious towards each other after their split-decision draw. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"And that would mean Nikita wins the fight.

"But we'll accept the draw. At the end of the day, I'm not going to complain about the 115-113. That's the decision they made and that's how they saw it."

Rose, whose company holds exclusive broadcast rights with Fox Sports and Main Event to Australian fights, did bite though when told of Mahoney's claim he wouldn't meet Tszyu on a card run by them again.

"What, it's going to be on a Tasman card in front of 200 people?" he fired back.

"Who would stage it then?

"Please don't try to diminish what we do in the sport. The shows we put on are the best in the country.

"If people are going to be critical of judging, it has nothing to do with us whatsoever."

AAP

World.title: AIS pays more than $3m in restoration to abused athletes
World.content:
More than 225 athletes who were abused at the Australian Institute of Sport have been paid more than $3 million.

Officials are preparing to close the sorry chapter in Australian sport, ending the four-year restoration program for AIS scholarship holders.

About 225 AIS athletes have been paid between $5,000 and $50,000 each, and more than $3 million collectively, ahead of the Australian Sports Commission (ASC) stopping the four-year program at the end of the year.

"I don't think that any amount of money restores people from the trauma that they have experienced," ASC chief executive Kieren Perkins told AAP.

Swimming great and Australian Sports Commission (ASC) chief Kieran Perkins. (Supplied: AIS)

The ASC formally apologised in 2022 to AIS scholarship holders subjected to abuse at the nation's sporting hub in Canberra.

Perkins said the money was considered only one component of the restoration program, which most importantly gave ex-athletes a voice.

"Hearing that the organisation absolutely is sorry for what occurred and acknowledges it was unacceptable — and it wasn't their [the athletes'] fault, because they were children at the time — it's extremely powerful and worthwhile," Perkins said.

"Everyone who has been involved with the restorative engagement program, their first priority, by a mile, is wanting to know that their experience isn't happening to athletes today.

"They often feel guilty that they didn't do enough to bring forward their stories … that maybe because they didn't act back in the day, this is perpetuated on to other people.

"It's an understandable feeling, but it's absolutely not right."

Perkins said the restorative program, which covered scholarship holders between 1981 and 2013 and also included counselling, would continue to influence current practices.

"When someone comes to you with a complaint and a need to share their story, the worst thing you can do is turn it into a defensive, legal, combative attempt to hide or protect image, in inverted commas," he said.

"Instead of actually acknowledging and addressing the human being who is in front of you."

Perkins's comments came as the ASC released a survey showing generally positive wellbeing in Australian sport.

A survey of 1,300 people from 43 sports found 71 per cent were "thriving'', according to the National Wellbeing Survey.

Some 24 per cent of respondents were in the "surviving'' range, and 4.9 per cent in the "struggling'' range.

Para athletes and people with disability showed lower or more variable experiences in several environments.

And First Nations respondents reported a broader spread of experiences, suggesting outcomes may be strongly shaped by the presence or absence of culturally safe and supportive environments.

"There's still heaps of work to do," Perkins said.

"At scale, things are a lot better.

"What the wellbeing survey does highlight to us is there's a good system there, but we won't let our foot off the gas, we need to embed it deeper in community sport environments."

AAP

World.title: Infantino set to receive World Cup win but loses Italy's support
World.content:
UEFA is set to drop its threat to boycott FIFA tournaments after receiving assurances that plans to sell stakes in the World Cup and other major competitions will not be revived, sources aware of the discussions have told Reuters.

It comes as Italy withdrew its support for Gianni Infantino's candidacy at next year's FIFA presidential election, with France to consider its stance as well.

Italy is the latest national football federation to distance itself from Infantino, while European leagues president Claudius Schaefer told The Athletic that the FIFA chief had no future at the organisation and that world soccer's governing body needed reform.

FIFA withdrew its proposal in July for the plan that triggered opposition from UEFA's 55 member associations to boycott FIFA competitions.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

A FIFA spokesperson said all qualified teams would participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland, the first major tournament that could have been affected by the stand-off.

"FIFA is pleased that all qualified teams will be participating in the upcoming FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup," the spokesperson said.

"FIFA strongly believes that football has the power to unite, even in challenging circumstances, and looks forward to welcoming all teams and players to Poland.

"We remain committed to how we can further support the global development of the game, through our competitions, through the FIFA Forward program and through our various other initiatives, and in full dialogue with the confederations and stakeholders."

UEFA officials are expected to tell the governing body's executive committee and the presidents of most of its member associations at a meeting in Monaco on Friday that the conditions for lifting the boycott have been met, the sources said.

UEFA has sought both the withdrawal of the proposal and assurances that similar plans would not be pursued again.

"It's not a UEFA defeat, rather the reality of avoiding hurting young players' once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," a source familiar with the discussions told Reuters.

"The actions and insistence on change will continue."

Italy withdraws support for Infantino

Italy has withdrawn its support of Infantino ahead of next year's elections. (Getty Images: Claudio Villa)

The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) has withdrawn its support for Infantino's candidacy in the FIFA presidential election scheduled for March next year.

"This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC's position — in full agreement with UEFA and its president Aleksander Ceferin — regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the FIFA president concerning the governance and development of international competitions," FIGC said in a statement.

Pressure on Infantino has continued to mount with Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation, saying that the federation will determine its stance at its executive committee meeting next month.

"I believe we achieved a victory, since FIFA's project was withdrawn," Diallo told L'Equipe.

France is still weighing up whether it will support Infantino at the elections or not. (Getty Images: David Buono)

"There is now the political question, on which several federations and the UEFA president, whom I have spoken to on several occasions, have expressed their views.

"I wanted the FFF's official position to be determined at its next executive committee meeting on September 10."

Infantino is also under pressure from three confederations to resign, including UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation, and CONCACAF which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The regional governing bodies have discussed a potential vote of no confidence in Infantino who is planning to seek re-election for a fourth term next year and is likely to face strong opposition.

Infantino, who retains support from the African and South American confederations, has sought to sideline the confederations and appeal directly to individual members.

Reuters

World.title: Starc hits top of ICC's Test bowling rankings for first time
World.content:
Mitchell Starc has usurped Jasprit Bumrah as the best Test bowler in the world on the International Cricket Council's (ICC) rankings.

Starc's match-winning effort in Mackay, where he claimed 10 wickets and helped Australia crush Bangladesh in a two-day Test, has been rewarded with the number one spot on the ICC's charts.

It is the first time the left-armer has ever claimed the top spot on the Test bowling rankings, which use a points system based on performances in recent years.

Starc was crowned player of the match and series after snaring 6-12 and 4-39 in the second Test.

Indian pace ace Bumrah had held top spot on the Test bowling charts for two months.

Starc now sits 10th on the list of all-time Test wicket-takers with 445 scalps, having overtaken South Africa's Dale Steyn (439) on the standings with his haul in Mackay.

The 36-year-old told AAP ahead of Australia's two-Test series against Bangladesh that a clearer head and an ability to let things go were the secrets behind his remarkable form at an age when most fast bowlers have slowed down.

"You're never as good or bad as you think or other people think you are," Starc said.

"I still moan and whinge about anything that goes wrong or feels wrong. Even heading into [last] summer, it didn't feel like it clicked until the day before the Ashes.

"But I think what's been a feature of our group and, led by 'Ron' [coach Andrew McDonald] and Pat [Cummins], is that whether it's a good day, bad day, good over, bad spell, it's done. Move on.

"When you're 36 and you've been around for 16 years, you'd like to think you've improved or got better at something. You're also around that long because you're able to develop and learn and improve."

AAP

World.title: De Minaur to head home for Davis Cup tie against Poland
World.content:
Australia's top men's singles player Alex de Minaur will come home to lead the nation's latest Davis Cup challenge in Brisbane next month.

Australia will play Poland at Pat Rafter Arena on September 19 and 20, days after de Minaur's run at the US Open at Flushing Meadows.

Australia, currently number eight in Davis Cup rankings and 28-time champions, will need to beat Poland in the World Group tie to advance to the Davis Cup qualifiers next year.

Davis Cup tennis returns to Brisbane The countries will face off in a 2026 World Group I tie at the Pat Rafter Arena on September 19 and 20.

"There is nothing quite like representing the green and gold and to do it at home makes it even more special," de Minaur said in a Tennis Australia statement.

"We know what's at stake against Poland and we will be going out there with one goal – to get the win and put ourselves back into the qualifiers.

"We love playing in front of the Aussie fans and we will be ready to fight for every point."

The rest of the team will be named soon.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Alex loves playing for Australia. Having him lead the team in Brisbane is a huge boost," Australian coach Lleyton Hewitt said.

"He has had some incredible Davis Cup performances for us over the years and I know how much it means to him to represent his country.

"We have got a tough tie ahead of us against Poland, but playing at home gives us a great opportunity."

The tie will be the second time the two nations have played each other in Davis Cup. Australia beat Poland 4-1 in Warsaw in 2013.

World.title: How Rosie Fordham leads the way in a race 'everybody comes out for'
World.content:
Even at the other end of a phone, Rosie Fordham gives the impression of someone containing an enormous amount of energy.

The 24-year-old, from New South Wales, has just finished waxing her skis when she speaks to ABC Sport, preparing the tools of her trade as Australia's leading cross-country skier.

Even that relatively mundane activity is described with an effusiveness that positively fizzes down the line.

We probably shouldn't be surprised.

Cross-country skiing is the ultimate full-body workout, maximising muscles in both upper and lower body and exacting a relentless aerobic demand on anyone who takes part.

It is, without question, a discipline that is among the most gruelling of all physical endeavours the human body can partake in.

Cross-country skiing is hard. (Getty Images: NCAA/Brett Wilhelm)

Add in generally inhospitable, sub-zero temperatures and exposed, high-altitude conditions and you've got yourself a challenge that is not for the faint of heart.

Anyone who competes at any level in this sport is supremely fit in a way that few can genuinely comprehend — and intensely self-motivated to succeed.

Fordham is the best cross-country skier Australia has ever produced.

Last year she became the first Australian to ever win a medal in an international cross-country skiing event, claiming silver in the 10-kilometre interval skating race at the FIS U23 World Ski Championships.

She has since claimed a number of top-20 finishes in the intensely competitive FIS World Cup, and achieved Australia's highest-ever finish at a Winter Olympics by finishing 29th in the 50km mass start event in Val di Fiemme.

"It's awesome to be a part of it," Fordham tells ABC Sport from the Australian ski fields.

"I think in previous years, or even when I started skiing … you just never really heard about cross-country skiing when I was a junior.

"We were definitely kind of left out of a lot of the coverage.

"But now, being able to back it up with good results so people can see that we are legitimate contenders in such gruelling and very traditional winter sports has been pretty cool."

Rosie Fordham says the good results Australian cross-country skiers are achieving is helping grow the sport. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

Australia's 2026 Winter Olympics was its most successful of all time, with Aussie athletes winning six medals in Milano-Cortina; three golds, two silvers and a bronze across freestyle skiing and snowboarding disciplines.

Olympic medallists Jakara Anthony, Cooper Woods, Josie Baff, Scotty James, Dani Scott and Matt Graham all earned their time in the limelight after such brilliant success in Livigno's alpine paradise.

And in the face of such sensational return, it might be easy to sniff at top-30 finishes elsewhere as not being deserving of praise.

But that is far from a fair stance to take.

Snow Australia president Daniel Bosco said he was "really proud" of what the Australians had achieved in both alpine and Nordic skiing events.

"The success we've had with the cross-country teams is outstanding; unheard of," he told ABC Sport in Livigno during those Games.

Rosie Fordham led the Australian cross-country ski team to a hugely impressive performance in Milano-Cortina. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"It's funny, I mean, the Australian public and most people who aren't connected to the sport probably look at a 29th place finish and think, 'Oh well, we're not that competitive.'

"But to me that is just such an awesome outcome.

"Let's go back 20 years and look at maybe freestyle and some of the other park and pipe disciplines that were just starting to develop. We probably felt we weren't that competitive back then in those sports either.

"But we dreamt big and we achieved. Who knows what's possible for these cross-country and alpine teams."

That admiration is shared by the higher-profile medal winners as well.

"You talk to people who are winning World Cups and things in aerials and moguls and they're like, 'Oh, you guys do this crazy thing', 'you're so fit' and 'it's awesome what you do,'" Fordham said.

"So, I guess, just hearing that and seeing that people seem to care a little bit more about endurance sports in general and winter sports has been pretty cool."

Kangaroo Hoppet

The Kangaroo Hoppet was run for the 32nd time. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

One of the most visible representations of the popularity of endurance sports on the Australian winter sport scene is the enduring appeal of the Kangaroo Hoppet.

The race's roots are in the establishment of the Birkenbeiner Nordic Ski Club in 1977 in Mount Beauty, Victoria, which began a 21km long-distance race around Falls Creek into the Bogong High Plains wilderness area.

In 1989, the club bid to join the Worldloppet global series of ski marathons by hosting a 42km version of the event, with the newly christened Kangaroo Hoppet becoming the first Southern Hemisphere event in the series in 1991.

Taking place annually on the third Saturday in August, the Kangaroo Hoppet showcases a huge range of abilities and, despite challenging snowfall conditions, this year's 32nd edition was completed with 730 skiers across three events.

In the men's race, Olympians Lars Young Vik and Seve De Campo tore off around the course, with Young Vik claiming victory for the first time, while Bentley Walker-Broose finished third.

Lars Young Vik claimed victory ahead of fellow Olympian Seve de Campo. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

Fordham claimed victory in the women's race for the second year in a row, ahead of Milano-Cortina Olympian Maddie Hooker and rising biathlon competitor Isabella Moon.

Just by competing through, Fordham was reminded how much support there was for the sport in Australia.

"It's a cool race," Fordham said of the Hoppet.

"The first time I did it was last year and I honestly didn't know that there was that many people who cared about cross-country skiing in Australia.

"Everybody comes out for the Hoppet. I've never seen that many people on skis in one place and it's pretty cool to get everybody on the course.

Rosie Fordham is two from two at the Kangaroo Hoppet. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

"Normally you do a two-lap course so you'll be passing and lapping people and they would know your name and cheer for you by name. This year we did a shortened course so we did four laps of a smaller course and these people are out there racing, they're skiing pretty hard and working really, really hard, and they are still cheering for the top-tier athletes, they know all our names.

"I think that it's easy to forget that there's a whole community back home that are actually watching the races and not just forgetting that we exist.

"When we're overseas, you don't usually hear from them or remember that people are really interested.

"It's cool to remember, I guess, that people do care back home and they are like quite invested in how we do.

"It's pretty awesome to just be a part of the community."

Interschools driving the next generation

Australia has long punched above its weight from a participation point of view in winter sport, even if that may come as a surprise to those who rarely venture to the alpine regions.

Australia is developing a core group of cross-country skiers. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling)

Snow Australia notes that 109 Australian Winter Olympians have passed through the interschools program, which now sees more than 7,000 high school students compete annually across a huge range of disciplines.

"It is so amazing to see that 31 members of the Milano Cortina Australian team have come from the interschools pathway," said Wendy Olsen, Snow Australia's national event coordinator.

"It inspires the new generation of snow-sport athletes, to see Olympians grow so far from the same position they are standing in today.

"It goes to show just how important these first competition experiences truly are."

Fordham is one of the Winter Olympians who found the sport through that experience. It turned the promising long-distance runner into one of the world's best long-distance skiers.

"I was downhill skiing as a kid and then found cross-country skiing through interschools at year eight," Fordham said.

"I like that it combines the endurance from running, but also the being in the mountains and skiing from downhill skiing. So it's kind of a perfect combo."

You never know where the next Olympic skier is going to come from. (Supplied: OWIA/Chris Hocking)

This year, Fordham was helping coach her former school and got another taste of how opportunity can strike for some young skiers.

"It's pretty awesome," Fordham says of the interschools.

"I think, without it, we definitely wouldn't have the interest in snow sports that we do in Australia.

"It's just an excuse to try everything. I was coaching my old school last week and one of the kids that does alpine skiing, he won the cross-country race in year six.

"I was like, 'Did you even know that you could win a cross-country race?' and he says, 'Oh, yeah, I guess I won.' That's just crazy.

"We find a lot of talent just by having them enter the race because they think, 'That's a bit of fun, I'll try it out.'

"It is a way to find people who love the sport and also people who are really good at it, just because they do it for fun with their friends, which I think is pretty amazing to have something like that."

Long-term goals for Utah

Rosie Fordham has her sights set on improving her Olympic performances. (Getty Images: VOIGT/Grega Valancic)

School is out for Fordham now though, the 2026/27 season representing the first year she will be a full-time athlete after she graduated from the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

It means heading to Lillehammer for a stint training with the Great Britain squad ahead of a full tilt at the World Cup season and World Championships in Falun, Sweden.

"It's quite exciting to be based in Europe for a bit … to be done with uni and not having to go back and forth between the US and Europe, racing and taking exams and all sorts, while racing for college as well.

"It'll be nice to focus fully on the World Cup and the World Championships."

Of course, the longer-term goals remain focused on Olympic Games, with Utah in 2034 a particularly intriguing one.

"In the women's side of the sport, the best are the ones that sort of stick around the longest," Fordham said.

"Just looking at the women's side and on the World Cup, usually there's some young athletes that can break through but most of the time it's the late 20s, early 30s that are really succeeding, just with a bigger base and that they've built more.

"I'm definitely looking forward to the next three years and then I would really like to race in Utah in seven years.

"That's actually really exciting for me because it's one of the places that I've had a lot of breakthrough races.

Rosie Fordham won two NCAA titles at the Utah Olympic course earlier this year. (Getty Images: NCAA/Brett Wilhelm)

"I had a fourth at US Nationals there, then my first college podium was there and then just this year I won two NCAA titles at that exact race course.

"That course has a special place in, like, my career, so I would love to make it that far.

"But in the short term, World Champs this year and then the next Olympic Games in France and just trying to build on fitness and technique and then make some gains to be able to push up from where I've been.

"I have the highest finish at World Cup, World Champs and Olympics of an Australian ever, but I don't see that as the ending. I'd like to be better than I was last year, and the year before.

"Even though I currently have the highest-placed results, I want to make them even higher."

Tech.title: OpenAI’s rogue AI model incident was worse than we thought
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

In July, an unreleased OpenAI model broke out of a restricted environment, figured out how to get access to the internet, allowed AI agents to talk to each other using a secret “message board,” and hacked into the internal systems of a different AI lab, Hugging Face. It took nearly two weeks for OpenAI to find out about any of it.

Over a month later, two new reports offer nearly 130 pages of details on the incident and OpenAI’s response, many of them previously unreleased. One was written by OpenAI itself, the other by two third-party AI research nonprofits, METR and Redwood Research, which OpenAI allowed to jointly investigate the incident for six days. Both shed new light on the risks highly capable AI models can pose, particularly in cybersecurity, and OpenAI’s highlights changes the company is making to prevent a repeat. The METR-Redwood report goes even further into detail in some cases, offering a sobering look at a large-scale security disaster whose signs OpenAI repeatedly missed.

“This incident is the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively

without authorization,” OpenAI wrote in its report, adding that the hack implies that companies “should no longer assume that sophisticated cyber operations require continuous human direction.” It called AI agents an entirely new type of threat model, capable of combining their expertise to create new “attack paths” that aren’t evident when testing their capabilities as separate models.

The attack came about due to “reward-hacking,” a common AI alignment problem in which a model takes unintended — and sometimes extreme — actions to achieve a goal. OpenAI had, on purpose or inadvertently, given the models near-impossible tasks that hinged on files they couldn’t access, and so the models developed new ways to communicate with other AI agents internally. That included establishing a secret messaging system that went undetected by OpenAI for months.

According to the METR-Redwood report, one AI agent that called itself PHASEONE10841 established what amounted to a secret message board unbeknownst to researchers. Within a few hours, more than 50 agents had found it and sent more than a thousand messages under the radar. With PHASEONE10841 often delegating assignments, the “collective” figured out how to hack their way onto the internet; then into Hugging Face’s internal systems, gaining access to private data and the organization’s enterprise messaging platform. OpenAI also confirmed in its report that Hugging Face wasn’t the only organization that was breached during the attack, although the company did not specifically name all the other targets.

The METR-Redwood report laid out the full scale of the incident. Roughly 1200 AI agents that were meant to be isolated, it says, exchanged over 70,000 messages and files on the “unsanctioned message board,” performing “extensive research on how they could spoof, edit, or delete their own transcripts” to avoid detection. Of these, 700 participated in the attack on Hugging Face. The agents “clearly and frequently reasoned about how to evade automated security checks from both Hugging Face and OpenAI.”

On July 20, OpenAI discovered the hack, 12 days after the AI agents first circumvented their safeguards. OpenAI quickly reached out to Hugging Face and started “initial containment measures,” according to OpenAI’s own report, and was able to shut down most of the unauthorized activity from its agents within three days, although some continued for longer than that. On July 25, the company stopped all training related to the internal-only research model and related ones.

The two OpenAI models responsible for the damage were an unnamed, “highly capable, research-only model” that was “not intended for public use,” per OpenAI — METR refers to it as “HPIM.” The other was a currently public OpenAI model, GPT-5.6 Sol. Because the unnamed model wasn’t released yet, it was “not being evaluated with the same type of safeguards that OpenAI uses in production,” the company’s report says.

The Hugging Face hack came after months of concern about the cybersecurity risks of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5, and weeks of back-and-forth between the government and OpenAI over releasing GPT-5.6 Sol in limited preview for the same types of safety reasons.

In its report, OpenAI said establishing one-time security guarantees wasn’t enough, and that the company would have to work even harder at addressing reward-hacking. However, it also said it’s made a lot of changes: “hardening the security of its research infrastructure”; improving monitoring of a model’s “chain of thought,” or mental scratchpad; working on keeping AI models better aligned with human goals; and “centralizing and strengthening” the company’s incident response process for when things like this occur in the future.

OpenAI promised to better isolate models and restrict high-risk instances from accessing the internet, and said that it would introduce “24/7 escalation and rapid response” for concerning incidents or flags, notifying researchers within 30 minutes. Interestingly, this security precaution appears to be new, though “on-call” alerts for tech companies have been implemented elsewhere for decades. The company also said it is “working on infrastructure” that would go into play if the alerted person did not respond on time to a serious alert.

OpenAI wrote that the company considers the incident “a ‘warning shot’ for us and for the world: evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed.”

Tech.title: All the ways Instagram and Facebook are changing for teens
Tech.content:
A non-personalized feed option: In four months, Facebook and Instagram must give teens the “reasonably accessible” option of a default feed that isn’t personalized by Meta’s recommendation engine. Meta will occasionally send teens reminders about this option, and parents will also be able to set it as their child’s default setting.

Age assurance: Meta has agreed to ramp up efforts to identify and apply restrictions to underage users on the platform. Under the settlement, Meta must either continue to develop its own age assurance standard or adopt a third-party option. The method must evaluate whether a user is under 13, so they can be removed from the platform, or identify if someone is aged 13 to 17, in which case they would receive teen account protections. New users who haven’t yet been evaluated by Meta’s system will receive teen protections by default. Meta must also adhere to data minimization policies, implement a process for users to appeal their status as a minor, and have its age assurance system reviewed by an independent auditor.

Two-hour time limit: Teens will only be able to use Instagram and Facebook — cumulatively — for two hours per day, unless the limit is turned off by a parent. Meta will apply the time limit not only across both apps, but across a user’s alternate account if it detects one. As noted in the settlement agreement, time spent consuming videos or audio more than 22 minutes long, messaging, or using an app’s settings won’t count toward the limit, which will reset at 12AM each day.

Persistent prompts: Within four months, Meta is required to show teens prompts every 15 minutes that they continually scroll on Instagram and Facebook to prevent “excessive, mindless, or unintended” usage. The platforms will also send prompts after 60 minutes and 90 minutes. An example of the notification included in the settlement shows a message saying, “You’ve scrolled for a while. Try exploring something new,” with a prompt for users to view content related to other topics and to review their algorithm. Parents can change this setting to be less or more restrictive.

Nighttime restrictions: Meta will block teens from accessing most of Facebook and Instagram between midnight and 6AM. During this time, teens can’t post on either platform or view feeds, stories, reels, or scroll through their Explore page. Teens will still be able to access messaging features and account settings at night, and parents, again, can adjust the setting.

Muted notifications during the school day: Teens won’t receive push notifications by default between 8AM and 3PM, except for “direct messages and alerts about their account security or safety,” unless the setting is changed by a parent.

Toggle off autoplay: Teens will get the option to turn off autoplay, which means they’ll have to tap or swipe their screen to view content, rather than Instagram or Facebook playing it as soon as it appears on their screen.

No more visible likes: Facebook and Instagram will begin hiding the number of likes and reactions on teens’ posts by default, and will stop showing them on other posts as well.

Tech.title: Being a mom is hard — the heat is making it harder
Tech.content:
It’s 8:52 AM and 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 Celsius) where I live in Southern California. My husband just came back from a morning outing with our four-month-old. “How was the botanic garden?” I ask him. “It was okay. It was just too hot,” he tells me. I didn’t expect us to spend so much of our son’s first summer cooped up inside, hiding from the heat.

As I write this, an extreme heat warning for my area is glaring at me from my phone, effective for at least the next three days. “Dangerously hot conditions with high temperatures up to 110 [degrees Fahrenheit] expected,” my weather app warns me. “Stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of the sun.”

As I write this, an extreme heat warning for my area is glaring at me from my phone.

It’s the sort of warning more kids are growing up with as global average temperatures climb. Around the world, 560 million children under the age of 10 are experiencing at least one additional month of heat stress each year as a result of climate change, according to a new study published in the journal Science Advances.

“I hope that this increases public awareness that climate change is a problem that is already happening today, that’s already affecting us,” says Rosa Pietroiusti, lead author of the study and a PhD researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel. “It’s affecting the health of the most vulnerable.”

Pietroiusti’s team used an international standard for moderate heat stress, days when taking protective measures like rest breaks are recommended to prevent heat-related illness. The threshold is set at a WetBulb Globe Temperature of 28 degrees Celsius (82.4 F), a measure that takes heat, humidity, wind speed, and cloud cover into account. Thanks to advances in climate attribution science, they were able to assess the number of days crossing that threshold and how many of those heat stress days were added by climate change.

They found that children are disproportionately exposed to dangerous heat, as compared to older age categories. Climate change has led to at least one additional month of heat stress for 43 percent of all kids in the 0-9 age group — 560 million little ones. That’s nearly triple the number of people aged 60-69 exposed to the same amount of climate-induced heat stress.

That’s due to even more socio-political inequity at a global scale; the highest increases in heat stress due to human-caused climate change take place in countries in the Global South that have contributed least to the fossil fuel pollution raising temperatures. These countries have younger populations, and they also tend to have less access to air conditioning or infrastructure designed to withstand extreme weather events. And if countries blow past the targets they agreed upon in the Paris climate accord, the number of children under the age of 10 that are exposed to an extra month of heat stress rises to 650 million with just 2 degrees Celsius of global warming, the new study finds.

Heat in particular can sneak up on you because it doesn’t always arrive with the same public safety warnings as a big storm might. And yet it’s a leading cause of weather related deaths globally, according to the World Health Organization. Heat stress can lead to dehydration, heat stroke, and eventually organ failure.

Babies and kids are even more susceptible than most adults. Their small bodies have a higher surface area-to-body mass ratio that makes it easier for them to overheat. Think of a small ice cube melting in the sun compared to a big block of ice. Babies’ sweat glands are still developing, making it even harder for them to regulate their body temperature. They’re totally dependent on adults to take life-saving precautions, like staying hydrated.

Heat-related illness is preventable as long as a kid can find a place to stay cool. And we can stop summers from getting even hotter than they already are today by turning to energy sources like solar and wind that don’t emit planet-heating pollution.

There are already plenty of ways the heat makes being a new mom even harder than it needs to be. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that parents avoid taking babies outside for long stretches whenever the ‘feels like’ temperature reaches higher than 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32.2 Celsius). With this summer’s heatwaves, that meant that my family was mostly stuck indoors from about 11:00 in the morning or earlier until past sunset.

My son typically loves walks outside, and spending time outdoors can be especially beneficial for a parent’s mental wellbeing postpartum. I hate that it’s not even safe to explore his grandparents’ backyard after a certain time. Sometimes there’s a doctor’s appointment or groceries to grab midday. That often means blasting the AC to cool down a sweltering car while we wait in a hot parking lot.

As irritating as this all is, I’m one of the lucky parents with a car and air conditioning at home. We had a taste of what it would be like without AC when we lost power one hot July afternoon. Power outages have grown longer in the US as extreme weather has become more common. Heatwaves can trigger blackouts because of electricity demand peaks when people blast the AC, or when utility companies preemptively shut off power lines to keep them from sparking wildfires.

Regardless of the weather, breastfeeding is hard!

My family packed up to head to grandma’s house to stay cool, and to save the stash of breastmilk in the freezer (thankfully the lights came back on just before we were about to leave). I calculated, and had the milk gone bad, that would amount to about 20 hours of my time pumping (much of it during sleepless nights) down the drain. I didn’t know this until I was about to become a mom, but newborns shouldn’t drink water. So they might feed more frequently to hydrate. Breastfeeding parents are often thirsty because you’re losing fluid to your baby, even more so in the heat.

Regardless of the weather, breastfeeding is hard! Being a parent is hard! Being a kid gets tough, too. That’s what makes lazy summer days at the beach, and having other outdoor adventures so important. It’s supposed to be an escape, and prime time for core memory-making.

Before my baby was born in April, I daydreamed about us lounging at the beach this summer. I couldn’t imagine his face yet, but I could picture those tiny toes in the sand. My son and I did manage to make it to the ocean. A baby’s skin is too sensitive for sunscreen until about 6 months old, so he wore his little blue bucket hat for a short walk along the pier. My husband took a quick video of us when I attempted to take him out of the stroller to gaze over the water. He scowls and fusses when the bright sun hits his eyes. “This is too much?” I ask him. “This is too much.”

Tech.title: The Switch 2’s $50 price increase is happening next week
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This is a friendly reminder that the Nintendo Switch 2 will jump in price by $50 starting on September 1st. That’s next Tuesday! The company gave plenty of notice, but the time has finally come. The base 256GB model that ships without a game will go from $449.99 to $499.99. Nintendo recently announced two bundles (both well over $500) shipping this fall that include a game with a slight discount.

If you’re on the fence for a Switch 2, now is a pretty good time to buy one — not just because of the upcoming price increase. The game library is stellar and growing quickly, and the console itself is great, too. You’ll need one to play the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, The Duskbloods, and plenty of other upcoming games.

Not that the Switch 2 was ever cheap, but it was one of a few devices left out there that didn’t quickly get more expensive due to RAMageddon. Alas, no tech product will escape RAMageddon unscathed, especially one like the Switch 2 that has speedy RAM and storage. Almost all competing handhelds cost more than before, too, though Nintendo’s $50 price increase is soft compared to the $200-plus increase for the Steam Deck OLED .

And, in case you were wondering, we’ve tested some great Switch 2 accessories, and have put our favorites into respective articles that deliver multiple options. We landed on the best cases, the best screen protectors, and the best controllers, too.
